title: 'Europeans balked': G20 foreign ministers' meeting opens without group photo. Here's why
text: Foreign ministers of the G20 largest economies began a two-day meeting in the US on Friday (local time), with the gathering notably skipping the customary group photograph. According to reports, US secretary of state Marco Rubio cancelled the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out over Russia's participation. Moscow is being represented by foreign minister Sergei Lavrov at the summit in Atlanta. Two US officials told The Associated Press that European officials "balked" at the prospect of being photographed with Lavrov, prompting Rubio to cancel the picture to avoid what could possibly become a âdistraction.â Several G20 countries had already raised concerns over the US inviting Russia despite Moscow's war against Ukraine, which began in February 2022. In a statement, the British Foreign Office reiterated the UK's longstanding policy of avoiding direct bilateral engagement with Russian ministers over the war in Ukraine, adding that it had "no plans" to change its stance. Polish deputy Prime Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski, who is also the country's foreign minister, called the cancellation of the group photograph âthe right decision.â Speaking to the media, he remarked: âI am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov.â German top diplomat Johann Wadephul stressed that âthere is no normality with Russiaâ, but added that differences must be asserted at the negotiating table. He also cautioned against sending âfalsely optimistic signals." Lavrov has made only occasional visits to Nato member states since the Russia-Ukraine war began and Western sanctions were subsequently imposed on Moscow. 'We are in a critical moment': Rubio Rubio opened the talks, which otherwise proceeded as planned, with an appeal for unity on issues threatening international security and global trade. âWe are in a critical moment â I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world,â Rubio told his counterparts. âWe are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises,â he added, citing disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. He warned that many of these developments posed âsevere threats to essential foundations of the global economic order." However, there were not many signs of consensus among G20 diplomats on several contentious issues, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and China's actions in the South China Sea. These tensions have contributed to rising global fuel costs and growing uncertainty over trade. The Atlanta meeting is intended to lay the groundwork for the G20 leaders' summit, which US President Donald Trump is scheduled to host at his Miami golf club in December. title: 1,200km reach, Western parts: How Russiaâs new Filin missile adds to Ukraineâs air defence woes
text: Kyiv has repeatedly urged Western allies to accelerate deliveries of air defence interceptors Russia has begun using a new cruise missile, the Filin, against Ukraine, adding to Moscowâs growing arsenal of relatively inexpensive long-range weapons designed to stretch Kyivâs air defences. The missile combines a Russian-made jet engine with electronic components linked to American and Chinese manufacturers, according to Ukraineâs military intelligence agency, HUR, as reported by Kyiv Post. The weapon reportedly entered combat use in late summer 2026. Its emergence highlights Russiaâs efforts to develop cheaper strike systems capable of reaching targets deep inside Ukrainian territory, potentially complicating Kyivâs efforts to intercept repeated waves of drones and missiles. On October 22, HUR released an interactive 3D model, technical specifications and a component database on its War&Sanctions portal. According to Militarnyi, the agencyâs findings indicate that the Filin combines standardised electronics and some 3D-printed components with a Russian propulsion system. Its advertised performance, however, has not been independently verified. Watch Beyond Fighter Jets India Builds New Drone And Missile Engines US electronics, Chinese navigation and Russian firepower According to Kyiv Post, HUR identified 35 electronic components associated with US manufacturers and 22 linked to Chinese manufacturers. The agency said the electronics resemble those found in other Russian missiles and drones, with standardised designs across different onboard units and circuit boards that could help simplify production. The missile was developed by Moscow-based NPO Molniya, part of Russiaâs Tactical Missiles Corporation. Its 3.5-metre-long fuselage and three-metre wingspan are made from carbon fibre and fibreglass composites, while some structural parts are manufactured using 3D printing, Militarnyi reported. The Filin uses a Russian-made R500 turbojet engine manufactured by Reynolds LLC. Its onboard equipment is assembled by St Petersburg-based PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing electronics for Russiaâs Garpiya attack drones, according to the Long War Journal. For navigation, HUR identified a Chinese-made inertial navigation system and a 16-channel Kometa antenna designed to improve resistance to electronic warfare interference. The missile launches from a ground-based platform using a solid-propellant booster and reportedly carries either a 50-kg or 100-kg warhead. Russian-advertised specifications cited by HUR put its maximum speed at 800 kmph and its range at up to 1,200 km. The missile can reportedly fly at extremely low altitudes or reach heights of six kilometres, according to Kyiv Post. A cheaper weapon as Ukraineâs air defences face pressure The Filin fits into a broader Russian push towards relatively inexpensive, mass-producible long-range weapons that complement more sophisticated systems such as the Kh-101 and Kalibr cruise missiles. The Long War Journal reported that Ukraine-based analyst Rob Lee said in August that Russia planned to procure more than 1,000 Filin missiles before the end of the year. However, the publication noted that the weapon had yet to see widespread use, leaving the status of those reported procurement plans uncertain. The development comes as Ukraine faces sustained aerial attacks. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 strike drones, 48 missiles and around 1,600 guided bombs in a single week, damaging infrastructure and civilian facilities across nine regions. Kyiv has repeatedly urged Western allies to accelerate deliveries of air defence interceptors. At the same time, Zelenskyy has said Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators were expected to hold technical-level talks in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.

title: Nuclear scare, fake radiation warnings: Cyberattacks hit Russia, Ukraine alert systems
text: Cyberattacks hit Ukraine, Russia emergency alert systems; fake threat warnings trigger alarm (Representative AI image) Ukraine and Russia have reported cyberattacks targeting their emergency alert systems, with hackers allegedly circulating fake warnings of radiation, chemical and nuclear threats, raising concerns over the disruption of public safety communications amid the ongoing war between the two countries. Ukraine's air raid alert application was reportedly compromised on Sunday, sending false warnings about chemical and radiation threats to mobile phones across the country. Loudspeaker systems in Kyiv also broadcast similar messages, prompting the Ukrainian Air Force to warn of possible external interference. Watch âNUKE MISSILE COMINGâ: Russia âNuclear Attackâ Alert Sends Ukrainians Into Panic, Then This Happened "Attention. The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," the Air Force said on Telegram, adding that, "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!" Ukraine's Central Intelligence Agency also reported a failure in the application and urged residents to consult alternative sources of information to verify warnings about possible air strikes. However, the Ministry of Digital Transformation later said the nationwide alert system was functioning normally. "The nationwide alert system is operating in normal mode. All threat signals are transmitted to regional administrations and, accordingly, to street alert systems," the ministry said in a post on X. Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations said its mobile application had been targeted in a massive cyberattack that enabled attackers to distribute false public safety information. Russian authorities also reported fake warnings about nuclear strikes inside the country, with a Ukrainian espionage group reportedly suspected of involvement. "The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app was subjected to a massive cyberattack, which allowed the attackers to distribute fake information to the public," the ministry said in a statement. According to TASS, the ministry said efforts were underway to eliminate the vulnerability in the application and restore its normal functioning. The incidents come amid continuing military operations and diplomatic efforts surrounding the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The false alerts in Ukraine were reportedly circulated shortly before the end of a localised ceasefire in the Oleshky area of Ukraine's Kherson region. On Sunday, US First Lady Melania Trump commended Moscow and Kyiv for their cooperation during the five-day humanitarian ceasefire, which concluded on November 1. title: India trying to bring Russia, Ukraine & Europe to the table on 3 fronts: Jaishankar
text: India's External affairs minister S Jaishankar has discussed the protection of civilian shipping with Russia, Ukraine, and European nations External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said India has held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on protecting civilian shipping, restoring grain exports through the Black Sea and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. According to news agency ANI, Speaking on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said India was engaging with the parties on three key aspects of the conflict, including the safety of civilian vessels and seafarers, the restoration of grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure. He said India was trying to bring the concerned parties together to address these issues. "One, not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers," he said, outlining the first of the three areas discussed with Russia, Ukraine and Europe. Watch Rubio-Jaishankar Meet: India Digs In Heels As U.S Reveals 'Trade Deal Bait' Vs Russian Oil Sanctions On the second issue, Jaishankar stressed the need to restore grain shipments from both Russia and Ukraine, warning that exports through the Black Sea had declined sharply amid the conflict. "The second, to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine, these are two major exporters of grain for the global markets, can be restored, because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said. Jaishankar further highlighted the complexities involved in ensuring the safety of energy infrastructure, saying different parties had different interpretations of what should be covered under such an understanding. "And the third is with regard to energy. Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players. There is energy infrastructure itself. To some, it would mean a refinery; to some, it would mean grids. There would be issues relating to ships carrying fuel," he said. He added that India is attempting to bring the concerned parties together to find common ground on these issues, particularly on the protection of energy infrastructure and fuel shipments. title: Ukraine peace, prisoner release & Trump meeting: What was discussed in Putin's meeting with US envoy Witkoff
text: Putin, right, greets Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday, as Washington intensified efforts to find a diplomatic solution to the nearly five-year-long war in Ukraine. The meeting came a day after Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, where the two sides discussed a possible peace framework. The US envoy arrived in Russia with fresh proposals aimed at bringing Moscow and Kyiv back to the negotiating table. Watch âZelensky CLUELESS, Doesnât Know What Heâs Talking Aboutâ: Trump Unleashes Fire On Ukraine President The discussions covered several issues beyond Ukraine, including the release of an American prisoner, renewed US-Russia economic cooperation, Russian diesel exports and the possibility of a meeting between Putin and US President Donald Trump in China. Ukraine peace proposals and trilateral talks Witkoff presented documents outlining possible ways to settle the Ukraine conflict, according to Russian news agency Interfax. He also urged Putin to consider resuming trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States to address technical issues surrounding a potential peace agreement. A US official told CNN that Washington and Kyiv had made "meaningful progress" during Tuesday's discussions in Norway. "Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability," the official said. Release of 74-year-old American prisoner Russia also released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher from Michigan who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Hubbard was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial in 2024. Russian prosecutors alleged that he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Moscow launched its invasion in February 2022 and fought alongside Ukrainian forces until his capture two months later. The Biden administration had designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. Witkoff thanked Putin for his release, saying, "Because of you, he's going home to his family." Putin confirmed that Hubbard was at St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport following his release. Possible Putin-Trump meeting in China Putin proposed meeting Trump in China, according to Russian state television, as quoted by Reuters. The Kremlin had previously raised the possibility of trilateral talks involving Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next month. No agreement on a meeting was immediately announced. US-Russia economic cooperation and diesel exports Putin also raised the possibility of restoring economic cooperation between Moscow and Washington. The discussions came as Russia prepared to dispatch its first diesel shipment to the United States on Thursday following an agreement with Trump. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the initial shipment would carry 40,000 metric tons of diesel, with further supplies expected. "Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States' needs, to the extent of our capabilities," Novak said, according to RIA. Witkoff also thanked Putin for lifting restrictions on Russian diesel exports, while Putin said diesel prices had declined following the agreement. Iran war and other discussions The two sides also discussed Russia's willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, according to footage of the meeting reported by CNN. Potential Russian fertiliser exports to the United States were among the other issues raised during the discussions, reflecting efforts to explore broader economic engagement alongside diplomatic negotiations. Why the meeting matters The meeting comes at a critical juncture in Washington's efforts to broker a settlement between Russia and Ukraine, with the two sides remaining deeply divided over territory and security guarantees. Ukraine has insisted that any peace agreement must include credible guarantees against future Russian aggression and cannot require Kyiv to surrender territory. Moscow, meanwhile, continues to demand control over the entire Donbas region, a reduction in Ukraine's military strength and assurances that Kyiv will never join NATO. The talks also come amid growing strains between Washington and Kyiv following Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia under legislation aimed at restricting Moscow's war financing, alongside the agreement to import Russian diesel. Ahead of the meeting, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned that Moscow would not make "political concessions" and said Russia did "not expect a miracle" from Witkoff's visit. title: 'To kill people': Musk accuses Ukraine military of misusing Starlink for drone strikes
text: 'Never been allowed': Musk says Ukraine violated Starlink terms for drone strikes Tech giant Elon Musk on Saturday (local time) accused the Ukrainian military of violating Starlink's terms of service by using the satellite internet system for offensive drone strikes. He said the loophole that allowed such use had been closed last week. In a post on X, Musk said the use of Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive operations was never permitted. He also distinguished it from Starshield, a separate satellite communication system controlled by the US government. "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it. Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them. Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he wrote on X. Musk also underscored Starlink's importance to Ukraine's defence, claiming that the system had played a crucial role in preventing Russia from overrunning the country in the early stages of the war. He asserted that SpaceX had contributed more to Ukraine's defence than any other private company. "Starlink remains critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now. Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact. Starlink was also crucial to preventing Russia from overrunning Ukraine in the early days of the war, as all other means of communication were destroyed or jammed by Russia. SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth by far," he added. Despite highlighting Starlink's role in Ukraine's defence, Musk reiterated his opposition to prolonging the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, criticising those advocating continued fighting without offering a practical resolution. "That said, I have nothing but utter contempt for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell," he said. On Friday, Musk also alleged that financial aid sent to Ukraine to support its war against Russia was being channelled back to the US through "multiple laundry" channels and used to finance the political campaigns of some politicians. Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said operational speeds for the Starlink and Starshield satellite communication networks had been restored to levels recorded before recent restrictions. title: US explores route to bring Russian gas back to Europe through Ukraine: Report
text: Trump eyes Russian gas return to Europe despite past warnings over dependence The US is exploring a plan to bring Russian natural gas back into the European market through pipelines crossing Ukraine, in a bid to secure an energy truce between Moscow and Kyiv before winter. The proposal is part of wider efforts to advance peace negotiations, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing officials from the US, Europe and Ukraine. The arrangement could see a US intermediary handle the sale of Russian gas, potentially bypassing European sanctions while giving American investors a stake in the business. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the proposal during their visits to Moscow and Kyiv in September, people familiar with the discussions told the WSJ. Watch Putin Warns Europe Is 'Paying The Price For Turning Away From Russian Energy Supplies' The idea faces a major obstacle: Europe's stated policy of ending its reliance on Russian energy. EU legislation requires member states to phase out all Russian natural gas purchases by the end of 2027. Several European leaders have also ruled out returning to dependence on supplies from a country they consider a major security threat. Yet Washington believes the prospect of reopening a lucrative European market could persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to agree to an energy ceasefire. The proposed route would use the Soviet-era pipeline system connecting Siberia's Urengoi gas fields to Europe through Ukraine. Kyiv, in turn, could earn much-needed money from transit charges. The proposal had lost momentum last month after Ukraine halted attacks on Russian refineries following pressure from US President Donald Trump . The pause lasted nearly two weeks, even as Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure continued and Moscow began sending diesel to the US. Washington subsequently turned its attention to the possibility of negotiating a wider peace settlement. That pause is now over. Ukraine launched attacks on three major Russian refineries over three days, beginning Friday, bringing the question of an energy truce back into focus. The renewed urgency comes ahead of planned three-way talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi in mid-November. Moscow has so far resisted US efforts to secure such an arrangement, according to the WSJ. A possible financial incentive for Moscow The White House has also discussed safeguards to prevent Russia from using gas revenues to bankroll its military campaign. Under one proposal, proceeds from European sales would be placed in an escrow account in a third-party jurisdiction, a senior US official told the WSJ. American negotiators have presented the arrangement to European governments as a way to ease energy costs at a time when the continent is preparing for winter with relatively low gas reserves. They believe access to the European market could give Putin a strong financial reason to accept a deal. The proposal would represent a dramatic shift in Trump's approach to Russian energy. During his first term, he repeatedly criticised then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel for backing the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, warning that the project would leave Germany âcaptive to Russiaâ. His administration imposed sanctions on the pipeline in late 2019. Russia's subsequent invasion of Ukraine reinforced European concerns about the risks of relying on Moscow for energy. Before the war, Russian gas accounted for 45% of Europe's supplies. That share has since fallen to 11%, with US liquefied natural gas now making up 30% of European consumption. The EU has since moved to dismantle its dependence on Russian gas, with a complete phase-out mandated by the end of 2027. Its stated position is that purchases should not resume even after a comprehensive peace agreement, much less under a temporary ceasefire that leaves Russia's war effort intact. EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen reiterated that position in an October interview with a Hungarian newspaper, which his office confirmed. âI certainly would not trust Russia. Even if there were peace tomorrow, which we all hope for,â he said. Europe's resistance faces a new energy test Despite the public opposition, the Trump administration believes economic pressures could make European governments reconsider. Some senior officials, however, have privately rejected the idea in strong terms. A senior Nordic official said buying Russian gas again would contradict everything Europe stands for. Another senior official from a large European country likened the proposal to former British leader Neville Chamberlain sacrificing Czechoslovakia to Hitler in exchange for business deals, the WSJ reported. Washington is also considering the possibility of restoring gas supplies through Nord Stream as part of a broader settlement. The US sees such an arrangement as potentially helping not only to end the Ukraine war but also to ease longstanding tensions between Moscow and America's European allies. A senior US official told the WSJ that Merkel's mistake had been to pursue the pipeline without first securing a broader security arrangement with Russia that Moscow could accept. The Nord Stream route, however, would be difficult to revive. Nord Stream 1 stopped deliveries in August 2022, while Nord Stream 2 never entered service. Both pipelines were badly damaged in underwater explosions in September 2022, which were attributed to Ukraine. Their restoration would require considerable time and the resolution of major political and regulatory obstacles. The route through Ukraine, on the other hand, offers a quicker alternative. The pipeline network connects to Slovakia and extends towards Austria and Germany. It could be brought back into operation almost immediately, as limited gas flows continued through it until January 2025, despite the ongoing war. US officials have also discussed other economic arrangements during negotiations. One proposal that could significantly lower gas prices across Europe has drawn interest from European leaders, a US official said. However, any such arrangement would be tied to a comprehensive peace deal. The energy situation could further complicate Europe's position. The conflict involving Iran has disrupted Qatari LNG shipments, leaving cargoes stranded inside the Persian Gulf. Energy prices have climbed globally despite an increase in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. According to the EU, the conflict has added 100 billion euros, or around $112 billion, to Europe's energy costs. Meanwhile, underground gas storage across the continent is about 75% full, leaving Europe on course to enter winter with reserves below the nine-year average, EU energy regulators said. The prospect of cheaper Russian supplies has also become a political issue in Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany has made restoring imports of low-cost Russian gas a central plank of its campaign ahead of the 2028 national elections. For Ukraine, the calculation could be different if renewed gas transit forms part of an agreement that protects its energy infrastructure. Diplomats told the WSJ that Kyiv's backing could make it easier for European governments to reconsider the proposal, particularly if a ceasefire prevents blackouts and a humanitarian crisis in major Ukrainian cities. A collapse of energy supplies could trigger another wave of refugees in the coming months. The risk is compounded by Ukraine's dwindling air-defence capabilities, with the US restricting supplies of Patriot interceptors amid a global shortage linked to the war on Iran. title: FREYJA missile shield: Ukraine's new bet against Russian ballistic missiles
text: German soldiers unload the US made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile (SAM) system Ukraine has completed its part of a new multinational missile defence system designed to intercept ballistic missiles, but the programme is still waiting for critical components from European partners before it can move towards testing. The development marks a major step in Kyiv's effort to build an alternative to US-made Patriot systems as Russia continues to intensify missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities. According to Defence News, the system, called FREYJA, is being developed through a coalition of Ukraine and European countries. Ukrainian defence company Fire Point has completed its assigned work on the FP-7.X interceptor and launcher, while European partners are responsible for supplying key technologies, including radar, infrared seekers and command-and-control systems. Watch Putin's Army ANNIHILATES Ukrainian Military Aircraft Mid-Air, 600+ Shot Down In 24 hours | Watch The programme is targeting initial testing by the end of 2026, with battlefield deployment planned for 2027. However, the timeline depends on the delivery and integration of the remaining European components. "Ukraine has done what it was supposed to do, and that is good news," Zelenskyy told journalists, adding that 10 countries were participating in the programme and working on their respective contributions. "People work on systems like this for decades. We want it very fast, because there is no time," he said, highlighting the urgency of developing an indigenous capability to intercept ballistic missiles. Which countries are involved and what are they contributing? The Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was formally established on July 13, 2026, in Paris. According to the joint declaration published by the Swedish government, its 10 founding members are Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. Ukraine is developing the FP-7.X interceptor missile and launcher through its defence company Fire Point. Germany is contributing radar technology through Hensoldt, including its TRML-4D radar, while Diehl Defence is involved in infrared seeker development. Norway's Kongsberg Defence and Aerospace is developing the command-and-control centre. Other potential technology suppliers include Sweden's Saab and France's Thales for long-range surveillance radar, and Denmark's Weibel Scientific and Italy's Leonardo for fire-control radar. These are proposed contributions in the preliminary design, not all confirmed contracts. Poland joined the coalition in September, while Canada has expressed readiness to contribute technology. How FREYJA will work and why Ukraine needs its own missile shield FREYJA is being designed as an integrated ballistic missile defence network combining Ukraine's FP-7.X interceptor and launcher with European radar, tracking, guidance and command-and-control technologies. Its surveillance radars will detect incoming ballistic missiles, while tracking radars monitor their trajectory and relay information to a central command centre being developed by Norway's Kongsberg. The system will use NATO's Link 16 communication standard to connect with Ukraine's wider air defence network, while the Asterix protocol will facilitate radar-data exchange. The initial FP-7.X interceptor is designed to engage threats at an altitude of approximately 20 to 25 kilometres using a blast-fragmentation warhead, with a hit-to-kill version planned for the future. The architecture is modular, allowing components from different manufacturers to be integrated or replaced. Ukraine's push to develop FREYJA is driven by its growing dependence on the US-made Patriot air defence system to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. However, the supply of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors remains limited, with high production costs and growing international demand adding to the pressure. According to Defense News, a PAC-3 interceptor costs approximately $3.8 million, while Ukrainian defence company Fire Point is targeting a production cost of less than $1.2 million for its FP-7.X interceptor in serial production. The shortage has become more pressing after the US-Israel war with Iran depleted an estimated two-thirds of America's prewar PAC-3 interceptor stockpile. With Russia continuing to launch ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and large numbers of drones against Ukrainian cities, Kyiv wants to build a more affordable and sustainable missile defence capability. FREYJA could help Ukraine expand its interceptor supplies, reduce dependence on American weapons and strengthen its domestic defence industry through European technological cooperation.

title: 'Real danger, real need': Why Ukraine needs Patriot missiles to fight Russia before winter
text: The urgency stems from Ukraine's limited ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles (Photo: Reuters). Ukraine is racing to secure hundreds of Patriot air defence interceptors before winter, as Russia intensifies attacks on critical infrastructure and Kyiv faces growing uncertainty over the availability of missiles from the United States and its European allies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the announcement of a proposed $2.1 billion arrangement involving 500 Patriot interceptors but expressed concern that deliveries could take years. Kyiv wants its partners to release missiles from their existing stockpiles immediately, arguing that the coming winter could leave millions of people vulnerable to Russian strikes on electricity, heating, water supply and transport networks. The urgency stems from Ukraine's limited ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. While the country has other air defence systems to counter drones and cruise missiles, Patriot systems remain among its few effective defences against fast-moving ballistic weapons. Watch 94 Years Of The IAF: The Road Ahead For India's Air Arm Damage to power stations and heating infrastructure becomes particularly dangerous when temperatures fall below freezing. Disruptions to electricity, water and heating can affect not only military operations but also civilian life, making energy infrastructure a key vulnerability as winter approaches. Patriot missile system The first two weeks of October reportedly saw more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of Ukraine's power grid. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs to be in a stronger position during negotiations and prevent Russia from breaking life in Ukrainian cities and communities. He has argued that this would only be possible if Kyiv had enough resources to defend itself. âFive hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon â this winter â they COULD make for a highly effective defence package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,â Zelenskyy said in an X post. âWe are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there,â he added. Kyiv has asked its American partners for a winter support package involving 100 Patriot interceptors a month. âWe are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,â Zelenskyy said. He has proposed that the US and its partners supply Ukraine with interceptors from their existing stocks during the winter and replenish their arsenals in subsequent years through production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and its partners. âThe United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,â he said, adding that supplying them immediately and replenishing the stocks later would be âentirely feasibleâ. Europe's stockpile dilemma Ukraine's demand for Patriot missiles is putting pressure on European countries, which have already supplied Kyiv with military equipment and financial assistance. Several of its leading European backers, however, are now facing a difficult choice between meeting Ukraine's urgent requirements and retaining enough interceptors to protect their own territory. Germany, one of Kyiv's biggest military aid donors, has transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. Berlin has supplied three systems from its military stocks and subsequently arranged two more through a deal under which the US would replenish the Bundeswehr. The Netherlands has also assembled the components for another complete system, including five launchers, a radar and missiles. But European governments are increasingly concerned about the availability of interceptors. Germany must balance Ukraine's needs against the minimum stockpiles required to protect its own territory and meet its Nato commitments. âWe are really reaching our limits here,â Brig. Gen. JÃ¼rgen SchrÃ¶dl, a senior German defence ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin after the NATO summit in Ankara. âWe also have to ensure our own protection.â Norwegian defence minister Tore O. Sandvik has also cautioned against placing the long-term burden of military assistance on Europe. âI think itâs not sustainable for Europe in the long run,â he told POLITICO. âAll the European countries have to step up.â The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors, which Ukraine relies on to counter Russian ballistic missiles. Kyiv is developing its own Freyja interceptor, but the system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can take on that role. Until then, Ukraine needs an immediate supply of Patriot missiles. âOne of the priority directions is Patriot â PAC-3 or PAC-2,â Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Ukraineâs presidential office, told POLITICO. âThe first [solution] is buying, or receiving from stockpiles, PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors.â The shortage is also linked to competing demands on US supplies. Most PAC-3 interceptors are produced in the US, making Washington central to decisions on their sale, supply and future production. US President Donald Trump had raised hopes at the Ankara summit by indicating that Ukraine could be allowed to produce US-designed Patriot interceptors under licence. Such an arrangement could eventually reduce Kyiv's dependence on American deliveries, but it would not address the immediate shortage. US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said a long-term production agreement would not be concluded before winter, while manufacturing the first missiles would take longer. Trump subsequently appeared to step back from the proposal, saying last week: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology." The war involving Iran has added pressure on US missile supplies, with Washington also seeking to replenish its own stocks. Asked on Thursday about Zelenskyy's calls for more Patriot missiles, Trump said: âWe want missiles too.â Ukraine has also signed an agreement to receive PAC-2 interceptors being manufactured in Germany, although deliveries are unlikely before next year. Pressure on Europe's arsenals The shortage has pushed Kyiv and its partners to look for interceptors across European military stockpiles. Countries such as Poland, Spain and Greece are among those facing pressure to contribute, but their willingness to release missiles varies according to their own defence requirements. Poland confirmed in July that it had released several PAC-3 interceptors following requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior US commanders. Polish media outlet Defence24 reported that only five missiles were transferred. The decision triggered a political backlash, with opposition lawmakers accusing the government of weakening Poland's defences at a time when Russian missiles and drones have repeatedly crossed or strayed into its territory. Countries closer to Russia are also reluctant to reduce their existing stocks, with their armed forces already considering their air defences insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat cited by POLITICO. This has shifted attention towards Southern European countries, which have contributed less to Ukraine's military effort than Germany and several Northern European donors. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez confirmed in 2024 that Madrid was sending missiles to Ukraine, but the government has not disclosed their type or quantity. Greece has not announced any Patriot transfers. Greek media reported in July that Ukraine had requested up to 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens. Kyiv has continued to negotiate with its partners to secure whatever missiles they can spare. During an earlier effort, Ukrainian officials and Rutte approached European governments with requests for interceptors from their existing stocks. âDear defense minister of Poland, can you give us five?â former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov recalled asking. Berlin also offered to contribute additional missiles if other countries released some from their stockpiles. âIf you get 20 out of all the countries, I'll give you an extra five,â Fedorov quoted German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius as saying. âThatâs the exercise we had to perform to get more than 20. And it is a hard mission.â Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said Kyiv is struggling to buy, exchange or secure available interceptors amid rising demand in the Middle East and the need for the US and European countries to replenish their own supplies. âWe are literally fighting for every missile,â Sybiha said. Ukraine war adds to Europe's economic strain The pressure to sustain military assistance to Ukraine comes as European governments face economic challenges, including high energy costs and inflation. The disruption of Russian gas supplies following the invasion of Ukraine has forced several countries, particularly Germany, to rethink their energy arrangements and seek alternative sources. The additional pressure on energy markets following the Iran war has added to concerns over fuel costs and household expenses. Speaking to TOI, Prof Rajan Kumar, professor at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the Ukraine conflict and the disruption of Russian gas supplies had compounded Europe's economic difficulties, particularly for Germany, which was previously a major buyer of Russian energy. "Europe's economic difficulties have been compounded by the Ukraine crisis and the disruption of Russian gas supplies. Germany had planned major energy infrastructure projects, including Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2, but the pipelines were destroyed,â Rajan said. âGas supplies were disrupted, and energy became increasingly expensive. Higher crude oil prices have added to the pressure, making energy costs unsustainable for several European economies,â he added. The economic strain has raised questions about how long European governments can sustain military assistance to Kyiv while meeting domestic spending and defence requirements. The pressure is particularly acute for countries that must simultaneously replenish their own weapons stockpiles and maintain support for Ukraine. For Russia, the challenge facing Ukraine and its European partners presents an opportunity. If Kyiv cannot secure enough interceptors before winter, Russian attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure could place further pressure on Ukraine's ability to sustain essential services. At the same time, divisions over military stockpiles and the cost of continued assistance could complicate Europe's response.

title: 'Can't use it to kill people': Musk admits restricting Starlink in Ukraine
text: 'That loophole was closed': Musk admits SpaceX restricted Starlink in Ukraine Elon Musk has acknowledged that his company, SpaceX, restricted Ukraine's Starlink satellite internet service last week, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved. In a post on X on Saturday, the tech billionaire accused Ukraine's military of violating the service's terms by using it for offensive drone strikes. However, he denied responsibility for simultaneous disruptions to Starshield, the US government-controlled, military-grade satellite communication system that supports Ukraine's drone operations and communications. "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. The issue emerged last week amid broader tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Restrictions affecting Starshield also raised concerns among Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. Musk maintained that the US government controlled any changes to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to Starlink. He also defended SpaceX's role in supporting Ukraine's defences since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, whose relationship had already been strained by US President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. title: Russia to send first diesel shipment to US on Thursday amid global supply crunch
text: Russia will send its first 40,000-tonne diesel shipment to the United States on Thursday, under an agreement with President Donald Trump to resume Russian fuel supplies, Russia's deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said. The move comes as global diesel markets face a supply squeeze, while Ukraine has warned that renewed Russian energy exports could help finance Moscow's war effort. According to Reuters, Novak said further shipments would follow the agreement between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump, adding that Moscow would meet US demand within its capabilities. The first cargo is part of a broader supply plan announced by President Trump. Trump has announced plans for Russia to supply 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel initially, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another 1 million tonnes thereafter. The arrangement is aimed at increasing fuel supplies amid a global diesel shortage and rising prices. Russia had imposed a ban on diesel exports after Ukrainian drone strikes on its oil refineries disrupted production and caused fuel shortages in the country. On October 9, Moscow lifted the ban, allowing Russian suppliers to resume diesel shipments to international markets. The development comes after US President Donald Trump pushed for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine targeting attacks on energy infrastructure. The proposed arrangement aimed to halt strikes on oil refineries, power facilities and other energy sites, as attacks on critical infrastructure disrupted fuel supplies and added pressure on energy markets. President Volodymyr Zelensky criticised the US-Russia arrangement, warning that allowing Russia to expand fuel exports while the war continues could weaken pressure on the Kremlin to end the conflict. title: Russiaâs 70-year-old Bear: The Tu-95 bomber that still patrols near Americaâs doorstep
text: Russia has sent its Cold War-era Tu-95MS strategic bombers, known by the Nato reporting name 'Bear', on a planned patrol near Alaska, highlighting the continued role of the decades-old aircraft in Moscowâs long-range military operations. According to Reuters, Russian news agency RIA cited the defence ministry as saying on Monday that the bombers had carried out a planned patrol over the Bering and Chukchi seas in Russiaâs Far East. The Bering and Chukchi seas lie close to Alaska, placing the patrol in a strategically important region between Russia and the United States. The area connects the North Pacific with the Arctic and remains significant for military activity by both countries. For Russia, such patrols demonstrate its ability to operate long-range strategic bombers near North America. They also allow crews to conduct extended flights over important maritime regions. But why is Russia still flying a bomber design that dates back more than seven decades, and what makes the Tu-95MS relevant to modern warfare? Why Russia still relies on its 70-year-old bomber First flown on November 12, 1952, the Tupolev Tu-95 was developed by the Soviet Union during the Cold War as a long-range strategic bomber capable of carrying nuclear weapons. Its later Tu-95MS variant, which first flew in 1979, was designed to carry long-range cruise missiles, transforming the aircraft into a standoff weapons platform. More than 500 aircraft of the wider Tu-95 family were produced, according to United Aircraft Corporation (UAC). The Tu-95 family served extensively with Soviet long-range aviation during the Cold War, carrying out strategic training missions, reconnaissance flights and patrols over the Arctic, Atlantic and Pacific. In the 1980s, an F-106 from the Massachusetts Air National Guard intercepts a Tu-95 Bear bomber off the coast of Nova Scotia (USAF) After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Russia retained the aircraft as part of its strategic aviation fleet. Russian Tu-95MS bombers later saw combat use in Syria in November 2015, launching cruise missiles against targets during Moscow's military campaign, and have been used to launch long-range cruise missiles against targets in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Tu-95MS is powered by four Kuznetsov NK-12MP turboprop engines, each producing approximately 15,000 horsepower and driving contra-rotating propellers. According to Rostec, the aircraft can reach a maximum speed of around 890 km/h, making it the fastest production turboprop-powered aircraft. Its reported range varies from 6,500 to 10,500 km depending on the weapons load and mission profile, giving it the endurance required for long-distance patrols over the Arctic and Pacific. The Tu-95MS has a maximum weapons payload of approximately 15,000 kg (15 tonnes). Depending on the variant, weapons can be carried internally in the fuselage weapons bay or externally on underwing pylons. Why the Tu-95MS remains relevant in modern warfare Despite being based on a design first flown in 1952, the Tu-95MS remains relevant because Russia uses it primarily as a long-range cruise-missile launch platform rather than a bomber that must fly directly over its targets. The aircraft can launch weapons such as the Kh-101 from a distance, allowing it to strike targets without entering the most heavily defended airspace. The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) identifies the Tu-95MS as Russia's primary launch platform for the Kh-101 cruise missile in the war against Ukraine. For Russia, keeping the Tu-95MS in service offers a way to sustain long-range strike capacity without depending entirely on newer and more expensive strategic bombers. Its continued patrols near Alaska also serve a signalling role, demonstrating that Russia can still deploy strategic aircraft across vast distances. Its relevance today comes less from the age of its airframe than from the long-range weapons it can carry and launch.

title: US tells European countries to not 'poke' Russia as Putin says 'ready for war'
text: Putin also warned against restrictions on navigation in the Baltic Sea The US has urged several NATO allies, including Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, to tone down their public warnings about the threat posed by Russia, cautioning European countries against rhetoric that could further strain relations with Moscow, according to a Reuters report. The messages, delivered by Pentagon officials during bilateral meetings in recent weeks, reflect the Trump administration's concern that some European leaders' statements about Russia could undermine continental security. Four people familiar with the discussions told Reuters that Washington had advised its allies to avoid publicly portraying Moscow as increasingly desperate or cornered as its invasion of Ukraine slows. Among the US officials conveying the message was Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who is also involved in an ongoing review of American troop levels in Europe. The Pentagon declined to comment on the reported exchanges. "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations," a Pentagon official told Reuters. Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians, Reuters reported. Russian President Vladimir Putin has issued another warning to Europe, declaring that Moscow is prepared for a potential conflict even though it does not want a war. title: Pentagon asks Baltic Nato allies to tone down rhetoric on Russia threat: Report
text: US tells Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia to be âmeasuredâ in comments on Russia Pentagon officials have privately urged several Nato allies in recent weeks to tone down their public comments on the threat from Russia, saying remarks by some European leaders could weaken security across the continent, news agency Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the discussions. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are among the countries that have received the message from Washington, the sources said. The conversations took place during bilateral meetings. It remains unclear whether the US has made similar requests to other European governments. The move comes as US President Donald Trump's administration renews its push to bring an end to the war in Ukraine through negotiations. Now in its fifth year, the conflict has become the focus of fresh diplomatic efforts by Washington, which has considered incentives for Moscow, including sanctions relief, while pressing Kyiv to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. A Pentagon official declined to discuss the reported conversations, saying: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations." According to one of the people familiar with the discussions, US officials have taken issue with remarks by some European leaders portraying Russia as cornered and increasingly desperate as its advance in Ukraine slows. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who is overseeing a key review of US troop deployments in Europe, was among those who conveyed the message, the sources said. Reuters could not establish who else from the US side was involved. The people, three European officials and one US official, said the exchanges were cordial and did not involve any confrontation. Pentagon's message: Avoid 'poking' Russia The reported US intervention highlights differences within Nato over how its members should speak publicly about Russia's growing assertiveness. Some Western officials believe strong warnings about Moscow's intentions could serve the Kremlin's interests by creating fear and weakening public support for Ukraine. Others argue that European governments need to openly communicate the Russian threat to their citizens. They say this is necessary to build support for the resources and sacrifices required to deter Moscow, particularly as concerns grow over an alleged Russian sabotage campaign across Europe. Russia has denied pursuing such a campaign. One person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Colby recently advised a Baltic official against "poking" the Russians. The official said Colby referred to comments suggesting Russia was "cornered like a rat", describing such language as unhelpful. It is not clear which specific remark he had in mind. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal had used the phrase "rat in a corner" for Russian President Vladimir Putin in late September. title: Hundreds evacuated from occupied Oleshky as Melania Trump brokers rare Russia-Ukraine ceasefire
text: People attend an evacuation from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. (Photo: Reuters). Hundreds of residents have been evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, with three planes carrying evacuees landing at an airport in Belarus on Saturday, according to media reports. The residents, who wished to return to Ukraine, were taken by bus through the Crimean peninsula to the Russian town of Anapa before being flown to Gomel in Belarus. They will travel onwards to Ukraine through a border crossing, Belarusian state news agency Belta reported, according to Reuters. The evacuation took place on Friday as part of a joint relief operation involving the opposing sides, marking the first operation of its kind in four years and eight months of the war. Residents were reportedly starving and exhausted. According to the BBC, Russian and Ukrainian authorities confirmed that hundreds of people had been evacuated from the devastated town. The operation was carried out during a temporary ceasefire that allowed the road out of Oleshky to be cleared of landmines. A ceasefire covering the entire frontline region of Kherson had been in force since Tuesday. The BBC described it as the longest and most extensive ceasefire since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Residents wishing to leave were given a four-hour window on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was deployed to transport up to 750 people from the town by 2 pm local time. Ambulances were also arranged for people with limited mobility. BBC reported. Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said the evacuation had taken place without incident. "Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," she said. Ukrainian authorities confirmed that the evacuees were travelling towards southern Russia before continuing to Ukraine through Belarus. Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders". Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart also made a joint appeal to the US first lady for similar humanitarian operations to be organised regularly. Speaking on Friday evening, Lantratova said they had requested that "humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump". title: 'Russia is a big machine': Trump says Ukraine 'has to want' to settle war with Putin
text: Trump said that Washington had spent heavily on Ukraine without receiving anything in return. (AP photo) US President Donald Trump placed the burden on Ukraine to end the nearly four-year war with Russia, arguing that Moscow's military strength and territorial gains leave Kyiv at a disadvantage. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, signalling that he expects Kyiv to move towards a negotiated settlement even as the fighting continues. Watch 'War Erasing Ukraine': Trump Tears Apart 'WARMONGER' Zelensky, Blames Him For High Oil Prices Trump pointed to Russia's ability to sustain its military campaign and capture territory, portraying Moscow as having the upper hand in the conflict. "Russia is a big machine - they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land," he said. His remarks came as his envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday as Washington continued its efforts to broker an end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Trump also questioned the value of American assistance to Kyiv, complaining that Washington had spent heavily on supporting Ukraine without receiving anything in return. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss," he said. The US president also pointed to the deep hostility between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy, suggesting that their personal animosity had become an obstacle to negotiations. He described the hatred between the two leaders as "tremendous". Trump further claimed that European countries were growing weary of the conflict, although European governments have been working to offset any reduction in American military support for Kyiv. Trump eases sanctions pressure on Russia Trump's push for a settlement comes as his administration has taken steps to ease economic pressure on Moscow, raising questions about whether the shift could strengthen Russia's position even as Washington seeks to end the war. On Friday night, Trump signed an executive order exempting Russia from sanctions under a new measure passed by Congress last month. The decision provides additional economic relief to Moscow at a time when the US is also seeking Russian cooperation to bring down fuel prices. The legislation, named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, was designed to squeeze the financial resources sustaining Russia's war against Ukraine. It also gave Trump additional authority to impose tariffs on countries that continue to trade with Moscow. The White House has broad powers to grant sanctions exemptions under the law. It requires the president to notify Congress if he decides against imposing the restrictions. Trump exercised that authority two days before the sanctions were due to take effect. âI am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for in the Graham Act,â Trump said in the order. âI have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.â The order did not explain in detail why lifting the restrictions would serve American interests or spell out the reasoning presented to Congress. The decision marks another shift in Trump's approach to Russia. In recent weeks, he has expressed frustration with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that the strikes have contributed to rising petrol and diesel prices. The administration has sought to ease fuel costs by allowing Russian diesel supplies into US and global markets, despite years of sanctions imposed on Moscow following its invasion of Ukraine. However, the war involving Iran remains the biggest factor restricting fuel supplies, limiting how much relief the Russian measures can deliver. US-Ukraine ties face growing strain The sanctions waiver adds to mounting tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump's latest remarks suggesting that his administration increasingly expects Ukraine to make concessions to end the conflict. The relationship has also been affected by disruptions to satellite support for Ukrainian drones, raising concerns about Kyiv's ability to sustain its military operations if American assistance weakens further. At the same time, Trump's decision to ease sanctions has drawn criticism from those who argue that reducing economic pressure could give Putin more resources to sustain the war rather than bring him closer to a settlement. The administration's approach reflects its competing priorities. Trump wants to end the fighting, reduce economic pressures at home and limit the cost of continued American involvement. But his willingness to relax restrictions on Moscow has raised questions about the leverage Washington may be giving up in negotiations. For Ukraine, the challenge is to secure an agreement that ends the fighting without sacrificing its territorial integrity or long-term security. Trump's latest comments make clear that he wants Kyiv to move towards a deal, while his assessment of Russia's battlefield advantage suggests he believes Ukraine has limited room to negotiate from strength. title: 'I don't believe in Russia's humanity': Truce brings hope to starving Ukraine city of Oleshky
text: A ceasefire has taken effect in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, offering a potential lifeline to residents trapped without food, water and electricity for years, as a humanitarian operation is planned to deliver supplies and evacuate civilians. Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed that Kyiv was honouring the truce, while Russia's defence ministry said it had halted fire towards the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson across the Dnipro River. The White House has credited US First Lady Melania Trump with securing the ceasefire, which is intended to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. Oleshky lies in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian-controlled territory. Russian forces seized the town during the opening days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The town had a pre-war population of around 24,000, but Ukraine estimates that about 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in Oleshky and its surrounding areas. The humanitarian situation has deteriorated sharply, with shops closed and residents deprived of electricity, gas and running water for three years. Attempts to deliver supplies have repeatedly failed, while mined roads and the threat of renewed fighting have made it dangerous for civilians to leave. With food running out, some residents have resorted to cooking weeds gathered from their gardens to survive. Others face shortages of medicine and inadequate access to medical care, leaving vulnerable residents particularly exposed as winter approaches. "I don't believe in Russia's humanity," one resident told the BBC, expressing doubts about whether the ceasefire would hold long enough for civilians to escape safely. The planned evacuation also carries risks. Roads remain mined, communications are patchy and residents fear renewed shooting, reprisals or detention if their phones and online activity reveal support for Ukraine. One woman told the BBC she was recovering in hospital after undergoing two surgeries following a landmine explosion and was worried she would be unable to join the evacuation. title: First time since 2020, Russia's flag and national anthem return to Olympics as IOC eases restrictions
text: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - Opening Ceremony - Abdoulaye Wade Stadium, Diamniadio, Senegal - October 31, 2026 Russia athletes during the opening ceremony Russia has returned to the Olympic stage with its national flag and anthem for the first time since 2020, with 13 athletes competing at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal. The return comes after six years of restrictions linked to the country's doping scandal and Ukraine war. Russian athletes had been required to compete under neutral identities at subsequent Olympic events. They were not allowed to represent their country through its flag, anthem or national symbols. However, the arrangement has changed at the Youth Olympics, which opened on Saturday, October 31. The development follows a gradual easing of restrictions by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 2026. In July, the IOC provisionally lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and withdrew its recommendations restricting the participation of Russian and Belarusian athletes in international competitions. Individual sports federations, however, continue to decide which athletes are eligible to compete. Ukraine has not boycotted sporting events in which Russian athletes have participated. Boycotts were once a common feature of international sport, with three successive Summer Olympics, from 1976 to 1984, affected by them. In the latter two cases, the IOC was more affected than the intended targets. Youth Olympics open in Senegal The Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal on Saturday, marking the first Olympic event to be held in Africa. The Games are also part of the continent's efforts to play a bigger role in international sport. Tens of thousands of spectators attended the opening ceremony at the Diamniadio Olympic Stadium, near the capital Dakar. Hundreds of drummers and dancers showcased Senegalese and African culture under the Games motto, âAfrica welcomes, Dakar celebrates.â Performers dressed in yellow, black and white traditional Senegalese gowns came together to form a giant map of Africa. The Games will also feature the first refugee team at a Youth Olympics. The six athletes, based in Kenya and Uganda, will compete in track and field, judo and taekwondo. Athletes will compete for medals across 153 events in 25 sports. Singapore hosted the first Summer Youth Olympic Games in 2010. title: âOreshnik is incomingâ: Hackers send fake nuclear warning through Ukraine alert app
text: File photo: This screenshot made on a smartphone shows a series of false alerts received late Sunday. Residents of Ukraine and Russia received fake emergency warnings through government-run mobile apps after the systems were hacked, authorities in both countries said. In Ukraine, some messages falsely warned of an imminent nuclear threat, while others claimed there were high radiation levels, a chemical danger and public disturbances in Kyiv. The attacks took place late Sunday in Ukraine and early Monday in Russia. It was not immediately clear whether they were connected. Ukraine temporarily suspended its app, which residents use to receive warnings about Russian missile and drone strikes, but said it was back online. A Russian Telegram channel linked to the countryâs security services said hacking group Hitcore had claimed responsibility for the breach of Ukraineâs system. Though the claim has not been independently verified. There was little indication that the messages caused widespread panic in Ukraine. Social media users instead responded with humour, sharing images of pets and AI-generated apocalypse scenes. Ukraineâs air raid alert channel said âunauthorized partiesâ had interfered with the app and urged users not to click links in suspicious notifications. The countryâs Center for Countering Disinformation advised residents to follow other emergency channels while the breach was being addressed. title: Bulgaria elects pro-Russia president Iliana Iotova in runoff, defeats pro-Western rival
text: Iliana Iotova has triumphed in Bulgaria's presidential runoff, unseating the pro-western contender, Andrey Gyurov. (Pic Credit: Reuters) Bulgaria's president Iliana Iotova, who supports diplomatic engagement with Moscow and opposes military assistance to Ukraine, has won the presidential runoff held on Sunday, securing a decisive lead over her pro-western rival Andrey Gyurov. The largely ceremonial presidential contest saw Iotova, an ally of prime minister Rumen Radev, face Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition. According to estimates released by several polling agencies, Iotova secured between 57.4% and 58.2% of the votes, comfortably ahead of Gyurov, who received between 38.6% and 39.6%. Celebrating her victory alongside Radev, Iotova said her campaign had centred on "incomes, peace and the challenges that lie ahead". European commission president Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Iotova on her win. In a message on X, she said she looked forward to continuing cooperation with Bulgaria on issues ranging from security and defence to competitiveness and energy independence. Black Sea tensions dominate election backdrop The election took place amid growing security concerns following a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. Several ships were hit off Bulgaria's coast in October, leaving 21 people missing. The incidents are believed to be linked to the wider fallout from the Russia-Ukraine war. Although Radev has said the attacks appeared to benefit Russian interests and summoned Moscow's ambassador, his government maintains that there is currently no evidence directly connecting Russia to the incidents. Following Iotova's victory, Radev said Bulgarians had chosen "the future over the past", adding that they had voted for normalcy and a stable, clear direction for the country. Iotova set to become Bulgaria's first elected woman president Iotova, 62, assumed the presidency earlier this year after Radev resigned to contest parliamentary elections. Sunday's victory will make her Bulgaria's first directly elected woman president. A former journalist and European parliament member, she was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021. She supports Bulgaria's membership of the European union and NATO but maintains that a resolution to the Ukraine conflict can be achieved only through negotiations. After casting her vote in Sofia, Iotova said she wanted Bulgaria to be strong within a strong Europe while retaining sovereignty over its decisions. Gyurov, 50, a former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, accepted the election outcome and stressed the need for national unity. "We have laid a solid foundation upon which we can build," he told reporters, while describing his preferred vision as one of a secure, stable and European Bulgaria. Low voter turnout highlights political divisions Bulgaria's close historical ties with Russia continue to divide public opinion over the country's approach to Moscow. Sociologist Boryana Dimitrova of the Alpha research institute said concerns about war had played a significant role in the campaign, adding that Iotova had presented herself as the "president of peace". She also described the election as crucial for Radev and his allies in maintaining political stability. The first round of voting, in which Iotova narrowly finished ahead of Gyurov, recorded a historically low turnout of 23%. Participation in Sunday's runoff was projected to be around 27%. Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round because he expected the contest to go to a runoff. He eventually voted for what he called "the lesser evil", explaining that neither candidate fully reflected his understanding of democracy. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Will back all meaningful efforts for Ukraine peace, PM Modi assures Poland's Tusk
text: PM Modi with Polish counterpart Donald Tusk at Hyderabad House Thursday. NEW DELHI: Looking to further expand their strategic partnership, India and Poland agreed to double bilateral trade by 2030 and announced dialogue mechanisms for defence industrial collaboration and counterterrorism cooperation as PM Narendra Modi hosted his counterpart Donald Tusk for talks Thursday. Modi and Tusk expressed deepest concern in a joint statement over the war in Ukraine, including its tragic humanitarian consequences and the impact on Global South. In his media statement, Modi assured Tusk that whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort for peace. Poland views the war in Ukraine as a direct threat to its national security and sovereignty due to its shared border, influx of refugees and the threat of future Russian aggression in eastern Europe. Watch Zelensky 'CAVES' To Putin: Ukraine Ready To FREEZE WAR; 'Russia Gets 25% Of Ukrainian Territory' âThey reiterated the need for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in line with international law, consistent with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity,â said the joint statement. The leaders also noted the negative impacts of the war on global food and energy security, especially for the Global South. Modi and Tusk, the first Polish PM to visit India in 16 years, also backed an MoU under negotiation for cooperation in critical minerals. Modi said the friendship between India and Poland was based not only on diplomatic ties but also on a shared heritage of humanity and empathy. He recalled how, during the Second World War, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur had provided shelter in India to thousands of Polish children and families. He also thanked Poland for helping India evacuate Indian students from Ukraine shortly after the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022. Modi said the world was passing through a period of uncertainty and change, and even in such times, both India and Poland were emerging as important hubs of growth, technology and innovation. âToday we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India,â he said. He also announced a startup bridge to facilitate cooperation in IT, Artificial Intelligence and critical technologies. âBoth India and Poland believe in democratic values and the rule of law,â Modi said, underlining that both sides considered reforms essential to make global governance institutions more empowered. The two countries agreed that the UN needed structural reforms, including expansion of UNSC in both permanent and non-permanent categories, to remain relevant, credible and effective. In the joint statement, Poland expressed support for Indiaâs membership of a more inclusive, reformed and expanded UNSC, as well as its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2028-29. Modi and Tusk unequivocally condemned terrorism, including cross-border terrorism, and stressed that there could be no justification for terrorism on any grounds. âThey condemned in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in J&Kâs Pahalgam on 22 April, 2025. They called for strong and concerted action against terrorists and terrorist entities, including those designated by the UNSC 1267 sanctions committee,â said the joint statement.
