title: Russia exits European anti-torture treaty, ends independent prison inspections
text: File photo: Russia formally leaves anti-torture convention amid allegations of abuse in detention Russia has formally withdrawn from the council of Europeâs Convention for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, bringing an end to the European bodyâs mandate to independently monitor conditions in Russian prisons, police stations and other places of detention. The withdrawal took effect on November 1, a year after Moscow notified the Council of Europe of its decision to denounce the convention on October 30, 2025. Russia had been party to the treaty since 1998. âThe withdrawal of the Russian Federation marks the end of the CPTâs monitoring mandate in the country. It also marks the end of any independent monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty inside the Russian Federation,â Alan Mitchell, president of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), said in a statement. The committee said it had received numerous accounts of alleged torture and ill-treatment by Russian officials since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The allegations concerned detention facilities both in occupied Ukrainian territories and inside Russia. However, the CPT said it had been unable to visit Russia to examine the allegations because of the Russian authoritiesâ lack of cooperation. It contrasted this with Ukraine, which continues to allow the committee access to any place of detention on its territory and supports the automatic publication of its reports. Russia blocked publication of most inspection reports During its membership, the CPT carried out 30 visits to Russia between 1998 and 2021, inspecting more than 450 places of detention. But Russia was the only party to the convention with a stated policy of refusing to authorise the publication of the committeeâs visit reports and government responses. Only four reports were approved for publication. The unpublished findings include those from periodic and ad hoc visits, among them 10 inspections in Chechnya and the North Caucasus between 2000 and 2017. Russia can still authorise their publication. The CPTâs monitoring covers prisons, police stations, immigration detention centres, juvenile detention facilities, psychiatric hospitals and social care homes. Its delegations have the right to enter places of detention without restriction, interview detainees in private and communicate with anyone who may provide relevant information. The committee sends governments confidential reports setting out its findings and recommendations after each visit. The system is intended to prevent torture and ill-treatment through independent inspections and dialogue with national authorities, rather than to investigate or prosecute individual cases. Mitchell said independent monitoring remained a fundamental safeguard against abuse of people deprived of their liberty. The CPT will continue its work across the Council of Europeâs 46 member states. title: Russia strikes 9 Ukrainian regions as new report shows spike in civilian casualties
text: Russia's recent strikes have plunged Ukraine into darkness, impacting electricity for hundreds of thousands and resulting in civilian injuries. (Pic Credit: Reuters & ANI) Russian strikes across nine regions of Ukraine disrupted electricity supplies to hundreds of thousands of households and injured at least 15 people, officials said on Friday. The attacks came as a new report revealed a sharp rise in civilian casualties since Russia launched its invasion. The latest wave of aerial attacks on civilian infrastructure has heightened concerns that worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington could leave Ukraine more vulnerable to Russiaâs intensifying assault as winter approaches. Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraineâs power infrastructure ahead of winter, seeking to weaken public morale by disrupting heating and water supplies. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended a summit of European union leaders in Brussels on Friday, where he received applause from leaders who share his concerns over Russian aggression and Moscowâs broader ambitions in Europe. The leaders pledged continued support for Ukraine and called on Washington to increase pressure on Russian president Vladimir Putin. Trump-Zelenskyy tensions raise concerns over US support Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy came under renewed scrutiny after the two leaders exchanged sharp public remarks, fuelling uncertainty in Ukraine and across Europe. On Thursday, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by the American president. Trump, meanwhile, openly criticised the Ukrainian leader during an interview with Newsmax, saying, âZelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with.â Speaking ahead of the EU summit, Zelenskyy thanked the 27-member bloc for standing by Ukraine, describing its leaders as âreal leadersâ. âWe want to end this war as (quickly) as possible,â Zelenskyy told reporters in English. âWe donât see now signals from (the) Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. Thatâs why we have to prepare for the winter.â The growing rift has raised fears that Washington could further reduce its support for Ukraineâs war effort. Ukraine faces shortages of Patriot missiles Ukraine continues to face a severe shortage of US-made Patriot air defence missiles, which are essential for intercepting Russiaâs destructive ballistic missile attacks. Zelenskyy has repeatedly urged Washington to supply additional systems and ammunition. Speaking in Brussels, he said Ukraine had received limited numbers of patriot interceptors in recent months. Some were purchased from the United States by European countries for Kyiv, while others came from the existing stockpiles of countries around the world. Zelenskyy also expressed concern over disruptions to Western intelligence-sharing arrangements and sudden speed restrictions affecting Starshield, the military-grade version of spaceXâs starlink satellite internet service. The technology plays a crucial role in Ukraineâs drone operations and military communications. Restrictions that reduced the speed of Ukrainian drone interceptors to 70 kph (43 mph) came as a âdangerous and unpleasant surpriseâ, he said. However, he added that higher speeds needed to intercept Russian jet-powered drones travelling at more than 400 kph (250 mph) were being restored. âHave they returned to previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back? Yes,â Zelenskyy told a news conference. He also criticised Trumpâs diesel deal with Russia, despite international efforts to impose sanctions and isolate Moscow diplomatically over its invasion of Ukraine. Although Trump had promised to end the war swiftly, Ukrainian officials have accused him of pressuring Kyiv to surrender territory to Russia. âThere are so many people with good hearts in America, who sincerely want evil to lose and Ukraine to stand strong,â Zelenskyy told the EU summit. âAnd at the end of the day, the American people will have their say.â Zelenskyy seeks â¬79 billion in European assistance The European Union is working to persuade Washington to maintain its backing for Ukraine, the blocâs foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said. âWe are trying to convince also our American partners that if we want to end this war, then we have to squeeze the aggressor,â Kallas said. âWith our American allies itâs very difficult at the moment.â Irish Prime Minister MicheÃ¡l Martin, whose country currently holds the EUâs rotating presidency, said there was widespread concern across Europe over the latest developments in Ukraine. Zelenskyy told European leaders that the war would cost Ukraine 155 billion euros ($174 billion) next year. He said the country would require at least 70 billion euros ($79 billion) in assistance from Europe. title: Beyond Starlink: How Ukraine plans to cut its reliance on Musk's satellite network
text: Beyond Musk's Starlink, Ukraine plots its own path to satellite independence Ukraine is exploring the development of its own satellite communications network to reduce its dependence on SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield systems, which have become critical to its military operations against Russia. The move follows restrictions on the satellite services earlier this month that disrupted Ukrainian military communications and drone operations, highlighting the risks of relying on infrastructure controlled by a private company and the US government. Watch Putin Crushes Trumpâs Ukraine Plans? âNo Deal Before We Complete Capture Of Ukrainian Territories' The Ukrainian military has signed a letter of intent with Finnish telecommunications giant Nokia and satellite manufacturer ICEYE to explore developing a sovereign satellite communications network that Kyiv would control. The announcement, made on October 22, comes as Ukraine seeks greater control over the communications infrastructure it relies on for battlefield coordination, intelligence and drone warfare, as cited by Space.com. "Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," ICEYE cofounder and CEO Rafal Modrzewski said in a statement. "We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today." The proposed partnership follows an October 1 announcement by Nokia and ICEYE that they would work together to help governments and defence customers establish secure, sovereign satellite communications capabilities. Starlink restrictions expose Ukraine's dependence Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Starlink has played a crucial role in maintaining communications between Ukrainian military units. The satellite network has helped sustain connectivity when terrestrial infrastructure has been damaged or disrupted by Russian attacks. Ukraine also relies on Starshield, a military-grade satellite communications system owned and controlled by the US government, for certain military operations. Its receivers provide communications links for Ukrainian drones, including those operating over long distances and deep behind Russian lines. The system's resistance to radio jamming makes it particularly valuable on the battlefield. However, the country's reliance on these systems has left its military communications vulnerable to decisions made outside Kyiv's control. On October 14, Ukrainian soldiers and officials reported significant restrictions on their access to Starshield, with reduced connection speeds affecting drone operations and frontline communications. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions hampered efforts to intercept Russian attack drones, while some drones carrying satellite terminals reportedly lost connectivity and fell from the sky. Sources told Reuters that connection speeds had fallen to about 160 kilometres per hour or less, disrupting military operations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said access to Starshield had been intentionally limited. The restrictions raised concerns among Ukrainian and European officials about the consequences of depending on satellite infrastructure that Ukraine does not own or control. The Ukrainian defence ministry said on Saturday that its monitoring systems had recorded a return to normal speeds for Starlink and Starshield, with connections operating at more than 400 kilometres per hour. "The Ministry of Defence's monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable," Defence Minister Evhenii Khmara told reporters. The ministry did not say whether the service had been fully restored. Neither SpaceX CEO Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for imposing the restrictions, with both publicly indicating that any such decision rested with the other. Reuters has reported that the order to restrict Starshield came from within the White House. US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but would resolve it if problems persisted. Musk and Washington's influence over satellite access The latest restrictions have renewed scrutiny of the relationship between SpaceX and the US government, as well as the extent to which a private company can influence communications vital to military operations and foreign policy. Musk has said that decisions about Starshield's use rest with the US government. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States)." The episode has also prompted questions about the broader dependence of governments on SpaceX's satellite infrastructure, particularly when access can be adjusted according to US national security and foreign policy priorities. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Democratic US Representative Jason Crow said on Friday, calling for greater clarity about the changes to Ukraine's satellite services. Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Kyiv wanted the service restored as quickly as possible. "To have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it," she said, describing Ukraine's priority. The restrictions have also strengthened calls in Europe for the development of independent military satellite communications capabilities, amid concerns that there is no viable short-term alternative to SpaceX's systems. US administrations have sought to control Starlink access The latest dispute is not the first time the US government has sought to influence the availability of Starlink in different countries. According to six former senior US officials cited by Reuters, both the Biden and Trump administrations have asked SpaceX to activate or restrict the service in various locations to support US foreign policy objectives. During former President Joe Biden's tenure, officials sought to prevent Iranian-backed armed groups, including the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon, from using Starlink terminals. They also pushed for the expansion of the service in Ukraine following Russia's invasion in 2022 and sought to make it available in Iran during protests in September 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini. Five former officials told Reuters that the Biden administration coordinated with SpaceX on several occasions to restrict access by US adversaries and expand connectivity for allies. Officials shared intelligence with the company about suspected Starlink use by the Houthis and Hezbollah through terminals diverted via intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, US intelligence officials informed the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah might have obtained Starlink terminals. Similar concerns emerged in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Houthis. The administration subsequently contacted SpaceX to identify and deactivate the terminals, with at least some of them switched off, according to two former officials. The Trump administration also discussed activating Starlink in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in June 2025 and February 2026, a former senior Trump administration official and another person familiar with the matter told Reuters. The move was intended to bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed whether those terminals were activated. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. The earlier requests, which Reuters said were being reported for the first time, illustrate how successive US administrations have relied on SpaceX to help implement foreign policy decisions. ICEYE's existing role in Ukraine's defence ICEYE already supports Ukraine's military through its Earth-observation satellite capabilities. The Finnish company and its US subsidiary jointly operate a fleet of satellites in low Earth orbit that use synthetic aperture radar to collect information about the Earth's surface. Ukraine uses data from the constellation for intelligence gathering and military planning, giving ICEYE an established role in the country's defence efforts. The company has also attracted Russian attention. A Russian inspection satellite, Kosmos 2612, recently made an extremely close approach to ICEYE-X36, operated by ICEYE US. The purpose of the manoeuvre remains unclear, with possible explanations including an attempt to assess the satellite's capabilities, interfere with its operations or signal Russia's ability to approach commercial spacecraft. Nokia, meanwhile, has highlighted the importance of satellite networks in maintaining connectivity when terrestrial communications are disrupted. "Nations need communications they can rely on in every situation. Satellite networks extend and protect connectivity when networks on the ground are disrupted," Mikko Hautala, Nokia's chief geopolitical and government relations officer and chairman of Nokia Defense, said in the October 22 statement. "This makes them a key part of any secure communications system," he added. "Through this Letter of Intent, together with Ukraine and ICEYE, we will explore how trusted, sovereign satellite communications can strengthen Ukraine's resilience and give it control over the connectivity it depends on." The letter of intent marks an initial step towards exploring a Ukrainian-controlled satellite communications network. While the agreement does not establish a deployment timeline or confirm that a system will be built, it signals Kyiv's intention to reduce its reliance on external providers for communications that have become indispensable to its war effort. title: Europe, India and Trumpâs peace initiative: Diplomacy, energy security and economic renewal
text: Europe cannot afford an indefinite war in Ukraine Europe cannot afford an indefinite war in Ukraine. After years of fighting, enormous military expenditure and devastating human losses, European leaders must confront a difficult reality: without a credible diplomatic strategy, the conflict risks further weakening Europeâs economic competitiveness, social cohesion and political stability. President Donald Trumpâs renewed peace initiative offers an opportunity to change course. Europe and India should support serious negotiations to end the war, restore economic cooperation and build a more stable international order. The precise terms of a settlement remain unresolved. Proposals discussed in the wider peace process have included territorial arrangements, restrictions on Ukraineâs future military alignment, security guarantees, reconstruction and the possibility of renewed economic cooperation with Russia. Any agreement would require difficult negotiations, credible guarantees and mechanisms for implementation. Nevertheless, the overriding objective should be clear: replacing a prolonged and destructive conflict with a sustainable political settlement. Europeâs economic difficulties make diplomacy particularly urgent. High energy costs have placed pressure on manufacturers, weakened competitiveness and threatened industrial employment. The automotive, chemical and steel industries face mounting challenges from international competition, expensive production and structural change. When companies reduce their workforces or relocate production, workers and their families bear the consequences. European governments cannot safeguard prosperity while overlooking policies that may undermine their industrial base. Affordable, reliable energy is essential for manufacturing, employment and growth. As part of a negotiated settlement, the possible resumption of Russian gas supplies under mutually agreed conditions deserves serious consideration. Europe should diversify its energy sources, but diversification should not automatically exclude commercially viable supplies. Energy security requires resilience, affordability and a realistic assessment of long-term needs. The consequences extend beyond industry. Europeâs welfare states depend on productive economies, secure employment and sustainable public revenues. When businesses struggle, household energy bills rise and living costs increase, governments face greater pressure on public finances. Their capacity to invest in schools, hospitals, public transport and social protection may consequently diminish. European leaders should therefore assess whether their approach to the war advances the long-term interests of their citizens. Norway, as a major exporter of oil and natural gas, occupies a different economic position from countries heavily dependent on imported energy. Higher prices may benefit exporters while burdening consumers and energy-intensive industries elsewhere. European policymakers must consider these differences and prioritise economic resilience and the welfare of their citizens rather than treating prolonged economic hardship as an unavoidable consequence of conflict. The partnership between India and the European Union offers a compelling additional reason to pursue peace. The two sides concluded negotiations on a landmark free trade agreement in January 2026. Once the agreement completes the necessary approval procedures and enters into force, it could connect markets representing approximately two billion people, creating substantial opportunities for trade, investment and employment. Europe and India should seize this opportunity. European companies can expand investment in Indian manufacturing, infrastructure, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals and technology. Indian businesses can contribute to European industry, research, digital services and advanced manufacturing. Both sides can benefit from more resilient supply chains, knowledge exchange and access to new markets. This partnership could strengthen economic growth at a time when geopolitical uncertainty is discouraging investment and diverting resources from development. However, the benefits will depend on practical cooperation rather than geopolitical confrontation. Europe needs new markets and competitive production opportunities; India needs investment, advanced technology and international market access. Together, they can reduce excessive dependence on individual suppliers and strengthen their economic resilience. A prolonged European security crisis would make these ambitions more difficult to achieve. Sanctions and energy policy should also form part of a broader diplomatic discussion. India has longstanding economic and strategic relations with Russia, including purchases of Russian oil. A comprehensive settlement could establish a clear, coordinated framework for easing relevant sanctions as Russia fulfils its commitments. Such arrangements should provide greater certainty for legitimate trade, respect applicable international law and avoid penalising Indian businesses merely for maintaining lawful commercial relations with Russia. India is well placed to encourage dialogue. Its longstanding relationship with Moscow, alongside its expanding partnerships with Europe and the United States, gives New Delhi a distinctive diplomatic position. Indiaâs tradition of strategic autonomy allows it to engage with competing powers without accepting that international politics must be organised into hostile blocs. It should work with European countries, including Austria, that favour diplomatic engagement, while respecting Ukraineâs sovereignty and the legitimate security concerns of all parties. Europe must stop treating diplomacy as a sign of weakness. Military assistance and deterrence may influence the calculations of the parties, but they cannot alone establish a durable European security order. Negotiations, verifiable commitments and credible security arrangements are indispensable to reducing the risk of renewed conflict. The resources consumed by war could otherwise support healthcare, education, scientific research, public transport and climate action. Europe and India have much to gain from cooperation in renewable energy, artificial intelligence, sustainable development and technological innovation. These are investments in the prosperity and security of future generations. Europe and India should therefore support a serious, inclusive effort to end the war, restore economic cooperation and establish a more balanced international order. A negotiated settlement would not resolve every disagreement, nor would it guarantee immediate economic recovery. It could, however, create the conditions for renewed investment, more stable energy markets, expanded trade and greater international confidence. Europe and India should back diplomacy, expand trade and invest in shared prosperity. The next generation deserves economic opportunity and international cooperationânot an inheritance of war, debt and deepening hostility. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: Chhattisggarh youth missing in Russia; family alleges pressure to join Ukraine war
text: Raipur: A youth from Bilha in Chhattisgarh's Bilaspur district who travelled to Russia in search of employment has been out of contact with his family since Oct 7, with his relatives alleging that he was detained, assaulted and pressured to join the Russia-Ukraine war. The family of Vineet Kumar Dubey has approached Bilaspur collector Sanjay Agarwal and SSP Rajnesh Singh, seeking urgent intervention to trace him and bring him back safely. Bilaspur police have written to the Russian embassy and the ministry of external affairs seeking information about his whereabouts and condition. There is, however, no official confirmation yet from Russian authorities or Indian agencies on where Vineet is, whether he is being held against his will, or whether he was actually pressured to join the war. According to his family, Vineet, who studied up to Class X, came across a job opportunity in Russia through a Telegram app group and reached Moscow on Oct 1. His sister Aashi Dubey said he messaged the family after landing and told them he had reached safely. âMy brother reached Russia on Oct 1. He informed us that he had arrived, but we have not been able to speak to him since Oct 7,â she said. Family alleges he was stopped from reaching embassy The family claims Vineet began facing trouble soon after reaching Russia. They allege that he was prevented from approaching the Indian embassy and initially kept at a hotel in Moscow. He was later taken to Volgograd, where he was allegedly kept in an apartment. According to information, some people took him away in a car at around 7am on Oct 7 to an unidentified location. His relatives allege that he was then pressured to obtain residency papers and join the war. The family has also alleged that he was warned that he could be implicated in a drugs-related case if he did not comply with the demands being made of him. WhatsApp contact became family's only source of information The family says details of what allegedly happened to Vineet came through a man who identified himself as Kishor, who contacted them on WhatsApp. Since then, they have had no direct communication with Vineet and remain uncertain about his location and condition. The family has urged the centre and the Indian embassy in Russia to establish his whereabouts at the earliest and facilitate his return. Handwritten note deepens family's concern Aashi also showed a handwritten note which she claims was sent by Vineet. In the message, he reassures his father that he is fine, asks him not to worry and tells him to take care of Aashi. But the note ends with the letters âOKHâ, which Aashi says had a private meaning between the siblings. She said the two would use âOKHâ as a code when one of them needed help but did not want to openly tell their parents. For the family, that detail has added to the fear that Vineet may have been trying to signal distress while appearing to reassure them. Police await response from embassy, MEA SSP Rajnesh Singh said police received a complaint from Vineetâs sister stating that he had been detained in Russia. âWe have written to the embassy on the basis of the complaint. Further action will be taken once a response is received,â Singh said. Collector Sanjay Agarwal said the administration had coordinated with police and was awaiting a response from the authorities concerned. The family says nearly three weeks have passed without direct contact with Vineet, and no official agency has yet been able to confirm his location or condition. title: Trumpâs Russian roulette: A high-stakes juggle between Vladimir Putin and the polls
text: Trump said Ukraine needed a new president and later cliamed Putin appeared more interested in reaching a deal than Zelenskyy. With US fuel prices soaring weeks before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump turned to a most unlikely supplier for relief. Russia. Moscow, which Washington has sanctioned for years over its war in Ukraine, is now being allowed to supply diesel to the US and global markets under a temporary licence issued by the Treasury Department. The decision came after a telephone conversation between Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin . The White House said the move will help bring down fuel costs for American farmers, truckers and families. But critics, including several Republicans, argue that the deal risks putting money into Moscow's hands while doing little to ease prices for American consumers. The timing is politically sensitive as Americans are preparing to elect a new Congress on November 3, and the cost of living remains a major concern. Watch 'Russia Won't Abandon Iran': Lavrov's Big Declaration As Tehran Hosts Russian Foreign Minister For Trump, the political calculation appears straightforward. If Russian supplies arrive quickly and in sufficient quantities, they could help ease fuel prices and give his party a political boost. If deliveries fall short or prices remain high, the administration could end up granting Moscow significant economic relief without delivering much for American consumers. Trump has waved many sactions days before they were due to take effect under Graham Act. How much difference can Russian diesel make? Diesel prices averaged $6.28 a gallon on October 11, up 71% from a year earlier. The American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices, put the average at $6.33 on October 16. The impact extends well beyond motorists because diesel also powers the lorries that transport goods, tractors used by farmers and cargo vessels that move products around the world. When diesel becomes more expensive, the cost of transporting food and other essentials rises, eventually feeding into household bills. Farm-state Republicans had pressed the White House to act, with Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa and others calling for a ban on fuel exports to protect domestic supplies. Trump initially backed the idea, but the White House later ruled it out. The administration subsequently turned to Russian diesel. In announcing the deal, Trump said bringing down prices for American farmers, ranchers and truckers was his highest priority. According to Trump's announcement, Russia would supply approximately 2.24 million barrels immediately, followed by 3.73 million barrels the next month, with subsequent supplies expected to roughly double. Russian oil imports by different nations. Russia said on October 21 that it would send its first diesel shipment to the US the following day, carrying 40,000 metric tonnes of fuel. More shipments are planned, although questions remain over whether Moscow can deliver enough diesel to make a significant difference to prices. The figures, however, offer a sense of the deal's limitations. The second shipment, spread over a month, would amount to around 124,000 barrels a day. Kpler, a market intelligence firm, estimates the global diesel shortfall at about one million barrels a day. The planned shipment would therefore cover only around one-eighth of that gap. And there is also no guarantee that Russia can deliver the promised volumes. The International Energy Agency has said Russian diesel production has fallen by about 30 per cent, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries contributing to the squeeze. Rachel Ziemba, an analyst specialising in economics and geopolitics, said the measure was unlikely to make a significant difference to the global diesel market in the near term. Kpler's Michelle Brouhard has also warned that Russia's ability to supply additional barrels remains uncertain. Even if Russian diesel reaches the market, lower wholesale prices may not immediately translate into cheaper fuel for Americans. Refining capacity, transportation costs and the time required for deliveries could affect how quickly consumers see any relief. A lifeline for Moscow While the benefit to American consumers is still unclear, the decision could offer Russia a more immediate advantage by opening a route to sell fuel that sanctions had restricted. The Treasury licence remains valid until April 7, 2027, making it significantly longer than the usual 30-day sanctions waivers. It is the first diesel waiver since the start of the Ukraine war to extend beyond that standard period. Putin had said days before the announcement that Russia had ample diesel supplies but was struggling to sell them abroad because of sanctions. News agency Reuters reported that his envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, had visited Washington the previous month seeking licences covering major Russian oil companies. Dmitriev welcomed the Treasury notice, saying Russian-American cooperation on diesel and energy would benefit the world. He later described the broader sanctions waiver as a historic moment. The move was followed by a broader sanctions waiver. On October 16, Trump signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs provided for under the newly enacted Graham Act, certifying that the decision was in the national interest. The waiver suspended new sanctions and potential tariffs under the law, including penalties targeting countries that purchase Russian energy. India and China were among the countries that could have faced additional trade restrictions. The White House argued that enforcing the measures would obstruct efforts to negotiate an end to the war. Together, the decisions marked a sharp shift from Trump's earlier approach. Last year, his administration imposed an additional 25% tariff on India over its purchases of Russian oil. On October 2, Trump and other G7 leaders had also pledged to maintain pressure on Moscow. A bipartisan group of US senators has since warned that easing restrictions would not serve American interests and would help finance Russia's war against Ukraine. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who learnt about the diesel deal after it had been finalised, called it unfair and dishonest, describing it as a sign of weakness. Trump responded by suggesting that Ukraine needed a new president and later said Putin appeared more interested in reaching a deal than Zelenskyy. Trump has also placed the burden on Ukraine to end the nearly four-year war with Russia, arguing that Moscow's military strength and territorial gains leave Kyiv at a disadvantage. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, signalling that he expects Kyiv to move towards a negotiated settlement even as the fighting continues. Trump pointed to Russia's ability to sustain its military campaign and capture territory, portraying Moscow as having the upper hand in the conflict. "Russia is a big machine - they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land," he said. Trump also questioned the value of American assistance to Kyiv, complaining that Washington had spent heavily on supporting Ukraine without receiving anything in return. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss," he said. The US administration has defended its decision by pointing to Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, which it says have contributed to higher fuel prices. A US official told Axios that Trump acted after Zelenskyy ignored repeated requests to stop the strikes. However, Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite an energy ceasefire announced by Trump, with no comparable punitive action from Washington. Republicans divided as election pressure mounts The backlash has exposed divisions within Trump's own party. Republican senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn and Thom Tillis joined Democrats in criticising the deal, calling it a betrayal of Ukraine and a gift to an adversary. Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has vowed to force a House vote to block the purchases, predicting overwhelming support for the measure. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-sponsor of the sanctions legislation, has also condemned the administration's decision. Other Republicans, including Anna Paulina Luna and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, have defended it. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said the deal would help farmers, truckers and families while Trump continued pressing both sides to stop attacks on refineries. The decision has also raised legal questions. Seven senators argue that allowing Russian petroleum products into the US violates a 2022 law barring such imports. Tillis has separately questioned whether the administration complied with requirements to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. The Treasury Department maintains that its actions comply with applicable laws. For European governments, the easing of pressure on Moscow is particularly uncomfortable as Nato allies contend with Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. Zelenskyy has warned that Russia could repay the concession with further attacks and deception. Domestic politics help explain why Trump is keen to show results quickly. A Pew Research Center poll found that 44% of registered voters viewed their congressional vote as a way to oppose Trump, compared with 19% who saw it as a way to support him. Trump has urged Republicans to campaign as though he were on the ballot, even as he insists that his own electoral victories are already settled. The Russian diesel deal is therefore more than an energy decision. It is an attempt to address a pressing economic problem while navigating an election, a costly war and competing demands from allies. With the November 3 election approaching, the central question is whether the promised fuel will reach the market in sufficient quantities to make a noticeable difference. For now, Washington has opened the door to Russian diesel, but whether the decision brings relief to American consumers remains uncertain. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Chhattisgarh man missing in Russia; kin allege he was pressured to join Ukraine war
text: Sister of Vineet Dubey showing his pic on her phone RAIPUR: A youth from Bilha in Chhattisgarhâs Bilaspur district who travelled to Russia in search of employment has been out of contact with his family since Oct 7, with his relatives alleging that he was detained, assaulted and pressured to join the Russia-Ukraine war. The family of Vineet Kumar Dubey has approached Bilaspur collector Sanjay Agarwal and SSP Rajnesh Singh, seeking urgent intervention to trace him and bring him back safely. Bilaspur police have written to the Russian embassy and the ministry of external affairs seeking information about his whereabouts and condition. There is, however, no official confirmation yet from Russian authorities or Indian agencies on where Vineet is, whether he is being held against his will, or whether he was actually pressured to join the war. According to his family, Vineet, who studied up to class X, came across a job opportunity in Russia through a Telegram app group and reached Moscow on Oct 1. His sister Aashi Dubey said he messaged the family after landing and told them he had reached safely. âMy brother reached Russia on Oct 1. He informed us that he had arrived, but we have not been able to speak to him since Oct 7,â she said. Family alleges he was stopped from reaching embassy The family claims Vineet began facing trouble soon after reaching Russia. They allege that he was prevented from approaching the Indian embassy and initially kept at a hotel in Moscow. He was later taken to Volgograd, where he was allegedly kept in an apartment. According to information, some people took him away in a car around 7 am on Oct 7 to an unidentified location. His relatives allege that he was then pressured to obtain residency papers and join the war. The family has also alleged that he was warned that he could be implicated in a drugs-related case if he did not comply with the demands being made of him. WhatsApp contact became familyâs only source of information The family says details of what allegedly happened to Vineet came through a man who identified himself as Kishor, who contacted them on WhatsApp. Since then, they have had no direct communication with Vineet and remain uncertain about his location and condition. The family has urged the centre and the Indian embassy in Russia to establish his whereabouts at the earliest and facilitate his return. Handwritten note deepens familyâs concern Aashi also showed a handwritten note which she claims was sent by Vineet. In the message, he reassures his father that he is fine, asks him not to worry and tells him to take care of Aashi. But the note ends with the letters âOKHâ, which Aashi says had a private meaning between the siblings. She said the two would use âOKHâ as a code when one of them needed help but did not want to openly tell their parents. For the family, that detail has added to the fear that Vineet may have been trying to signal distress while appearing to reassure them. Police await response from embassy, MEA SSP Rajnesh Singh said police received a complaint from Vineetâs sister stating that he had been detained in Russia. âWe have written to the embassy on the basis of the complaint. Further action will be taken once a response is received,â Singh said. Collector Sanjay Agarwal said the administration had coordinated with police and was awaiting a response from the authorities concerned. The family said nearly three weeks have passed without direct contact with Vineet, and no official agency has yet been able to confirm his location or condition. title: US clears $2.1 billion Patriot missile deal for Ukraine, with Europe and Canada footing bill
text: As Zelenskyy welcomed the move, he also urged Washington to facilitate faster deliveries, saying the missiles are needed to counter Russian attacks during the coming winter (Photo: Reuters). The US state department on Friday approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptors to Ukraine, in a deal estimated to be worth $2.1 billion and funded entirely by Kyiv's partners and allies. Ukraine has been facing shortages of US-made Patriot air defence systems and PAC-3 interceptors, which can be used to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. Intensified Russian attacks over the past two months have forced people across the country to increasingly seek shelter, with air raid alerts becoming part of daily life. Watch Russia Pounds Ukraines MOST Protected Weapon, Energy Site Kyiv Faces Massive Blow Watch However, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the move, he also urged Washington to facilitate faster deliveries, saying the missiles are needed to counter Russian attacks during the coming winter. âFive hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon â this winter â they COULD make for a highly effective defence package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,â Zelenskyy said. âWe are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,â he added. According to the US state department's notification, Ukraine has requested to purchase 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, along with classified and unclassified spare parts and other related logistics and programme support. The purchase would be funded through donations from Canada, Germany and Norway via the Jumpstart programme, as well as national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan. âNo U.S. funds are involved in this sale,â the notification said. The principal contractor for the proposed sale is Lockheed Martin. According to the state department, the proposed sale would improve Ukraine's ability to respond to current and future threats by strengthening its integrated air and missile defence capabilities. It would also sustain the operation of existing Patriot systems against ongoing aerial threats. Zelenskyy seeks immediate supply of interceptors While welcoming the authorisation, Zelenskyy said Ukraine needed the interceptors during the winter of 2026-2027 rather than several years later. He said Russia had continued targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure, with more than 30 strikes on critical parts of the country's power grid during the first two weeks of October alone. âRight now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day,â Zelenskyy said, adding that Russian attacks were targeting electricity, heating, water supplies and bridges, as well as life in Ukrainian cities and communities. The Ukrainian president said Kyiv had asked its American partners for a winter support package involving 100 Patriot interceptors a month. Zelenskyy proposed that the US and its partners supply Ukraine with interceptors from their existing stocks during the winter, and replenish their arsenals in subsequent years through production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and its partners. âThe United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,â he said, adding that supplying them immediately and replenishing the stocks later would be âentirely feasibleâ. Previously, the US secretary of state Marco Rubio described the interceptors as the as the âmost in-demand productâ in the defence sector. âWhen a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own. We have minimum standards that we have to meet internally in our base presence all over the world,â Rubio said. He added that the US maintained a global defence footprint, with many of its installations around the world relying on air defence systems. âSo there's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,â Rubio said. On Friday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's long-range strike capabilities were an important element of its security. âUkraine's long-range strike capabilities are one of the real guarantees of our independence now, during this war, and they will remain one of our long-term security guarantees after it ends,â he said in an X post.

title: US says ending Ukraine conflict top priority amid talks of trilateral meet between Putin, Xi and Trump
text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio (Photo: AP). US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Monday said ending the Russia-Ukraine war remained a top priority for President Donald Trump , adding that Washington would continue exploring ways to bring the conflict to an end. Rubio remarked as he addressed reporters during his visit to Uzbekistan. Rubio said the US had spent nearly two years trying to facilitate an end to the conflict. It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting,â Peskov said. title: 'No military solutions': EAM Jaishankar reveals PM Modi-Putin talks on Ukraine conflict in Delhi, Bishkek
text: File photo: PM Modi with Russian President Vladimir Putin NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar has said Prime Minister Narendra Modi discussed the Ukraine conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin in New Delhi and earlier in Bishkek, as India continues diplomatic engagement with Moscow, Kyiv and Washington on measures to protect civilian shipping, restore grain exports and safeguard energy infrastructure. Speaking exclusively to news agency ANI on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta on Saturday, Jaishankar said India had held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on three key aspects of the conflict. "Prime Minister himself had a discussion with President Putin in Delhi and before that in Bishkek," he said, referring to India's diplomatic engagement. Watch EAM Jaishankar Highlights Israelâs Support In Wars, Calls It Vital For Defence Technology Jaishankar said he had also discussed the conflict with Russian and Ukrainian officials, including during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, and in talks with Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov. "We have also been coordinating this with the Americans because they have their own peace mediation initiative. So Secretary Rubio knows properly what is going on here," he said. India focuses on civilian shipping, grain exports and energy security Explaining the three areas under discussion, Jaishankar said India was first seeking to ensure that civilian vessels and seafarers were not targeted in the conflict. The second priority was to restore grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, both major suppliers to international markets. He said shipments through the Black Sea had fallen sharply because of the conflict. "One not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers. The second is to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine. Then these are two major exporters of grains for the global markets. Find a way of restoring that flow because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said. The third area concerned energy infrastructure and shipments. Jaishankar said this was the most complicated issue because the concerns differed among the parties involved. "Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players," he said, referring to refineries, electricity grids and ships carrying fuel. He added that India was trying to bring the parties together to address these concerns but could not publicly disclose the current status of the discussions. Jaishankar calls for diplomatic solutions to global conflicts At the G20 meeting, the external affairs minister reiterated India's position that major international conflicts required diplomatic engagement rather than military escalation. "Look, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications," he said, adding that "there are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway." Jaishankar also flagged the impact of disruptions in energy markets and fuel distribution on developing economies. "This distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful," he said, adding that the Global South was bearing the brunt of energy shortages. He also raised concerns over disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions along the Persian Gulf and Red Sea corridors. On supply chain resilience, which was the focus of the G20 meeting's concluding plenary session, Jaishankar called for greater diversification of global production and manufacturing networks. "Today we need more diversified supply chains," he said, advocating "more globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing." In a post on X after the session, he said securing resilient supply chains was central to the well-being of the global economy. He also called for promoting the "right to industrialise", resisting "predatory practices" and pursuing the "de-politicisation of markets". Jaishankar meets Russian, Polish and South Korean counterparts On the sidelines of the G20 meeting, Jaishankar held separate discussions with his Russian, Polish and South Korean counterparts on the Ukraine conflict, West Asia, bilateral ties and multilateral issues. After meeting Lavrov, Jaishankar said the two sides had discussed the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf situation and multilateral issues. He also met Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, with discussions focusing on the Ukraine conflict, India-European Union ties and the G20. "My meeting with DPM & FM RadosÅaw Sikorski @sikorskiradek of Poland focused on the Ukraine conflict, India-EU ties and the G20," Jaishankar said. Poland is participating in this year's G20 meetings as a full participant following an invitation from the United States. It has also expressed interest in securing permanent membership of the grouping. title: Tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel heads to US after Trumpâs surprise deal with Moscow
text: A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel is headed for New York, according to ship-tracking data released on Friday, following a deal reached between Moscow and Washington earlier this month. The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulphur diesel at Russiaâs Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, Reuters reported, citing LSEG shipping data. The vessel is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. Also Read | Trumpâs Russian roulette: A high-stakes juggle between Vladimir Putin and the polls The identities of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The shipment would mark the first US import of Russian oil or petroleum products since then-President Joe Biden announced a ban on such imports in 2022. The development comes after US President Donald Trump announced the surprise deal on October 9 as part of efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. The agreement also involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports. Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Moscow and threatened to ban diesel exports to Europe unless countries released more fuel from their emergency reserves to help ease prices. Further shipments to follow? As announced by Trump on October 9, Russia was to "immediately export" 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak indicated that further shipments would follow as Russian and US companies finalise delivery contracts. He also projected that Russia could raise its diesel exports to their usual levels of 3 million to 3.5 million tons per month by the end of the year. Last week, Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russiaâs sovereign wealth fund, revealed that the US Treasury had approached the fund for assistance in resolving complex payment issues related to the agreement. Since the European Union imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, which began in February 2022, Russia has primarily exported diesel to Brazil and Turkey, as well as to countries across Africa. title: Putin proposes trilateral summit with Trump, Xi to discuss Ukraine war: Report
text: Putin Floats a Summit With Trump and Xi to Discuss Ukraine Deal Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss the Ukraine conflict, with Moscow seeking a peace deal favourable to its interests, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported. Putin reportedly raised the proposal during a telephone conversation with Trump on October 9. The Kremlin has confirmed that discussions about a possible meeting are underway, although no final decision has been made. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told WSJ that the three sides had yet to agree on the meeting or its agenda. âThere is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,â Peskov told WSJ. Watch Ukraine Hits Putinâs Baltic Fuel Hub Days After Trump Moves To Bring Russian Diesel Back To Market A senior US official told the newspaper that Trump had not formally agreed to the summit but could be open to the proposal as he seeks to end the Russia-Ukraine war. According to the report, the Kremlin suggested holding the trilateral talks alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, China. Russian diplomats have reportedly presented the proposal to Chinese officials, who indicated they would not object if Trump agreed to participate. The proposal has raised concerns in Ukraine and among Washington's European allies, particularly over the absence of Ukrainian representation in discussions about the conflict. Trump says negotiations making progress On Sunday, Trump said negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict were making "great progress" while defending his administration's diplomatic approach towards Moscow. He also accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of failing to secure a better deal two years ago. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he wanted to avoid actions that could push Russia away from the negotiating table. He also referred to ongoing hostage negotiations and said he could sign the relevant document at a later date. "My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and donât want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations! Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!" Trump wrote. Moscow and Washington discuss energy cooperation The proposed summit follows a 90-minute telephone conversation between Putin and Trump earlier this month, which Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov described as "very substantive" and friendly. According to Russian state news agency TASS, the two leaders discussed economic initiatives, energy supplies and international issues. They also expressed satisfaction with communication channels between their countries. Ushakov said the presidents had not agreed on a specific date for an in-person meeting but could meet on the sidelines of the upcoming APEC summit in China if both attend. Also Read: âWant to try your luck again?â: Iranâs Araghchi warning to Trump against renewed war "An important international event is coming up in China - the APEC summit. At least for now, both the Russian and US leaders are interested in attending. Accordingly, if both leaders are at the same international venue, I assume they will find an opportunity to meet, shake hands and talk," Ushakov said, as quoted by TASS. Energy cooperation was another key subject of the conversation. Ushakov confirmed that the leaders discussed possible Russian petroleum product supplies to the United States and international markets. Following the call, Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to American and global markets, with further shipments expected in the coming months. The proposed trilateral summit would bring together the leaders of Russia, the United States and China, but Ukraine's absence could complicate efforts to reach a settlement acceptable to Kyiv and its European partners. title: Maria Sharapovaâs personal mission reaches new milestone with $210,000 Chernobyl scholarship fund
text: Maria Sharapovaâs personal mission reaches new milestone with $210,000 Chernobyl scholarship fund Maria Sharapovaâs connection to the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster goes back to before her birth. Her parents left Gomel, Belarus, after theaccident and moved to Siberia, where she was born in 1987. Years later, the five-time Grand Slam singles champion used her success in tennis to support young people living in areas affected by the disaster. Through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and her foundation, she backed university scholarships, youth projects and sports facilities, giving families in affected communities more opportunities to build their futures. How did the Chernobyl disaster change Maria Sharapovaâs life The nuclear accident at the Chernobyl power plant in Ukraine on April 26, 1986, changed the course of Sharapovaâs family history. Her parents, Yuri and Yelena, were living in Gomel, Belarus, when the disaster happened. They left the area because of concerns about radiation and moved to Siberia, where Sharapova was born on April 19, 1987. Sharapova later moved to the United States with her father to train as a tennis player. She was seven when they arrived in Florida in 1994, with about $700 to support their move. Her career went on to bring her five Grand Slam singles titles and worldwide recognition. However, her familyâs experience of leaving Belarus gave her a personal reason to support young people affected by the disaster. In 2007, Sharapova became a Goodwill Ambassador for the United Nations Development Programme. She chose to focus much of her work on young people in areas affected by the Chernobyl accident, including parts of Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. What did Maria Sharapovaâs $210,000 scholarship fund achieve One of Sharapovaâs major projects focused on education. In 2008, her foundation and the UNDP launched a $210,000 scholarship fund for students from Chernobyl-affected areas of Belarus. The programme aimed to help talented young people attend university, giving them access to opportunities that might otherwise have been difficult to afford. The scholarships supported students studying at two leading institutions in Belarus: Belarusian State University and the Belarusian State Academy of Arts. The first recipients began their studies in the 2009-10 academic year. The programme was designed to help 12 young people pursue higher education. For Sharapova, the goal was not limited to paying university fees. She wanted young people in the affected areas to have a fair chance to build careers and improve their lives. Addressing the purpose of her work, Sharapova said: âIt has always been my dream to contribute to the recovery of a region where I have a personal connection. Enabling talented young people to pursue higher education is part of a broader effort to build a brighter future for the regionâ. The scholarship programme also recognised that the effects of a disaster can continue long after the immediate emergency has passed. Education can help young people find better work, develop skills and contribute to their communities. How did Maria Sharapova support children and local communities Education was only one part of Sharapovaâs efforts. In February 2007, she announced an initial $100,000 contribution to recovery projects in rural communities across Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. The funding supported seven youth-focused projects, including facilities for sports, computer access and environmental education. Some projects also helped local institutions provide better activities and support for children. In Belarus, funding from her foundation helped equip rural music schools and create a room for childrenâs relaxation and psychological support at a district hospital. These projects addressed everyday needs rather than focusing only on the disaster itself. Children needed places to learn, take part in activities and meet other young people. Access to computers and sports facilities could also help them develop skills and take part more fully in community life. Sharapova later increased her support for sports programmes. During a two-day visit to Belarus on June 30 and July 1, 2010, she met children in affected areas and announced a further personal contribution of $250,000. The money was intended to expand a programme offering sports and physical activities to young people in Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. Her visit also brought attention to the communities behind the projects. By meeting young people and seeing the work in person, she could connect her public role with the needs of those receiving support. What has Maria Sharapova done beyond Chernobyl recovery Sharapovaâs charitable work has also reached children affected by other crises. In March 2022, following Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine, she announced a donation to Save the Childrenâs crisis relief fund. The organisation was providing food, water and other essential support to children and families affected by the conflict. In a public message shared at the time, Sharapova wrote: âWith each day that goes by, I am more and more heartbroken and deeply saddened by the images and stories of families and children affected by this escalating crisis in Ukraine. I am donating to Save the Childrenâs crisis relief fund, an organisation working tirelessly to provide food, water, and aid kits to support those in need. Please join me in making a donation. I pray for PEACE and send my love and support to all those affected.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Her response to the Ukraine crisis was separate from her earlier work in Chernobyl-affected communities, but both efforts involved helping children and families facing difficult circumstances. Sharapovaâs work with the UNDP ended after nearly 10 years, according to the organisation. Her earlier projects included scholarships, youth centres, community facilities and sports programmes. These efforts show how her familyâs experience influenced her decision to support people whose lives were affected by the same disaster that forced her parents to leave Belarus. For Sharapova, success has meant more than achievements on the tennis court. Her work in Chernobyl-affected areas gave young people access to education, sports and community resources at a time when those opportunities mattered. title: US says Europe refused to join push for tariffs on India, China over Russian oil
text: File photo: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on India and China for purchasing Russian oil, questioning why the United States should bear the burden of pressuring Moscow alone. Speaking to NBC News' Meet the Press on Sunday, Bessent said the Trump administration had approached European allies in the spring to seek coordinated action against countries buying Russian energy. âSo we have askedâin the spring, I asked our European allies to join us in putting secondary tariffs on China, on India. They refused. So why should the US bear the burden?â Bessent said. He added that Washington could re-engage with its European partners, reiterating that President Donald Trump wanted to end the Russia-Ukraine war. âPresident Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop. And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation,â Bessent said. US defends 60-day pause on sanctions legislation Bessent's remarks came after Trump temporarily waived certain provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving his administration 60 days to assess the potential consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs. Defending the decision, Bessent insisted that the administration had not lifted sanctions on Russia. âNo sanctions were lifted on Friday,â he told NBC's Meet the Press, referring to Trump's executive order granting the waiver. The legislation, which received strong bipartisan support in Congress, provides for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China. Bessent said the pause would allow the administration to evaluate the situation before deciding on further measures. He also defended Trump's record on Russia, citing sanctions imposed on Russian energy companies Rosneft and Lukoil. âPresident Trump sanctioned the two largest Russian energy companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, which dealt a catastrophic blow to the Russian energy industry,â he said. âSo no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump.â US secretary of state Marco Rubio also defended the pause, saying the administration needed time to assess the consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs on the global and American economies. âI think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,â Rubio told reporters on Saturday. Rubio said the administration was also considering pressures on global energy supplies arising from the Iran war, attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Bessent accuses Europe of financing Russia's war effort Bessent also criticised European countries for continuing to purchase Russian oil and gas while supporting Ukraine. Citing shipments from Russia's Yamal facility, he said 140 cargoes had left during the first six months of the year, with 136 going to European countries, including Belgium, Spain, France and the Netherlands. Those shipments were worth more than $8 billion, he said. âThe Europeans have given Russia and Vladimir Putin more money than they've given the Ukrainians. They continue to gorge on Russian energy,â Bessent said. He added that the United States imported $4 billion worth of Russian products, including $1.8 billion in fertilisers, while European countries imported more than 10 times as much. Bessent also pointed to the UK's decision in May to waive its embargo on diesel and jet fuel made using Russian crude, questioning why similar criticism had not been directed at other countries. Rubio calls India an important ally Rubio said Washington needed to consider the energy requirements of countries such as India before deciding whether to impose tariffs or sanctions. âThese sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countriesâIndia, for example, and others,â Rubio said. He added that countries such as India had diversified their energy supplies but could not immediately stop importing Russian energy. The comments came amid criticism of Trump's decision to pause enforcement of the sanctions legislation. Indian-American lawmakers Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam criticised the move, arguing that it weakened pressure on Russia and undermined Congress' authority. Bessent questioned over whether Ukraine is a US ally During the same NBC programme, Bessent was asked three times whether the United States considered Ukraine an ally. He did not give a direct yes-or-no answer. âWe provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so thatâs what you do for an ally. Weâre not providing those to Russia,â he said on the second occasion. title: Fired US general admits leaking classified Iran, Ukraine information to journalists: Report
text: File photo: Fired Lt Gen Brett Sylvia The US Army general fired by defence secretary Pete Hegseth admitted to leaking classified information about the wars in Iran and Ukraine to journalists over a period of roughly a year, according to an internal investigation report reviewed by Axios. Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, who headed the Joint Chiefs of Staffâs Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate, known as the J5, acknowledged sharing classified information with two reporters from separate media outlets, according to the report. A US official told Axios that Sylvia made the admissions on video after failing multiple polygraph tests during the investigation. Sylvia was dismissed by Hegseth on Wednesday over what the Pentagon described as severe misconduct. The investigation, which has been referred to the Department of Justice for further action, remains ongoing. According to the report, the disclosures began as early as June 2025 and continued after the Pentagon tightened restrictions on media access. Sylvia allegedly communicated with reporters through the encrypted messaging application Signal and also met one journalist in person at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia. The report said the diner meeting took place after the journalistâs access to the Pentagon had been revoked. During the meeting, Sylvia relied on notes he had made while reviewing a classified report to orally share information about US assistance to Ukraine. The journalist was working on a book and met Sylvia twice, the report said. Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagonâs public affairs office or seek clearance before sharing the information. Investigation points to deleted messages The investigation also raised questions about Sylviaâs handling of communications with one of the reporters. According to the report, he received a Signal message sometime in June or July that he believed concerned Iran. Sylvia said he could not recall its precise contents and claimed he had deleted the message, believing he had accidentally erased the entire conversation thread. This also removed Signal messages and calls that could otherwise have been recovered from his personal phone. US officials suspect Sylvia deliberately deleted the communications and presented the action as accidental. The report also said he admitted to being one of 20 officials cited in a media story critical of Pentagon leadership. Another US official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and his office had lobbied the Joint Staff to issue a statement supporting Sylvia in an effort to limit the damage from any future allegations of leaks. The Joint Staff later withdrew the statement after someone in the Defence Department informed it of the reasons behind Sylviaâs dismissal. US president Donald Trump, asked about the firing on Thursday, said Sylvia had âbig problemsâ and that the administration was âvery much looking for leakersâ. Trump appeared to refer to Sylvia using female pronouns. Separately to the Axios report, a defence department official also confirmed to Al Jazeera that Sylvia was under investigation for leaking classified information concerning the Iran war, Russiaâs war against Ukraine and other matters. The official said he had failed three polygraph tests and accused him of putting national security at risk. The official also stressed that Sylvia was not a central planner for the Iran war, saying that responsibility rested with Centcom and its commander, Adm Brad Cooper. Hegsethâs wider crackdown on leaks Sylviaâs dismissal is the latest action in Hegsethâs campaign against unauthorised disclosures to the media. In July, the Pentagon announced a joint task force with the Justice Department to identify leakers and directed its Office of General Counsel to prioritise prosecutions over the unauthorised release of classified information. The Pentagon had also introduced restrictive rules governing journalistsâ access and reporting in October 2025, prompting several news organisations and defence reporters to surrender their press credentials. Sylvia is the second officer to be removed from the J5 position under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt Gen Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement in October last year. No immediate replacement has been named for Sylvia, according to an official cited by The Associated Press. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: India-EU landmark FTA likely rollout in mid-2027, says top EU lawmaker

McAllister also said the EU would particularly welcome progress on the investment protection agreement as it would strengthen the confidence of European investors in the Indian market, encouraging greater European investments and contributing to job creation in India.
