title: Ukraine's drone ops slow after Musk's Starlink curbs as Trump warms to Putin
text: Starlink restrictions hit Ukraine's drones as Kyiv worries about US backing Ukrainian drone operations slowed after restrictions were suddenly imposed on the battlefield use of the country's US-made Starlink communication terminals, officials said Wednesday, as Kyiv endured a second consecutive night of missile attacks. Zelenskyy's drone arsenal slows after Musk's Starlink curbs as US support wanes and Trump warms to Putin. Ukraine also did not receive the usual advance warning from its Western partners about devastating Russian ballistic missiles targeting Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The development has raised concerns that Ukraine may be losing access to vital intelligence, particularly from the US. Watch Zelensky Pleads NATO To Stop Putinâs China-Backed Starlink Rival, Fears Russia Could Dominate War Zelenskyy did not specify which partners he was referring to when he spoke about the lack of warning. US President Donald Trump has said Washington has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. The developments have frustrated the Ukrainian military and fuelled fears that Kyiv's relationship with Washington is deteriorating. Ukrainian officials are concerned that US support for the war effort could be weakening after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine and isolate Putin. Trump has also criticised Zelenskyy. On Saturday, he said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy had failed to do enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US. Trump's efforts to end the fighting have yielded no progress. Starlink is essential for Ukraine Ukrainian officials fear that US support, particularly military intelligence sharing and access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications system, could be at risk. SpaceX , Musk's company, imposed a speed limit on Ukraine's Starlink terminals mounted on drones overnight, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on social media. The restriction disrupted operations and made slower-flying attack drones more vulnerable to Russian air defences. By late Wednesday, drone operators were reporting improved data connections, with speeds reaching 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said. However, a Ukrainian official said the speed remained insufficient to intercept jet-powered Russian drones and that all restrictions needed to be lifted. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because the details involved sensitive military information. Musk said on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the US military and Trump. The Pentagon and US Space Force did not immediately respond to questions about whether the American military had imposed any restrictions on satellite communications services in Ukraine. Starlink is a crucial tool for Ukraine's military, supporting both offensive and defensive operations. The network is used for long-range drone missions, interceptor air-defence systems and frontline logistics, Beskrestnov said. âObviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,â Beskrestnov said, without elaborating. The White House did not immediately comment. Kyiv received no warning before initial ballistic missile attack Ukraine's air force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said Kyiv received no warning before an initial Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday night, although warnings were issued ahead of three subsequent waves of missiles. A lawmaker on Ukraine's parliamentary Defence Committee told The Associated Press that intelligence sharing with international partners had not stopped. The lawmaker spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the press. Five people were killed and 36 wounded in a Russian attack on Kyiv that lasted from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning, police said. Russia continues strikes on Ukraine's power grid despite Trump's truce demand Zelenskyy expressed outrage Wednesday over Russia's continued aerial bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure, apparently defying Trump's call for a ceasefire. âWe ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond â and to respond forcefullyâ to Russia's continued aerial attacks, Zelenskyy said in a social media post. âRussia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,â he said. Russian forces targeted Ukraine's power grid, oil facilities and gas infrastructure for a third consecutive night, Zelenskyy said. The attacks came after Trump claimed Russia and Ukraine had agreed not to target energy infrastructure, more than four years after Moscow launched its invasion. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy has agreed to halt Ukraine's months-long campaign against Russian oil refineries, which had caused fuel shortages in Russia. Ukraine's last widely reported strike on an oil refinery took place on Friday. Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak accused Ukraine of attacking more refineries on Wednesday, but local officials and independent media did not report such attacks. Ukraine dismissed the allegation as false. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that details of the energy ceasefire were still being worked out. âThe work in that direction is continuing,â he told reporters. Russia's Defence ministry said its forces had attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the wider Kyiv region and the northeastern Kharkiv region overnight, striking six power plants. Russian forces struck all three of Kyiv's combined heat and power plants overnight into Wednesday, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity, Zelenskyy said. Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and other infrastructure in Kyiv, the surrounding region and Kharkiv overnight, Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy visits London to seek further support Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday for talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who announced the accelerated delivery of British-made air-defence systems to Ukraine. Before their hour-long meeting at Downing Street, Burnham told Zelenskyy that Britain's support for Ukraine would remain unchanged, acknowledging that recent days had been âdark and difficultâ for the country. Zelenskyy also met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace. European leaders remain concerned about Moscow's broader ambitions on the continent and have accused Russia of sabotage as part of a hybrid war. They are seeking to ensure Washington continues to support Kyiv. Ukraine claims battlefield gains against Russian forces Ukrainian officials said their forces were pushing back Russian troops in eastern Ukraine, where Moscow's larger army has been trying to make advances for years. Ukraine has recaptured 277 square kilometres (107 square miles) in an operation that began in the summer, said Brig Gen Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, on Wednesday. The claim could not be independently verified, and Russian officials did not comment. Russia's defence ministry said its air defences had shot down 902 Ukrainian drones over several Russian regions, Crimea, which Moscow illegally annexed, and the waters of the Sea of Azov overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones had flown towards the capital region. Most were intercepted far from the city, while 180 were shot down as they approached Moscow. He did not report any damage or casualties. Russian state-backed lender Sberbank confirmed that its data centre in Saratov had come under attack. The facility had once been planned as Europe's largest data centre. Russian state news agency Tass quoted a member of Sberbank's board as saying the bank's systems were operating normally. title: âVery risky choiceâ: Italy's Meloni warns US-Russia diesel deal could help fund war in Ukraine
text: Meloni warns US-Russia diesel deal could benefit Moscow Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday criticised the United States' agreement with Russia on diesel supplies, calling it a âvery risky choiceâ that could undermine efforts to bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table over the war in Ukraine. Speaking in the Italian parliament ahead of a European Union summit this week, Meloni said the agreement could provide Moscow with additional revenue to fund the war and weaken the impact of sanctions imposed over its invasion of Ukraine, according to Reuters. Watch Giorgia Meloni Unveils Plan To Ban Burqa & Niqab In Italian Schools âThe outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear,â she said. âIt provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions,â Meloni added. The United States and Russia said last week they had agreed on an initial supply of more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets. US President Donald Trump has defended the arrangement, saying it would help bring down energy prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Meloni calls for EU representative in Russia-Ukraine negotiations Meloni also urged the 27-member European Union to appoint an authoritative representative to negotiate on its behalf over the Russia-Ukraine war. She did not rule out giving a formal mandate to the E3 group, comprising France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to represent the bloc in such discussions. âIf France, Germany, and Great Britain believe they can do better on their own than we could all do together, and so far that is the choice they have made, then at least let them do so on behalf of everyone and with an official mandate,â Meloni said, according to Reuters. Her remarks come ahead of an EU summit at which support for Ukraine, including its war funding, is expected to be a key issue. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Sunday that Ukraine's financing would be âfront and centreâ at the meeting. Trump defends diesel deal as Ukraine objects Trump has defended the agreement on the grounds of American interests, arguing that increased supplies would ease fuel prices. In a post on his Truth Social platform, he said he had made the right choice for Americans, while also accusing the media of overlooking European payments to Russia for energy. Russian deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said Moscow could supply as much as 3.5 million tonnes of diesel a month to global markets by the end of the year. The arrangement has drawn criticism from Ukraine, which has argued that additional Russian petroleum revenues could help fund Moscow's war effort. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the proposed suspension of sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027 would undermine Ukraine's efforts to restrict Russia's income from energy exports. âGifts to Putin will not lead to peace,â Zelenskyy said on Saturday. He added that easing sanctions without a clear and lasting agreement to de-escalate the conflict would be âan obvious sign of weaknessâ. The EU, meanwhile, has continued to pursue economic pressure on Moscow. The bloc announced a fresh sanctions package targeting individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial network. The contrasting approaches to Russian energy supplies have exposed differences between Washington and European governments over how to pressure Moscow and pursue an end to the war in Ukraine. title: 'No drones or artillery shells flying into your courtyard': Oleshky evacuees reach Ukraine after journey through Russia
text: Emotional scenes as some of the residents of the frontline city met relatives they had not seen for years (Reuters) Hundreds of residents from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory after undertaking an extraordinary journey through Crimea, Russia and Belarus under a temporary ceasefire. According to BBC, the evacuees arrived in Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Saturday after travelling for nearly 19 hours to escape the humanitarian crisis in their city. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the successful completion of the humanitarian operation, saying that all evacuated residents had crossed into Ukraine through the Chernihiv region. He said roads leading to Oleshky were cleared of mines during the temporary ceasefire, allowing humanitarian supplies to be delivered and residents requiring evacuation to be brought out. He also expressed hope that humanitarian access to Oleshky would continue and thanked the US and First Lady Melania Trump for their mediation efforts. The evacuation brought an emotional end to years of separation for several families. Relatives waited at the Belarus-Ukraine border to reunite with family members who had remained in Oleshky under Russian occupation. Among them was 19-year-old Liza Paliy, who had not seen her father for more than two-and-a-half years after he stayed behind when she, her mother and sister fled the city. "We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," Liza told the Associated Press. Another evacuee, speaking to Reuters after reaching Gomel in Belarus, described the constant threat of attacks in Oleshky and why leaving had become unavoidable. "Here, there are no drones or artillery shells flying right into your courtyard. Many times we were literally on a brink of death back there," the resident said, adding that large craters had appeared in their vegetable garden. Valera recalled how the prolonged isolation had pushed residents to the brink, with food becoming increasingly scarce and families relying on whatever they could grow in their gardens. "There was no bread. Nothing," he told AFP, describing the struggle to find even basic food. He said residents planted vegetables and ate whatever was available to survive. Why did evacuees take such a long route to reach Ukraine? Despite Ukrainian military positions being only around 5 km from Oleshky, residents could not take a direct route into Ukrainian-controlled territory because of the active frontline, the Dnipro River and the danger posed by landmines and drone attacks. The city lies on the eastern bank of the river, opposite Kherson, which remains under Ukrainian control. Destroyed bridges and mined roads made crossing directly towards Ukrainian positions extremely dangerous. Independent attempts to escape had also resulted in casualties. According to the head of the exiled Oleshky City Military Administration, Tetiana Hasanenko, one person was killed and four others injured by landmines while trying to flee the area in September. The evacuation therefore required a carefully coordinated route through Russian-controlled territory before residents could return to Ukraine. Under the temporary ceasefire, designated roads leading out of Oleshky were cleared of mines. A convoy of 25 buses, accompanied by ambulances and humanitarian vehicles, entered the city on October 30. Residents were given a four-hour window to leave, until 14:00 local time. The residents first travelled by bus to Armyansk in occupied Crimea, before continuing to Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar region. title: Drones fall, strikes stall: How Musk's Starshield curbs hit Zelenskyyâs war against Russia
text: Trump growing closer to Putin? How Musk's Starshield curbs cost Ukraine $1 million in drones A disruption in the US military satellite internet service Starshield caused Ukrainian drones worth more than $1 million to fall from the sky and forced troops to halt almost all operations for three days, The New York Times reported, citing Ukrainian military commanders. A senior Ukrainian commander, identified only by his first name, Oleh, said dozens of armed drones were heading towards Russian military targets last week when their video feeds suddenly went fuzzy. The drones had lost their connection to ground-based pilots through Starshield, a Pentagon-funded satellite internet service, he said. Watch 'Drones Dropping Like Flies': Big Win for Russia As Ukraine Suffers $1 Mn Loss Due To Starlink Curbs Many of the drones crashed, costing his units more than $1 million worth of weaponry, according to the report. The development comes days after Donald Trump âs reported engagement with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin over efforts to end the war in Ukraine. The MAGA supremo also recently eased sanctions on Russian oil. Oleh said the disruption forced his units to suspend almost all operations for the next three days, including strikes on Russian command posts and fuel hubs. Such attacks help protect Ukrainian troops on the front lines and slow Russian advances, he said. The reported disruptions have added to the growing tensions between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Ukrainian troops said connectivity had improved after a week, but problems persisted. The Trump administration has issued mixed statements on the issue, denying that any changes were made to satellite internet services in Ukraine while also saying that service had been restored. Ukrainian officials fear the disruptions were ordered to punish Kyiv for attacks on Russian oil refineries and pressure it into making concessions in the war. Ukraine has also reported gaps in US military intelligence sharing and delays in deliveries of American interceptor missiles. US officials have denied deliberately disrupting these services. What is Starshield and how does it affect Ukraine? Starshield is a military-grade satellite communications system developed by SpaceX, the company owned by Elon Musk . It is a more advanced sister system to Starlink, which is widely used by Ukrainian forces for communications and drone operations. European countries pay for Ukraine's access to Starshield. However, the advanced system is not available to all Ukrainian troops. Many units rely on it to operate drones while using standard Starlink connections for basic communications. Ukrainian officials have reported slowdowns affecting both Starshield and Starlink. Musk has said that Starshield is controlled by the Pentagon. However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio added to the confusion when he said on Wednesday that SpaceX determined access to both Starlink and Starshield. According to Ukrainian officials, the initial disruption caused drones to lose their connections at speeds as low as 40 miles per hour. Connectivity has since improved, but drones reportedly continue to lose their connections when travelling faster than 100 miles per hour. While some drone models can operate at these lower speeds, others need to fly faster to hit their targets, the report said. The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones used to bring down Russian drones targeting Ukrainian cities, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine is now looking for alternative ways to operate its drones, fearing that satellite connectivity could be restricted again or cut off entirely. Military commanders said the search for alternatives was diverting soldiers' attention from battlefield operations. US denies deliberately restricting satellite services Ukrainian officials have sought clarification on who ordered the reported restrictions on Starshield and Starlink and why. A White House official told The New York Times that there had been no changes to satellite internet services in Ukraine. Trump also denied responsibility for any changes, saying on Friday that it âwasnât meâ and that âfrom what I understand, itâs the same as itâs always been.â Rubio said a day later that a Starlink slowdown in Ukraine had âsort of happenedâ but added that âmy understanding is itâs been restored.â Zelenskyy has described the changes to Starshield as âa planned operationâ. On NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said that âPresident Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.â The issue has also drawn criticism from US lawmakers across party lines, with calls for the Trump administration to restore Ukraine's satellite connectivity. After a group of lawmakers spoke with Zelenskyy over a video call on Monday, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said the Ukrainian president had âconfirmed ongoing Starlink disruptions, reported interruptions to critical US intelligence sharing and raised concerns about delays in air-defense interceptors.â Tillis also criticised Washington's approach towards Moscow, saying: âDegrading Ukraineâs satellite communications, weakening its air defenses and easing sanctions against Russia only embolden Putin and prolong this war.â He was referring to a move by Trump to allow the US to buy Russian diesel fuel. On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he had a âsubstantive discussionâ with Rubio about Starshield, shortages of missile interceptors and recent disruptions to early warning systems for Russian ballistic missile attacks. Rubio rejected claims that the US had withheld warnings about Russian attacks on Ukraine, calling them âsimply not accurateâ. He also said Patriot interceptors were in short supply worldwide. âNothing is being deliberately denied to Ukraine,â Rubio said. Ukrainian troops struggle to adapt to restrictions Despite the conflicting statements from Washington, Ukrainian commanders said the effects of the reported restrictions were evident on the battlefield. Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, who recently took command of thousands of troops in the Center Grouping of Forces in eastern Ukraine, said Ukrainian forces were adapting to the new speed limits. Before the restrictions, Ukrainian drones using Starshield could fly at speeds of up to 250 miles per hour while maintaining a stable connection, Biletsky said. The formal speed limit had already been 100 miles per hour, but it had not been enforced, he added. This could allow the US to maintain that the system's rules had not changed, even as Ukrainian forces experienced a significant impact on the battlefield, the report said. Biletsky said that even if Ukraine managed to modify its attack drones to operate within the speed limits, interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered weapons would remain at a disadvantage. These interceptors need to fly faster than incoming drones to bring them down. Russian jet-powered drones can travel far faster than 100 miles per hour. âReducing the speed limits for air defense is a painful decision that literally undermines the protection of our cities, first and foremost,â Biletsky said. âSo when the Pentagon took this step, it was undoubtedly an unfriendly move toward Ukraineâs civilian population.â Ukrainian commanders told The New York Times that they believed the restrictions were the result of a political decision rather than a technical problem. They said troops had long feared that Washington could use satellite connectivity as leverage to push Kyiv into making concessions. Oleh recalled receiving a series of angry calls from soldiers as his drones fell from the sky last week. Troops scrambled to redirect the drones and save as much equipment as possible. He said soldiers felt abandoned and argued that Ukraine should stop viewing the US as an ally. Lieutenant Yuriy Butusov, a company commander with Ukraine's 23rd Assault Regiment in the Khartia Corps, said the slower connections had severely affected his troops' operations. He said the disruption had effectively given Russian forces âa vacation dayâ. âThis day without Starlink saved many lives and many trucks for Russia, unfortunately,â Butusov said. âItâs a big cost for us,â he added. âAnd much more blood. title: 'India an important ally': US state secy Rubio explains why Trump paused sanctions on Russia oil buyers
text: Marco Rubio says US President studying impact of possible tariffs US President Donald Trump has waived key sanctions provisions under the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, putting on hold proposed tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including India and China. Rubio, explaining the decision on Saturday (local time), said that the administration wanted 60 days to assess the implications of imposing the measures. He cited Indiaâs continued reliance on Russian oil, its importance as a US ally and mounting pressure on global energy supplies among the factors being considered. While India has diversified its energy sources, it continues to obtain a substantial amount of energy from Russia, Rubio said, adding that shifting away from these supplies could not happen overnight. The law would have allowed the US to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China. The waiver has put the relevant provisions on hold while the administration evaluates their potential impact. "These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countriesâIndia, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said. Indiaâs energy needs in focus Rubioâs remarks put Indiaâs energy requirements and its relationship with Washington at the centre of the explanation for the pause. While India has voluntarily diversified its energy portfolio, it continues to source a substantial amount of energy from Russia. According to Rubio, shifting away from these supplies cannot happen overnight. "You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added. Rubio is scheduled to visit India later this month, including Jamnagar, which is home to one of the world's largest refineries. Energy supply pressures add to the uncertainty The administration is also weighing developments in the wider geopolitical landscape since the Graham bill was passed. Rubio pointed to growing pressure on global energy supplies, including the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia, the situation around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, and the Russia-Ukraine war. He said attacks on energy infrastructure linked to the war between Russia and Ukraine were also affecting global prices. The expanding range of pressures on energy supplies, he indicated, made it necessary to study the likely consequences of the proposed measures before deciding how to proceed. "I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies that are happening not just because of Iran and not just because of the Straits of Hormuz, but increasingly because of the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, and because of the war with Ukraine and Russia, where energy infrastructure is being hit, and so that's having an impact on global prices as well," he said. The pause, therefore, gives the US administration time to consider the consequences of targeting countries that buy Russian energy while global supplies face pressure from multiple conflicts. What the waiver means under the Graham Act Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act on Friday. The provision authorises the President to waive the application of sanctions against a foreign person, restrictions relating to a person, and duties under the law. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said in the order. The waiver applies to duties under Sections 112 and 113 of the Act. These provisions allowed Trump to increase duties on all goods imported into the US from Russia to as much as 500% ad valorem, meaning duties calculated relative to the value of the goods. They also allowed duties of up to 100% ad valorem on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. India and China were among the countries covered by this provision. Diesel deal with Russia preceded the waiver The decision came after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia. Under the arrangement, Russia would immediately supply more than 3,00,000 tonnes of diesel fuel, followed by another 5,00,000 tonnes during November and 1 million tonnes immediately thereafter. Rubioâs explanation for the waiver centred on the need to assess the economic consequences of the proposed tariffs and sanctions, Indiaâs continued energy dependence on Russia despite diversification, and the pressure on global supplies amid geopolitical conflicts. The 60-day window is intended to give the administration time to examine these factors before determining the appropriate combination of measures. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: 'Will happen shortly': US secretary Marco Rubio on progress of trade deal as he arrives in India
text: Rubio hailed strategic ties with India and called it a "strong partner" US secretary of state Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday and spoke about the trade and "strategic" relations with India and what they plan to do as he was about to meet EAM Jaishanakar. He also talked about the Russia oil buying, Ukraine war as he talked to reporters in Mumbai. About the trade agreement, while clarifying that state department is not responsible for that he said, "As far as the trade agreement is concerned, the State Department doesn't negotiate trade agreements, but we are very much involved in what's happening. My counterpart, the National Security Advisor, and I care a lot about it. We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement. I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly. We're hoping, which it should, and hopefully have some good news to announce soon and sign it thereafter. So, we're very optimistic that we will have something in place here very soon." However, he also said that Us delegation "will discuss with Reliance about producing oil in Venezuela", claiming that "India made 'substantial progress' in diversifying oil purchases" which is a "smart thing to do". On being asked what role India can play in meeting the world's energy demand, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says, "India is a refining superpower. They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, it's something they can do. They also, by the way, have pre-existing oil concessions in Venezuela that can produce more themselves." "So, all these are positive things. I'm not claiming to you that Venezuela alone can fill the hole that could be caused by some of the things that are happening around the world, but I think over time, it most certainly can, and in the short term, it can certainly help. So, that's one of the things we'll talk about. With India, we've talked about it in the past, and they sound ready. They're willing to do it. There might be a few impediments that stand in the way in terms of sanctions and so forth that we'll have to work through," he added. He also talked about his India visit adding, "First of all, I will point out that the Foreign Minister of India has been to the United States four times this year. This is the most populous country in the world. It's the largest democracy in the world. It's an important commercial partner and business partner of the United States. We also do a lot of defense cooperation. They're a key member of the Quad. They're a strong strategic partner. I actually don't think we've come enough, and I think we need to have more of them." Post-meeting Jaishankar, Rubio said "In Mumbai, Indian External Affairs Minister @DrSJaishankar and I discussed energy security and defense cooperation while reaffirming the importance of advancing the U.S.-India strategic partnership," the US Secretary of State said on social media. Meanwhile, in his media interaction, Rubio also addressed other geopolitical situations like the Ukraine war, US arms control. 'Nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine' Rubio clarified that 'nothing being deliberately denied' to Ukraine after reports emerged that Trump administration has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine from countries that have already acquired the American-made weapons. He further added that Trump is 'frustrated' at accusations he harming Ukraine. "The president made it very clear, and there are no such changes. So none of that has changed. And I see reporting that it has, which is not accurate," he clarified further. 'China, Russia, US arms control talks would help world' Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that an arms control discussion between China, Russia and the United States would be a positive thing for the world. title: Ukraine has 500 Patriot missiles on order, but Russia's winter offensive exposes a critical supply gap
text: A Patriot missile launcher deployed to protect Ukrainain airspace. (Image credit: Defence Ministry of Ukraine) Due to the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, air defence stockpiles around the world are being depleted faster than factories can replenish them. Russia continues to fire ballistic missiles and drones at Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, while sustained operations in West Asia have drawn down stocks of similar weapons in other parts of the world. The interceptors at the centre of this problem were designed in an era when militaries expected short-duration but intense conflicts and did not anticipate firing such weapons in large numbers. These air defence missiles were expected to be used largely against combat aircraft and occasional surface-to-surface missiles. The Patriot missile is the central feature of the Ukrainian air defences against Russia. The proliferation of drones and cruise missiles, along with the growing use of ballistic missiles, has changed air defence dynamics. Under these new conditions, Ukraine's need for the Patriot system's most advanced interceptor is now running up against the pace of American production of PAC-3 missiles, which are seeing a massive surge in demand. On October 30, the US State Department approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine, valued at an estimated $2.1 billion. The US is not funding this procurement. Instead, the purchase is to be financed by Canada, Germany and Norway through the US JUMPSTART programme, alongside funding linked to the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, with Lockheed Martin as the primary contractor. The deal comes just before the onset of an extremely cold winter, with Russia targeting Ukrainian power infrastructure to put pressure on Kyiv. The Ukrainian armed forces have ordered 500 Patriot missiles from the  United States. An approval is not a delivery The approval is an important step, but it does not mean 500 missiles are sitting in a warehouse. It is clearance for a possible sale, and the missiles still have to be built, tested and shipped. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that they may not arrive for several years, even though Kyiv needs interceptors for the coming winter. Reuters, citing two sources, reported that the newly approved missiles are not expected until the 2030s. A procurement decision cannot refill an air defence magazine emptied in combat, and that gap between paperwork and delivery is at the heart of the story. The recently approved sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors to Ukraine by the Americans, is a typical example of what can befall a country that relies heavily on import of defence stores to fight its wars. The deal for the Patriot missiles will take years to roll out, while the threat to Ukraine is immediate. In fact, Zelensky has already approached the US for faster deliveries. The defence industry takes time to grow its roots and develop a domestic eco-system. In fact, Zelenskyy has often been forced to modulate his war plans in consonance with limitations imposed by his war fighting inventory, restrictions imposed by supplier nations and such like factors. These limitations have adversely affected the course of battles Ukrainians have fought. In todayâs world, technological superiority, and the ability to manufacture cutting edge platforms are an integral component of military capability of a nation. The more self-reliant the State is, better is it for its sovereign decision making. Brigadier SK Chatterji (Retd), author and strategic affairs expert The factory floor To understand the gap, it helps to look at what Lockheed Martin can actually build. The company delivered a record 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025. In January 2026, the firm announced a seven-year framework agreement with the US government to raise annual production capacity from roughly 600 missiles to 2,000, more than a threefold increase. If output continues at the 2025 pace, an order of 500 missiles would equal about 81% of a full year's output. If production eventually reaches 2,000 missiles a year, the same order would equal about three months of production. Neither figure is a delivery forecast, because Lockheed Martin also supplies the US military and several international customers, and a factory's annual output is not the same as the number of missiles available for export. The air defence missiles needed by Ukraine will take years to be delivered. Why 500 missiles can take years There are three constraints at work here. The first is the manufacturing cycle. The New Voice of Ukraine reported that producing one missile can take as long as 24 months. That does not mean each missile sits on the production line for two years, since work on different missiles overlaps and components are made in parallel. It does mean an order for hundreds of advanced interceptors cannot be filled like an order for a standard commercial product. The second is competition for the same missiles. The US armed forces need PAC-3 interceptors, as do America's European, West Asian and Indo-Pacific allies that operate Patriot systems. Any increase in production has to serve this wider demand, not just Ukraine. The third is the industrial base behind the final assembly line. Missiles depend on a network of suppliers, specialised components, skilled workers, testing facilities and manufacturing equipment. Lockheed Martin's expansion agreement is designed to grow capacity across that network, but the investment takes time to translate into completed, tested missiles. In effect, the 500-missile sale is a long-term replenishment measure and does not answer how Ukraine will defend its cities before the new production arrives. The repeated use of the Patriot missiles by Ukraine and other nations is fast depleting the size of the reserves . How long would 500 missiles last? The pressure on stocks becomes clearer when set against Ukraine's own estimates of what it needs. In September, Defense Express reported Zelenskyy's estimate that Ukraine would need 100 to 120 ballistic-missile interceptors every month during the coming winter. On October 24, Kyiv Post reported Zelenskyy as saying Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the United States over the previous three months. The arithmetic is sobering for decision-makers in Kyiv. At 100 interceptors a month, 500 missiles would last five months; at 120 a month, about four months. These are illustrative calculations, not forecasts, since they assume all 500 missiles are available on day one and that consumption remains constant. Actual usage would depend on the number and type of incoming missiles, the number of operational Patriot batteries and the availability of other air defence systems. Not every Russian missile needs a PAC-3 MSE, and using these scarce, expensive interceptors against threats that cheaper systems can handle would only deplete stocks faster. PAC-3 Edge: The capability bet Lockheed Martin's answer is a new variant called the PAC-3 Edge, a more capable future interceptor for the Patriot family. This variant is intended to improve range, altitude and manoeuvrability over the current MSE version. The planned changes include a new seeker, an upgraded control system and a more advanced solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman. It is aimed at more sophisticated threats, including advanced ballistic and hypersonic missiles. Lockheed Martin has said testing is expected to begin in 2027, with initial deployment targeted for 2031. These are programme targets, not proof that the missile is ready. The company plans to build Edge on its existing PAC-3 production line in Camden, Arkansas, with factory modernisation supporting the transition. It says production of the new missile could rise as MSE output tapers off, while retaining the ability to increase production when demand spikes. Steelfin: The volume bet Missiles such as the Steelfin would tremendously improve the air defence lsituation for the US and its partners across the world. Against this backdrop, the American defence industry is pursuing two different answers. The first came on October 12, when Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of modular surface-to-air missiles. The idea behind the missile is to build a common airframe, avionics, software, flight controls and interfaces, and then vary the booster and terminal-stage components to suit the threat. This family of missiles is meant to cover missions ranging from point defence against aerial threats to lower-tier air and missile defence and some ballistic missile defence roles, with compatibility planned for existing launchers such as the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System (VLS) deployed across US Navy ships and selected Patriot-related equipment. The most consequential claim is about scale. Anduril says it is planning near-term production of several thousand missiles a year, with capacity that can shift towards whichever variant is in demand. The US-based firm has not disclosed a detailed production schedule or contract quantities, and flight testing of Steelfin variants is planned for 2027. The cost comparisons the company has made against more expensive interceptors are likewise company claims, not independently demonstrated results. The logic of modularity is simple: If one design can be adapted for different missions, the manufacturer needs fewer separate production processes and can move between variants without building a new production line. But commonality does not remove every bottleneck. Different seekers, rocket motors and terminal stages still need to be qualified and tested. The bigger lesson Air defence forces need enough missiles to sustain operations and interceptors capable enough to defeat the hardest threats. A cheaper, high-volume interceptor could help preserve the most advanced weapons for targets that require them, while an improved top-end missile would widen the range of threats that can be engaged. The PAC-3 MSE is the only one of the three that is operational today. Steelfin and Edge are both in development, and neither will help Ukraine this winter. That is the larger point: The Patriot shortage is as much a question of industrial speed as it is of money or political will. The capacity expansion from roughly 600 to 2,000 missiles a year is significant, but it will take years to build, while missiles are being used up now. For Ukraine, the near-term question is whether its partners can release interceptors from existing stocks while an expanded production base catches up. The number that matters most is not what a company says it can eventually build, but how many working interceptors it can deliver each month, how fast that rate can rise, and how much of that output reaches the places where it is urgently needed.

title: Trump blocking Russia curbs historic moment: Putin envoy
text: Russian President Putin and US President Trump US President Donald Trumpâs decision to waive a new package of sanctions on Russia is a âhistoric momentâ, a Russian presidential envoy said Saturday. The Kremlin and Putin ââ who appeared in military uniform Friday and said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine ââ have not yet reacted to the move, which is a major diplomatic win for Russia. Dmitriev said the act would have caused âserious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global marketsâ. "I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies that are happening not just because of Iran and not just because of the Straits of Hormuz, but increasingly because of the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, and because of the war with Ukraine and Russia, where energy infrastructure is being hit, and so that's having an impact on global prices as well," he said. title: Trump votes in Florida midterms, defends controversial ad, doubles down on Iran war

title: Trump calls Ukraine attack on Russian oil refineries 'a disgrace', irks Zelenskyy
text: Donald Trump had called for a new Ukrainian president while defending a diesel supply deal with Russia. European leaders are preparing to reassure Ukraine of their continued support as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets them in Brussels, with Kyiv facing intensifying Russian attacks, uncertainty over US assistance and mounting financial needs ahead of winter. The summit comes amid fresh tensions between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Ukraine's fresh attacks on Russian oil refineries and accused Kyiv of driving up global energy prices. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy infrastructure, an announcement that took Zelenskyy by surprise last weekend. Trump reiterated his criticism after Ukraine struck a refinery southeast of Moscow that helps supply the Russian capital. "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet. The Ukrainian president, meanwhile, said there was little indication that Moscow was ready to end the war and warned that Kyiv needed to prepare for the coming winter. "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter," Zelenskyy said as he arrived at the summit. "The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defence and funding," he said, adding that he would discuss Ukraine's requirements for the rest of this year and 2027. Ukraine seeks billions in military aid Financial and military assistance is expected to feature prominently in discussions as Kyiv faces a substantial funding shortfall. Zelenskyy told Reuters earlier this month that Ukraine had agreed on a plan with European partners to cover a $27 billion deficit in military spending this year, allowing it to order drones needed to sustain its war effort into early 2027. However, finance minister Sergii Marchenko recently said Ukraine still faced an unfunded budget gap of $32.6 billion for next year. That figure does not include an estimated $40 billion in direct military supplies expected from allies. Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten expressed disappointment at the level of new financial commitments made by European countries, while indicating that further military assistance could be announced. "I am unhappy with the number of countries that have been willing to pledge new financial support to Ukraine. But we will see several countries pledging more military support soon," Jetten said. He added that the discussions would focus on helping Ukraine navigate the diplomatic challenges and withstand the winter. "Today will be more about talking to Zelenskyy about how to deal with the complex diplomatic situation that has arisen and how to survive the winter." Jetten also criticised Trump's language towards Ukraine, arguing that Washington had a stake in helping Kyiv defend itself. "This is not the right language. It is also in the interest of Trump to defend Ukraine in this war," he said when asked about the US president's latest remarks. Russian attacks deepen Ukraine's winter concerns Russian continues to target Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, increasing concerns over the country's ability to maintain electricity supplies as temperatures fall. Drone attacks on Kharkiv killed three people, according to local authorities. Strikes in the Volyn region, which borders Poland, left 370,000 people without electricity, while emergency power cuts were introduced in Kyiv during Russian attacks, private energy provider DTEK said on X. Russia, however, has played down the impact of Ukraine's attacks on its oil infrastructure. President Vladimir Putin said the strikes had caused "nothing particularly significant". Moscow has also placed local assets belonging to French, German, Swedish and Dutch companies under temporary management, a move described as retaliation for the European Union's support for Ukraine. The dispute over energy infrastructure has added another complication for European leaders, who are already grappling with higher energy prices following the war involving Iran. EU leaders criticised Trump's proposed arrangement concerning diesel supplies, while divisions over the energy crisis emerged among member states at the summit on Thursday. Belgian prime minister Bart De Wever warned that Ukraine's funding needs would remain substantial even with the support already pledged by Europe. Zelenskyy, he said, "will probably look everybody straight in the eye and say, thank you for the 90 billion, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing." De Wever said European governments would need to decide whether they were prepared to sustain their commitments. "So are you, as a European family, still willing, ready and able to put your money where your mouths are and support Ukraine and keep Ukrainian society and Ukrainian defence up and running?" he said. Trump weighs sanctions relief as tensions grow The uncertainty surrounding US support extends beyond Trump's criticism of Ukraine's military strategy. A US official said on Wednesday that the administration was considering easing sanctions on vessels belonging to the so-called shadow fleet, which has transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia. The possibility of sanctions relief has added to European concerns over Washington's approach to Moscow, particularly as Ukraine continues to rely on Western intelligence, weapons and financial assistance. With Russian attacks continuing and Ukraine preparing for another winter of war, Zelenskyy's Brussels visit is expected to focus on securing the support needed to sustain the country's defence and keep essential services running into 2027. title: Kyiv apologises again as Russia diverts Ukrainian drones into Baltic states; what is GPS spoofing
text: Russia has increased the number of GPS spoofing antennae in its Kaliningrad exclave from three in early 2025 to 36 now, Darius Kuliesius, deputy head of Lithuania's communications regulator said. Ukraine apologised to Lithuania on Sunday after its drones may have strayed into Lithuanian airspace during an operation against Russian military targets. Ukraine's foreign ministry said the incident may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare. The apology comes amid repeated drone incursions into Baltic airspace and Lithuania's warning that Russia can falsify GPS signals across a radius of up to 450 km from its Kaliningrad exclave. "We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia," spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X. "We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused. We are committed to sharing all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident." An earlier version of Tykhyi's post also mentioned Latvia. Watch Ukraine Hits Putinâs Baltic Fuel Hub Days After Trump Moves To Bring Russian Diesel Back To Market Russia expands GPS spoofing network near Baltic states Russia has increased the number of GPS spoofing antennae in its Kaliningrad exclave from three in early 2025 to 36 now, Darius Kuliesius, deputy head of Lithuania's communications regulator, told Reuters on Tuesday. Kaliningrad is a heavily militarised Russian territory between NATO members Lithuania and Poland on the Baltic coast. Kuliesius said Russia's GPS spoofing capability could reach up to 450 km from the exclave. "The occasional interference began with the 2023 NATO summit in Vilnius. Now they have built up the infrastructure and the interference has become systemic, permanent, unending Russian provocation against European security," Kuliesius said. A map from Lithuania's regulator indicated that the interference could reach across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, most of Poland, and parts of Finland, Sweden and Belarus, as well as the Baltic Sea. The regulator estimated the range by analysing disturbances in aviation surveillance ADS-B transmissions, Kuliesius said. Russia has frequently denied accusations of electronic interference. The Russian embassy in Vilnius did not immediately respond to a request for comment. What is GPS spoofing? GPS spoofing involves broadcasting false GPS signals to confuse navigation systems. Kuliesius said Russia's expanded antenna network could falsify signals across a radius of up to 450 km from Kaliningrad. The interference has also affected mobile phone networks near Kaliningrad, degrading their quality on some frequencies, Kuliesius said. He added that spoofing and jamming intensify during Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia. "Online bus schedules in Klaipeda stop working during the spikes, because they rely on tracking buses by GPS", he said, referring to a town 50 km from the Kaliningrad border. Most modern passenger aircraft and major airports have a variety of navigation tools available if GPS encounters problems. NATO jet shoots down suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia On May 19, a Romanian NATO fighter jet shot down a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia after it entered the country's airspace from Russia, the Estonian military said. The drone entered southeastern Estonia around noon local time and was shot down at 12.14 pm with a single missile. "The incident occurred under the conditions of heavy electronic warfare, including GPS spoofing and jamming, by Russia," the Estonian military said. NATO confirmed that a Romanian jet had shot down a drone over Estonian airspace and said an investigation was under way. It also said the alliance was ready and able to respond to potential air threats. Latvia issued an air threat alert on the same day after a drone entered its airspace. Residents near the Russian border were told to stay indoors, while NATO Baltic Air Policing jets were summoned to the area. The alert led to train suspensions, the stoppage of national examinations for ninth-grade students and the closure of grocery shops, according to local media reports. It was not immediately clear whether the drone that entered Latvia was the same one reported in Estonia or a separate aircraft. Both Baltic countries blamed the incursions on Moscow and said Ukraine had the right to strike Russian military targets to weaken Russia's ability to wage war. They stressed that they had not allowed Ukraine to launch attacks on Russia from their territories. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the previous week that Ukraine would send experts to Latvia to help protect its skies. Previous GPS interference affected European leaders' flights Last year, a Spanish military jet carrying Defence Minister Margarita Robles experienced GPS disruption near Kaliningrad. A plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was also jammed while travelling to Bulgaria. Estonia and Finland have also blamed Russia for jamming GPS navigation devices in the region's airspace. On May 15, Finnish authorities warned of suspected drone activity in the country's capital region. Helsinki airport suspended traffic for three hours, while the Finnish defence forces scrambled fighter jets and other emergency services. No drones were eventually found. Since March, several Ukrainian military drones have strayed into the airspace of NATO members Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, all of which border Russia. Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russia, including around the Baltic region. The Latvian government resigned the week before the May 19 incidents over its handling of the drone incursions.

title: âThey both want it to endâ: Trump denies US halted sharing intel with Ukraine
text: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday denied that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine and said he was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Addressing reporters before departing for a campaign in Alaska, Trump said both countries wanted the conflict to end but did not know how to reach that point. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market. Because the world market suffers from high prices. Asked whether Russia had violated the energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, Trump declined to give an immediate assessment. "I'll let you know about that later," he said. title: 'Game of Thrones' actor Nikolaj Coster-Waldau spends night in Kyiv Metro amid Russian air raid threat

title: Defence, space & nuclear energy: PM Modi, Poland's Tusk bat for deeper ties, doubling trade by 2030
text: PM Modi reaffirms support for peace in Ukraine, West Asia as India and Poland deepen strategic ties NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday reaffirmed India's commitment to supporting peace efforts in Ukraine and West Asia during bilateral talks with his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk, as the two countries agreed to deepen cooperation across strategic sectors amid growing global instability. The leaders held wide-ranging talks at Hyderabad House in New Delhi, exploring avenues for cooperation in defence, space, nuclear energy, critical minerals, green technologies and artificial intelligence (AI). They also discussed regional and global developments and agreed to work towards doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Tusk is on a three-day visit to India amid renewed international efforts to end the war in Ukraine. India, Poland to deepen strategic cooperation Announcing the decisions taken during the talks, PM Modi said India and Poland would expand cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy, while encouraging Polish companies to participate in joint projects. Watch Polish PM Tusk hails ties with India, calls PM Modi a 'friend' "Today we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space, and nuclear energy. We invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India in all these strategic areas," PM Modi said. "In critical minerals and coal gasification too, we will develop new partnerships with Polish expertise," he added. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said the discussions aimed to build on the strategic partnership established between the two countries in 2024 and expand cooperation across several areas. "A new phase in the India-Poland Strategic Partnership. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland held wide-ranging talks today. Building on the Strategic Partnership established in 2024, the leaders explored new avenues of cooperation in areas including AI, green technologies, critical minerals and defence, while further deepening ties in trade, investment, education, culture and people-to-people exchanges. " The two leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to a rules-based international order and reforms of global institutions, including the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). India, Poland aim to double bilateral trade by 2030 PM Modi highlighted the growing economic engagement between the two countries, describing India and Poland as emerging centres of growth, technology and innovation amid global uncertainty. "The world is going through a period of uncertainty and change. Even at this time, both India and Poland are emerging as important centres of growth, technology, and innovation," he said. He said the growing economic strength of both countries had created new opportunities for bilateral cooperation, with the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) expected to further expand trade and investment. "And the India-European Union free trade agreement has further expanded these opportunities. Upon entry into force, this agreement will open up new opportunities for exports of machinery, chemicals, plastics, and engineering goods from India to Poland," he said. "Additionally, we will attract new investments from Poland in sectors such as railways and mobility, advanced manufacturing, food processing, and biotech," he added. PM Modi also expressed confidence that the two countries would work together to develop trusted global supply chains and achieve their shared goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030. The MEA underlined the importance of the India-EU FTA in strengthening economic engagement. "Both leaders agreed to work together to double bilateral trade by 2030. The leaders underscored the importance of the India-EU FTA, which is set to unlock new opportunities for businesses and industries, giving fresh impetus to economic engagement. The two leaders also exchanged views on regional and global developments, reaffirming their commitment to a rules-based international order and reform of global institutions, including the UN Security Council," it said in a statement on X. PM Modi recalls shared history of India-Poland ties PM Modi said the friendship between India and Poland was rooted not only in diplomatic relations but also in a shared legacy of humanity and compassion. "During World War II, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur sheltered thousands of Polish children and families in India. Poland also extended this spirit of humanity by supporting the safe return of our students from Ukraine in 2022," he added. Jaishankar calls on Polish Prime Minister Earlier on Thursday, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met Tusk and discussed ways to deepen cooperation between India and Poland across various sectors. "Pleased to call on Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland. Appreciated his sharing thoughts on deepening India-Poland cooperation across a wide range of domains," Jaishankar said in a post on X. Tusk on three-day visit to India Tusk arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday evening for a three-day official visit aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation in defence, trade and strategic sectors. He was received at the airport by Union Minister of State for Food Processing Industries and Jal Shakti Raj Bhushan Choudhary. Welcoming the Polish leader, the MEA said the visit would provide fresh momentum to bilateral ties. "A warm welcome to Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland on his arrival in New Delhi. He was received at the airport by MoS Raj Bhushan Choudhary. The visit will provide fresh impetus to the India-Poland Strategic Partnership and further deepen our longstanding ties," the MEA posted on X. title: Russia detains Japanese journalist for spying on strategic island
text: A person watches a news feed running a Russia's FSB security service footage of the operation to detain a Japanese journalist accused of espionage, on a smartphone in Moscow on Oct 13 Russia has detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, accusing him of gathering information about the country's defence capabilities on the far eastern island of Sakhalin, amid strained relations between Moscow and Tokyo over the Ukraine war and a longstanding territorial dispute. According to The Guardian, Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said the journalist, who works for Japan's Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was detained in the Sakhalin region. Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified him as Imai Yuki and alleged that he had been conducting espionage on Russian territory. The charges carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. The FSB alleged that the journalist collected and stored information about Russia's defence capabilities for transfer to Japanese intelligence. He was subsequently transferred to Moscow, where a court ordered his pre-trial detention. Zakharova criticised Tokyo, saying the use of foreign correspondents to gather information that could undermine Russian security was regrettable. She warned that the arrest would further strain relations between the two countries. Japan's embassy in Moscow said the government was seeking to establish the circumstances of the journalist's reported detention. His newspaper, Hokkaido Shimbun, was also verifying the details. Sakhalin Island lies in Russia's Far East, north of Japan's Hokkaido island and west of the Kuril Islands, a chain extending towards Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The region provides access to key maritime routes and the Sea of Okhotsk, which is important to Russia's Pacific naval operations Russia-Japan ties strained over Ukraine war and territorial dispute Russia and Japan have seen relations deteriorate since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Tokyo joined Western sanctions against Russia, prompting Moscow to designate Japan as an âunfriendlyâ country. Russia has repeatedly criticised Japan's support for Kyiv and its alignment with Western security policies. The two countries also remain locked in a territorial dispute over four islands in the Kuril chain, controlled by Russia but claimed by Japan as the Northern Territories. The dispute dates back to the final days of the Second World War and has prevented the signing of a formal peace treaty between the two countries. The islands hold strategic importance because of their location between the Sea of Okhotsk and the North Pacific, giving Russia a crucial position in the region. Tensions intensified in August when Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Iturup, one of the disputed islands, prompting protests from Tokyo. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
