title: Russia sold Alaska for peanuts. Now it guards America against Moscow
text: Neither side could have foreseen how dramatically Alaska's economic and military importance would grow. Look at a map of the world and Alaska seems out of place. It belongs to the United States, yet sits apart from the rest of the country, separated by Canada and facing Russia across the narrow Bering Strait. How did this vast territory become a part of America? In 1867, the Russian Empire sold Alaska to the United States for $7.2 million in gold. Covering nearly 600,000 square miles, the territory cost the Americans less than two cents an acre. In hindsight, it looks like one of the greatest real-estate bargains in history. But the deal was more than a cheap purchase of land. For Russia, Alaska was a remote and expensive colony that had become increasingly difficult to defend. For the United States, it was an opportunity to expand its territory and influence in the North Pacific. The Alaskan timeline. Neither side could have foreseen how dramatically Alaska's economic and military importance would grow. More than a century and a half later, the sale remains a striking example of how a decision shaped by the strategic calculations of one era can transform the balance of power in another. A colony that never paid its way Russia's story in Alaska began with exploration. In 1741, expeditions led by Vitus Bering and Aleksei Chirikov reached the territory, paving the way for fur traders to venture across the North Pacific. Their principal prize was the sea otter, whose valuable pelts fuelled a lucrative trade. The business came at a heavy cost to Alaska's Indigenous peoples. According to the US National Park Service, Russian traders, known as promyshlenniki , often coerced Aleut and Alutiiq people into hunting sea otters and supplying provisions. In 1799, Tsar Paul I consolidated Russian trading operations under the Russian-American Company, granting it a monopoly over trade in Russian North America and responsibility for administering the colony. Intensive hunting soon depleted sea-otter populations around the early settlements, forcing the company to seek resources elsewhere. The declining fur trade, however, was only part of the problem. Alaska lay thousands of miles from Russia's political and industrial centres. Transporting food, supplies and people across such distances was expensive and difficult. The US National Archives notes that the Russian-American Company depended on substantial subsidies from an imperial treasury already under strain. Russia's presence in the territory was also limited. According to the US Department of State, the permanent Russian settler population never exceeded 400, with imperial authority concentrated in coastal settlements and trading posts. Maintaining Alaska was costly. Defending it against a determined foreign power could prove costlier still. The fear of losing it for nothing The decisive argument for selling Alaska was strategic. Three factors behind the 1867 decision. The Crimean War of 1853â1856 exposed the limits of Russian military and naval power. Britain, one of Russia's principal adversaries in the conflict, controlled neighbouring British North America, much of which would later become Canada. Russian officials feared that another war with Britain could leave Alaska vulnerable to seizure. If that happened, Russia might lose the colony without receiving a penny in compensation. The idea of selling the territory had been gaining support for years. In 1857, Grand Duke Konstantin Nikolayevich, the younger brother of Tsar Alexander II, argued that Russia should dispose of its North American possessions before the United States acquired them anyway. The Library of Congress identifies him as a leading advocate of the sale within the imperial court. Russia offered Alaska to the United States in 1859, according to the US State Department, but the American Civil War put negotiations on hold. Once the war ended, talks resumed, with Russia increasingly inclined to part with its distant colony. The empire also had other priorities. It was consolidating its position in mainland Asia, including the Amur region and the Pacific coast. These territories were more closely connected to Siberia and offered greater opportunities for settlement, economic development and military expansion. In December 1866, Alexander II and his senior officials decided to proceed with the sale. The transaction promised immediate revenue, relieved Russia of the expense of defending an exposed possession and reduced the danger of Alaska falling into British hands. Transferring it to the United States would also strengthen an emerging Pacific power whose interests could help counterbalance Britain. For Russia, the calculation was straightforward: better to sell Alaska than risk losing it in a future war. A deal struck overnight The negotiations brought together two key figures: US secretary of state William H. Seward and Eduard de Stoeckl, Russia's minister in Washington. President Andrew Johnson supported the acquisition, while Alexander II authorised the transfer. According to the US National Archives, the negotiations advanced rapidly in March 1867. After an overnight session, Seward and Stoeckl signed the treaty at about 4am on March 30. The agreed price was $7.2 million in gold. Based on the commonly cited area of 586,412 square miles, or approximately 1.519 million square kilometres, that amounted to roughly 1.9 cents an acre. The US Senate approved the treaty on April 9. The United States ratified it on May 28, and the two countries exchanged ratifications on June 20. Alaska was formally transferred at Sitka on October 18, 1867. The transaction redrew the map of North America. Yet the people who had lived in Alaska for generations had no say in the decision. Indigenous communities were neither consulted nor represented in the negotiations. From ' Seward's Folly ' to an American prize The purchase initially attracted scepticism in the United States. Critics mocked it as "Seward's Folly" and "Seward's Icebox", questioning why Washington would spend millions on a distant, icy territory that appeared to offer little economic return. But the familiar story of a nation united in opposition to the deal may be overstated. In a 2019 article in Western Historical Quarterly , historian Michael A. Hill argued in "The Myth of Seward's Folly" that the extent of public hostility to the purchase has been exaggerated. Transfer of Alaska. Subsequent discoveries gave Alaska a very different reputation. The Klondike gold rush began after gold was discovered in Canada's Yukon in 1896. According to the National Park Service, more than 100,000 people headed towards the goldfields between 1897 and 1900. Many passed through the Alaskan ports of Skagway and Dyea, stimulating commerce, settlement and transport infrastructure. Although the original Klondike deposits lay across the Canadian border, major gold discoveries followed within Alaska, including at Nome and Fairbanks. Oil transformed the territory's fortunes again. The discovery of the Prudhoe Bay oilfield in 1968, followed by the opening of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline in 1977, established Alaska as a major source of American crude. The US Energy Information Administration reports that the state's oil production peaked at more than two million barrels a day in 1988. At the end of 2024, Alaska held approximately 3.1 billion barrels of proved crude-oil and lease-condensate reserves, according to the agency's figures. The territory's military value also became increasingly apparent. During the Second World War, Japanese forces occupied Attu and Kiska in the Aleutian Islands, bringing the conflict to American territory. Alaska also served as a transfer route for US aircraft delivered to Soviet crews under the Lend-Lease programme. During the Cold War, Alaska's position along the shortest northern approaches between the Soviet Union and North America made it central to early-warning radar, air defence and military surveillance. The bargain had become much more than a bargain in land. Alaska was emerging as an economic asset and a strategic outpost on the edge of two competing powers. Still, judging the 1867 decision solely by what followed would be misleading. Russia could not have known the scale of Alaska's future oil wealth or anticipated how developments in military technology would transform the Arctic. Nor does the territory's subsequent value prove that selling it was irrational at the time. The sale made sense within the constraints Russia faced: a distant colony, mounting costs and the risk of losing it to a rival without compensation. The United States, meanwhile, acquired a territory whose economic and military significance would become clearer over the decades that followed. Two rivals, 55 miles apart The sale did not create the rivalry between Russia and the United States. But it placed American territory directly opposite Russia's far eastern frontier, giving that rivalry a distinctive geography. At their closest points, mainland Alaska and mainland Russia are separated by roughly 55 miles, or 89 kilometres. The Russian-owned Big Diomede and American-owned Little Diomede islands lie much closer together, separated by approximately 2.5 miles, according to the National Park Service. That proximity makes Alaska central to US homeland defence and Arctic operations. The Pentagon's 2024 Arctic Strategy describes the region as a northern approach to the United States and emphasises missile warning, surveillance, communications and military readiness. Alaska hosts missile-defence interceptors, radar installations, fighter aircraft and military bases supporting operations across the Arctic and North Pacific. The strategic tension is visible in the skies above the region. On July 24, 2024, the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) detected and intercepted two Russian Tu-95 bombers and two Chinese H-6 bombers flying together in the Alaskan Air Defence Identification Zone. NORAD said the aircraft remained in international airspace. Entering an air defence identification zone is not, by itself, a violation of national sovereignty, but such flights require monitoring because of their potential military significance. The Arctic's economic importance is growing as well. According to the Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment working group of the Arctic Council, the number of unique vessels entering the Arctic Polar Code area rose 37 per cent between 2013 and 2023, from 1,298 to 1,782. The total distance sailed increased by 111 per cent to 12.9 million nautical miles. Changing sea-ice conditions and resource projects, including Russia's Yamal gas development, have contributed to the increase. Moscow views the Northern Sea Route along its Arctic coastline as both an economic corridor and a strategic asset. Yet the growth in shipping should not be mistaken for an imminent transformation of global trade. Ice, inadequate port infrastructure, insurance costs and the difficulty of mounting emergency responses continue to constrain navigation through Arctic waters. Alaska's importance extends beyond military deployments and shipping lanes. It has also become a venue for high-level diplomacy. Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump met at Joint Base ElmendorfâRichardson in Anchorage on August 15, 2025, to discuss the war in Ukraine and broader bilateral relations. The summit ended without a signed peace agreement. Putin has occasionally addressed the historical question of Alaska's transfer with apparent nonchalance. During a televised question-and-answer session in 2014, when asked about the possibility of Russia reclaiming the territory, he responded: "Why do you need Alaska?" He also told the questioner not to get worked up about it. In January 2026, while discussing Trump's interest in Greenland, Putin again referred to Alaska as a historical sale that had already been completed. The bargain that changed sides In 1867, Alaska was a remote possession that Russia struggled to maintain and feared it might lose. Today, it is a major American military platform facing the Russian Far East, a gateway to Arctic waters and a critical component of the defence of North America. The $7.2 million purchase looks extraordinary when measured against the territory's subsequent mineral wealth, oil reserves and strategic importance. But its deeper significance lies in the contrast between what the two empires could see in 1867 and what the world would come to see in Alaska later. Russia sold a vulnerable colony to reduce its financial and military risks. The United States acquired a vast frontier whose value expanded with the discovery of natural resources, the rise of air power and the growing strategic importance of the Arctic. It was not necessarily Russian folly. It was a calculation made under the pressures of its time. The irony is that the very geography that once made Alaska difficult for Russia to defend now makes it indispensable to the United States. What Moscow saw as a costly outpost became Washington's front line in the Arctic, and a reminder that the value of territory can change far more dramatically than the borders drawn around it. title: No Patriot missiles for Ukraine? Trump holds up transfer as tensions with Zelenskyy rise
text: The development adds to a growing rift between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump repeatedly criticising Zelenskyy The Donald Trump administration has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine from countries that have already acquired the American-made weapons, The Washington Post reported. This comes as tensions between the POTUS and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy deepen. The delay comes as Kyiv faces intensified Russian missile and drone attacks and warns that its stockpile of interceptors is running dangerously low. The development adds to a growing rift between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump repeatedly criticising Zelenskyy, easing pressure on Moscow and questioning Ukraine's leadership. The strain has also extended to military communications and intelligence support, raising concerns that the shifting US approach could weaken Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russia. Watch Russia Batters Ukraineâs Energy Grid; Kyiv Plunged Into Darkness As 550,000 Households Lose Power According to The Washington Post, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has neither formally rejected the proposed missile transfers nor completed the necessary steps to approve them. The report, citing a US official and three people familiar with the diplomatic exchanges, said Hegseth had continued to authorise some other forms of US assistance to Ukraine. Also Read: Snow On Fire: Ukraineâs Winter Of Reckoning Ukraine running low on Patriot interceptors The United States retains control over the transfer of its weapons to third countries under agreements requiring Washington's approval before they can be passed on to another recipient. This means countries seeking to send their Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine need clearance from the US administration. A Ukrainian official told The Washington Post last week that only a couple of interceptor missiles remained in the country's stockpile. Zelenskyy also told lawmakers during a briefing on Monday that Ukraine had "almost no Patriot interceptors left from the United States" and alleged that the Pentagon was delaying missiles that Kyiv's partners had already paid for. The shortage comes as Russia continues to target Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine had again received no advance warning from partners, including the US, about the latest Russian attacks. He said six people were killed, including a mother and her child, who was just over a year old. Washington has maintained that it has not stopped providing intelligence to Kyiv. However, separate concerns have emerged over restrictions on Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade satellite communications system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications and drone operations. Moscow welcomes rift but remains cautious The growing confrontation has been welcomed by Russian officials, although Moscow remains wary of Trump's unpredictable approach, Reuters reported. The news agency said Kremlin hardliners had seized on the public dispute, but there was little consensus that the tensions had yet translated into a decisive strategic advantage for Russia. Trump has repeatedly attacked Zelenskyy in recent days and said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Russian Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev mocked the Ukrainian leader on Telegram, while Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued that Zelenskyy's criticism of Trump would have significant consequences. The tensions have coincided with Trump's decision to ease certain restrictions affecting Russian fuel supplies and refrain from imposing additional sanctions on buyers of Russian oil. However, some Russian commentators have questioned whether these moves would deliver substantial benefits to Moscow, with one pro-Kremlin lawmaker suggesting that Trump's decisions were driven largely by domestic political considerations ahead of the US congressional midterm elections. title: US grand strategy falls short of delivering victory in Iran
text: A Patriot missile launcher stands on guard as a B-1 bomber of the US Air Force takes to the air. (Image credit: US DoW) In spite of glaring differences in capabilities of the US-Israeli combine vis-Ã -vis the Iranians, Operation Epic Fury has not led to a victory for the Americans. Somewhere in their planning process, the strategic, political and economic aspects were not enmeshed adequately to arrive at the grand strategy required to achieve victory. A bleak situation has evolved, with Houthis re-entering the fray, and putting under the scanner Saudi Arabiaâs military capabilities. An analysis of the US miscalculations leads to the conclusion, that much as the Americans have achieved militarily, they have not been able to impose their will on Iran. As the shortfalls are studied, itâs also essential to identify major dilemmas that await the Americans at the next turn. American miscalculations impeding evolving of grand strategy Underestimating the Opponents Capabilities. The renowned military thinker Sun Tzu has stated, âIf you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will suffer a defeat.â Incorrect appreciation of the enemy capabilities can be the gravest of flaws in battle. The American assessment of Iranians resilience, especially the ability to absorb loss of top rung leaders, destruction of critical military and industrial capabilities, was flawed. They expected the Iranians to foldup once the decapitation campaign was successful. The resounding success in Venezuela, leading to capture of Maduro in January, 2026, possibly fanned euphoric deductions that proved untenable in Iran. The deduction that simultaneous with a successful decapitation campaign, the Iranians would rise up against an oppressive regime, proved wrong. Iran has a history that goes back thousands of years. It provides the nation a strong foundation and identity. These factors surface sharply to complement national cohesion when a nation is in danger. The US miscalculations are not new, though. When the US led coalition entered Baghdad, Iraq in April 2003, they expected a rousing reception that wasnât quite there. Damage to Global Trade by Denial of Straits. The criticality of Strait of Hormuz was well known before the first American salvoes of missiles, aircraft, drones were released, however, did the Americans evaluate the force required to fully dominate the Hormuz with multi-layered Air Defence cover, physical occupation of its banks, disallowing Iranian minelaying endeavour, and also sustaining such deployment? Further, It doesnât require sinking a super tanker to initiate a spike in freight costs. The insurance companies need barely an assessment of heightened risks to hike their rates. The possibility of Bab el Mandeb further choking global trade wasnât perhaps fully factored into the costs of war. That the Houthis will resurface as a force in being, wasnât possibly fully considered either. US Defence Pacts with Other Nations: The Myths. The US has its bases all over the West Asian region to create a defensive envelope that host countries had mostly taken as an impregnable shield. However, the Iranians have been able to penetrate the shield, fairly successfully. The US bases in the region include those at Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Jordan. These bases have faced Iranian attacks. The faith nations had in the US to be possessing the will and capability to protect allies and partners has been substantially eroded. Disproportionate Costs of Sustaining War. The American economy has produced the worldâs greatest military machine. They have run possibly the best intelligence-based operations that we have witnessed. The flip side of the coin is its cost thatâs straining the worldâs largest economy. When a USD 35,000-dollar UAV of the Iranians triggers the launch of a top end 2.1-million-dollar interceptor of the US Navy, the cost of the war pinches. Admiral Brad Cooper, Commander of U.S. Central Command is on record stating that the Persian Gulf countries are split over their support to a war against Iran. These countries, having allowed the use of the bases to the Americans for striking Iran, invited waves of attacks from the Iranians. Under such circumstances itâs not strange for alliances being stressed, differences arising and well entrenched relationships feeling the tug. Geo Economics: The Tariff Battleground. With a tariff war running the course simultaneously, nations have begun to wonder, which way are geopolitical alliances headed. President Trump has literally opened an economic warfare battlefront against most of the world. The price of a gallon of petrol was already shooting up when his tariff follies hit across geographies for citizens to feel the pinch in procuring their daily bread and butter. Unfazed, the President has turned his guns on old friends like Canada, EU, Quad partner India and many more. In fact, the Canadian story promises to occupy considerable media space, soon. A ding-dong tariff battle is also being witnessed with Trump blowing the whistle for more tariffs today, and taking an U-turn, tomorrow. Road ahead: Issues meriting close calculations American Boots on Ground. As of now, there is no tenable reason to believe that the war will stop very soon. However, the US cannot afford to put boots on ground. The IRGC has displayed adequate tenacity already to deter Trump, hopefully. The US has ordered a heavy escalation for a major assault, post elections. Saudi Arabia has High Stakes. They are the biggest oil exporters and also one of the top importers of weapons, globally. They should be able to take the fight to the Houthis. Reliance on air power alone will not do, and the Mecca agreement will take time to be productive! The World Order. It may witness changes, notwithstanding the results of November, 2026 elections in the US, or the post Trump era. Some old geopolitical alignments are already on crutches, while new ones are developing shoots. Bipolarity is mostly anticipated. The Chinese President Xi Jinping said during his recent visit to the US, â Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and making America Great Again, can go hand in hand. â Russian Decline. Though being often referred to as a declining power, Russia has displayed its ability to stall NATO spreading further East, The expansion of NATO at this stage, needs to be reviewed in-house, keeping in view its triggering an escalation in Ukraine. Most of the world is looking for peace in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon to start with, and deescalation in other conflict-ridden areas. The Iran War is also a loud warning to great powers not to underestimate the middle powers, or even well-armed militias with State backing. They may not be able to tilt the scales decisively, but the can certainly increase the costs disproportionately.
author: Brig. SK Chatterji

title: US has âtwo very different sets of intelligence reportsâ: Trump rules out Sunday strikes on Iran
text: US President Donald Trump ruled out immediate military strikes against Iran on Sunday US President Donald Trump on Sunday ruled out an immediate military strike against Iran, saying Washington had no plans to launch an attack that day, even as conflicting intelligence assessments and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts continued to shape the US approach to Tehran. "Would I tell you that? But the answer is no. There will not be a strike," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Michigan, responding to a question about whether military action against Iran could take place as soon as Sunday. "We have two very different sets of intelligence reports," Trump said, describing the incoming information as "very advanced." Watch Netanyahu Pushes Back At Trump Power Narrative, Denies Israel Needed US Green Light For Iran Strike The president maintained that Washington was doing "well with Iran," although an unnamed US official told Israeli news channel i24NEWS that Trump was prepared to "shift gears on Iran" and that military strikes no longer appeared to be "a question of if, but of when." The remarks came after Trump presented Tehran with a stark choice between reaching a diplomatic agreement and facing further military action. "Do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off? That's the only question," Trump told Fox News, framing the next phase of the conflict as a choice between negotiations and escalating military operations. Despite ruling out a strike on Sunday, Trump has continued to signal that Washington could pursue further military action if negotiations fail to produce an agreement. Trump claims US controls Strait of Hormuz Trump also asserted that American forces had established maritime dominance over the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route and a major point of contention in the conflict with Iran. "Remember, we now control the Hormuz Strait. They get nothing. Yes, we get everything." He maintained that commercial activity through the chokepoint had exceeded pre-war levels and described the US Navy's enforcement of a blockade on Iranian ports and shipping as "unbelievable." On Saturday, Trump had suggested that Washington could either launch fresh military strikes or secure a comprehensive agreement with Tehran. He questioned whether Iran would honour any commitments under a potential deal, while arguing that either outcome would amount to an American victory. Control over the Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of friction in the conflict, which erupted in late February following joint US-Israeli strikes. The confrontation has continued despite a ceasefire and a memorandum aimed at securing a final peace agreement. Trump signals Russia-Ukraine peace talks Turning to the war in Eastern Europe, Trump indicated that high-level diplomatic engagements involving the United States, Russia and Ukraine could take place soon. "We're going to be having some pretty soon, and I think they both want to make a deal," he said, expressing optimism about the prospects of negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv. Trump did not provide further details about the proposed engagements or specify when the talks would take place. On Brazil's presidential election, the US president refrained from endorsing either candidate, saying his administration was "watching" the race. Trump links European unrest to immigration Trump also criticised immigration policies in European countries, linking protests and unrest in France, Italy, Belgium and Spain to what he described as inadequate border enforcement. Contrasting the situation in Europe with US border controls, he claimed that the United States had prevented unauthorised crossings over the preceding 18 months. "I closed the border. You know that we've had zero infiltration," Trump said, asserting that "zero illegal aliens" had entered the country during that period. He also claimed that previous US administrations had allowed millions of people to enter illegally. Referring to his conversations with French President Emmanuel Macron, Trump said he had previously warned the French leader about the consequences of immigration policies. "'You are destroying France. You're letting people come in that hate your country.'" Trump said he had told Macron. He also cited migrant arrivals in Spain as evidence of what he described as wider instability across Europe. Trump accuses Taiwan of taking US chip industry On semiconductor manufacturing and trade, Trump accused Taiwan of taking over the US chip industry through low-cost production, renewing his criticism of the island's position in the global semiconductor supply chain. "They stole our chip business, all of it, 100%, because they made chips at a ridiculous price, and they just pushed them in," Trump said. He argued that stronger executive leadership in Washington could have prevented broader tensions with China over trade and technology. Trump's comments come amid continuing US efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing and address Washington's strategic competition with Beijing. You use AI every day. title: Zelenskyy sounds alarm as Russia hits Ukraineâs energy sites despite Trumpâs ceasefire announcement
text: (Source: Kharkiv prosecutor's office): An explosion from a Russian strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kharkiv Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday accused Russia of continuing to attack Ukraineâs energy facilities despite US President Donald Trumpâs announcement about energy infrastructure ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv. Zelenskyy said Russian strikes had hit a power plant in Kharkiv, a gas production facility and a civilian gas station. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learnt about the purported agreement through media reports. He said Russia had not publicly confirmed its acceptance of the proposal. âWe support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side,â Zelenskyy said. Referring to Trump's announcement on Truth Social, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been âhorribly surprised" by the strikes that followed the US president's post. Watch Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Could Hold Elections If Russia Agrees To 60-Day Ceasefire âIt was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,â Zelenskyy said. Trump had announced the purported agreement on Sunday, saying it took effect immediately but providing few details about its terms or implementation. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready to honour ceasefire In a separate statement on Monday, Zelenskyy reiterated Ukraine's willingness to support the ceasefire and said Kyiv was awaiting details from Washington. He stressed that Russia must also agree to the arrangement for it to work. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said, "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace." Zelenskyy also said Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. He urged Trump to press the Kremlin to agree to the arrangement. Warning of a possible escalation if Russia refused to comply, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would respond if Moscow did not agree to an energy ceasefire during the winter. "We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said. "This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war." Trump had previously announced a similar arrangement that did not result in a lasting halt to attacks. In a social media post on September 14, he said Russia and Ukraine had agreed ânot to hitâ each other's energy infrastructure, but provided no details about the proposal. Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the war, disrupting electricity, heating and water supplies for civilians. Ukrainian officials have described the strategy as âweaponizing winterâ and fear Moscow could intensify attacks as temperatures fall. Ukraine has also targeted Russian energy facilities, including oil refineries deep inside Russian territory. EU chief doubts Russia will honour truce European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Monday welcomed the prospect of a halt to energy strikes, particularly with winter approaching, but questioned whether Russia would respect the arrangement. âWe havenât yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,â Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg. âPersonally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy.â Kallas also pushed back against Trump's comments on Saturday that Ukraine should elect a new president. She said elections should not be held during the war without a ceasefire. Estonian foreign minister Margus Tsahkna questioned Trump's reported deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel amid high fuel prices in the US. Tsahkna said he did not believe the deal âis actually going to change anythingâ in terms of fuel prices, adding that it was âmuch more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S." Ukrainian and European officials have criticised the reported diesel arrangement, arguing that it could help fund Russia's war effort. Zelenskyy says elections impossible during war Zelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine remained impossible while Russian attacks continued, including strikes carried out during the day and night. âUnder such circumstances, itâs impossible to hold elections,â he said. However, he added that he would be ready to work towards holding elections if Ukraine secured a full ceasefire lasting at least 60 days. His remarks came after Trump said on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to have a new president and criticised Zelenskyy for not doing enough to end the war. Russian drone attack kills three in Kharkiv region A Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office. Investigators said the attack took place at around 7.25pm in a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores. It also sparked a fire. Ukraine's Air Force said its air defences had shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones launched overnight into Monday. The attack also involved a Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and included 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Strikes were recorded at 15 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at four sites. Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences had intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian regions, Crimea, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014, and the waters of the Black Sea. In a separate statement, the ministry said Russian forces had carried out overnight drone strikes on unspecified Ukrainian port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Odesa with military cargo on board. title: 'You'll figure it out': Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver as Republicans, Democrats criticise decision
text: US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia, which Congress had overwhelmingly approved for supporting Ukraine US President Donald Trump has defended his decision to exempt Russia from sweeping sanctions under a new law, calling it a âvery good decisionâ amid criticism from lawmakers across party lines. Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida on Saturday evening, Trump said the implications of his decision were not yet fully understood. âA lot of you donât know what my decision is yet, but weâll figure it out, and youâll figure it out,â Trump said, news agency PTI reported. âItâs a very good decision, and itâs going to be a decision thatâs good for the country, and I think good for the world because weâre really at a world stage,â he added. Trump on Friday signed an executive order exempting Russia from a new sanctions measure passed by Congress last month. The order also granted a waiver from 100% tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India. The exemptions will remain in effect until Trump or the secretary of state, in consultation with the treasury secretary and the US trade representative where appropriate, determines that further action is necessary. Lawmakers from both parties criticise Trump Trumpâs decision has drawn criticism from Republicans and Democrats who had supported the legislation, known as the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. Republican Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina questioned the decision, saying she would prefer to maintain pressure on Moscow to end the war and bring down energy prices. âPersonally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down, because I donât trust Putin, and I donât trust Russia,â she said. title: Armyâs Land Warfare Doctrine 2026, released by Rajnath, draws lessons from recent conflicts, stresses on advanced tech, drones, AI, multi-domain ops & Atmanirbharta
text: NEW DELHI: Indian Armyâs Land Warfare Doctrine 2026, released by defence minister Rajnath Singh on Friday, drew lessons from âcontemporary conflictsâ like Ukraine-Russia & Iran-US conflicts and last yearâs Operation Sindoor against Pakistan âwhere unmanned systems, persistent surveillance, contested communications and information warfare have emerged as critical factors on the battlefieldâ. âThe revised doctrine outlined a roadmap for preparing the force for future conflicts characterised by advanced technology, drones, artificial intelligence, precision warfare and multi-domain operations,â sources told TOI. âAligned with Defence Forces Vision 2047, the doctrine emphasises jointness among the armed forces, integration of capabilities across multiple domains and the continued centrality of land power in achieving decisive military and political outcomes,â they said. Rajnath, along with MoS defence Sanjay Seth, Chief of Defence Staff General N. S. Raja Subramani, Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth and defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, launched the new doctrine during the final day of the biannual Army Commanders' Conference. A land warfare doctrine is a high-level military strategy and set of guiding principles that explains how an army prepares for, plans, and conducts combat and security operations on land. The Armyâs doctrine also places considerable emphasis on empowering the soldiers and, man-unmanned teaming as enabler for future conflicts. It also highlights human leadership, resilient logistics and the ability to operate effectively even in technologically-contested environments. The doctrine provides commanders the flexibility to adapt operational approaches according to the threat, terrain and mission requirements. A key focus of the doctrine is on Atmanirbharta and a whole-of-nation approach, recognising the importance of indigenous defence capabilities, national infrastructure and coordination with institutions beyond the military in future wars, they said. Rajnath has been an advocate of Atmanirbharta in defence forces who has time and again stressed that self-reliance directly enhances military capabilities and acts as a force multiplier on the front lines. âThe revised doctrine signals the Indian Armyâs efforts to transform into a future-ready, technology-enabled and adaptable force, capable of fighting and winning wars across the full spectrum of conflict,â the sources told TOI. Alongside the doctrine, the Army is progressing several training initiatives, including a five-year roadmap for multi-domain operations training, a three-level AI skill development programme for officers and a new philosophy to make drone operations a secondary skill across the force. The Armyâs last land warfare doctrine was released in Dec 2018, following the armed forcesâ joint doctrine issued in April 2017. The 2018 doctrine covered the geostrategic environment, different levels of conflict, hybrid warfare, multi-front operations, surveillance, precision strikes, information warfare, space warfare and special forces. It also provided a foundation for developing strategies for India's northern and western fronts. Several developments have changed India's military planning since the previous doctrine was released in 2018. The Army has faced a prolonged stand-off with China along the Line of Actual Control in Ladakh, while conflicts in other parts of the world have demonstrated the growing role of drones, missiles and electronic warfare.

The waterway remains central to concerns over global energy supplies. Before the conflict began in late February, it carried around a fifth of the world's crude oil and natural gas. The sharp reduction in shipping traffic since then has kept supply risks elevated. At the same time, both sides have indicated that the door to negotiations remains open. Iran said contacts with Washington were continuing after talks with Qatari mediators ended without a breakthrough, although revised proposals were put forward. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, cast doubt on whether he would resume threatened military strikes and said an agreement with Tehran was still possible. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government certain powers to pursue peace talks. The competing signals have left oil markets balancing the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough against the threat of renewed military action. Brent had already climbed to a six-month high at the end of October amid concerns over an escalation in the Middle East. High fuel prices are also adding to pressure on Trump to bring the conflict to an end, with the war emerging as a key factor behind rising gasoline costs in the US. Separately, Washington is scheduled to host Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 for discussions on ending the war in Ukraine, post-war security arrangements and de-escalation. title: Russiaâs digital Achillesâ heel? How Ukraine data centre strikes are disrupting daily life
text: Ukraine hits Russiaâs tech nerve centre as data outages disrupt daily life (Representative Image) Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes, exposing the vulnerability of services used by millions of Russians. This comes as Kyiv expands its campaign against Moscowâs technology infrastructure. The attacks, carried out over several days in October, targeted data centres operated by Yandex, Russiaâs largest technology company, followed by a facility owned by Sberbank, the countryâs largest bank. A data centre belonging to technology group VK was also reportedly targeted. Watch Russia Goes After Ukraineâs Battlefield âBrainâ, Claims Strikes On Data Centres Supporting Military Yandex, often described as âRussiaâs Googleâ, provides search, email, navigation, music, ride-hailing, food delivery, cloud computing and digital payment services. Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30 per cent of normal levels following the October 8-11 strikes, The Moscow times reported, quoting internet monitoring group NetBlocks. Disruptions also affected third-party businesses that depend on its infrastructure, with users reporting problems accessing files, ordering taxis and entering residential buildings after digital keys stopped working. Yandex confirmed that one data centre had sustained significant damage, another had been shut down, and a third had suffered infrastructure disruptions. Although access to Yandex Pay was subsequently restored, several people reported that the service displayed an incorrect account balance. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.â State agencies and private businesses relying on Yandex infrastructure, including dating apps and access systems for residential complexes and smart homes, also faced disruptions, The Moscow Times reported. Taxi drivers were also affected. Three drivers told NBC News they could not track their earnings or withdraw their money during the outage. One said the application had displayed error messages and, at times, dispatched multiple cars for a single customer. On October 14, Ukrainian drones struck a Sberbank data centre in the Saratov region. However, the bank said its systems remained operational. âWe confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. Russiaâs digital development minister Maksut Shadayev said officials were working with the defence ministry on measures to protect data centres, according to The Moscow Times. Ukraine has described the strikes as retaliation for Russian attacks on its own digital infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of trying to âleave Ukrainians without the internetâ. The attacks have exposed the risks posed by Russiaâs reliance on a relatively small number of major technology providers. Meanwhile, Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraineâs digital and energy infrastructure. However, Russian data centres were potentially more vulnerable because many are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, whereas Ukraineâs are more widely dispersed. title: Nukes, Netanyahu, and November: Tucker Carlson raises nuclear war alarm for Nth time
text: Tucker Carlson has raised eyebrows with his assertion that Trump might order a nuclear strike on Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site TOI Correspondent From Washington: Somewhere in Washington DC, the nuclear clock is apparently ticking. At least according to Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host and penitent Trump loyalist, who says the U.S President may be hours away from ordering a nuclear strike on Iran under pressure from Benjamin Netanyahu. The target, according to Carlson, is Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified underground complex near Iran's Natanz nuclear facility. âBibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day,â Carlson quoted an âinformed observerâ as saying in a lengthy post on X, claiming that the Israeli PM is âcornered and desperateâ after last weekâs election results, and he canât form a government unless Trump helps him. "The only military option is a nuclear strike," Carlson wrote, alleging that the Trump administration has quietly rewritten the U.S nuclear doctrine since February to make battlefield nuclear weapons easier to use. Carlson also dragged in India, Pakistan, and other nations into his alarmism. A U.S strike, he warned, would unleash radioactive contamination across the Persian Gulf, potentially trigger nuclear escalation involving Russia, India, Pakistan and North Korea, and bring about World War III. "After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final,â he wrote, without explaining why others would get involved. Carlson has been sounding variations of this alarm for months, suggesting that even Armageddon has trouble keeping appointments. The latest post was greeted with ridicule in serious policy circles despite the adventurism of Trump and his MAGA cohorts. Indeed, there is a rather significant gap between the gravity of the claims and the evidence offered to substantiate it. Neither the White House nor the Pentagon has confirmed a change in nuclear doctrine. Carlson identifies no named American official, produces no documentary evidence and relies on anonymous sources for his central claims. Trump himself told Newsmax in October: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to." Still, U.S hardliners have been raising the prospect of an imminent nuclear confrontation with Iran for months, repeatedly drumming up the bogey of Tehran acquiring nuclear weapons within weeks or months. Carlsonâs own interview in March with former National Counterterrorism Center director Joe Kent was revealing. Asked whether Iran had been on the verge of acquiring a nuclear weapon, Kent replied: "No, they weren't three weeks ago when this started, and they weren't in June either. " He also said there was no intelligence indicating that Iran was about to abandon its policy against developing nuclear weapons. The American bogey of Iran getting nuclear weapons within weeks has now acquired a life of its own with one widely circulated meme features an ancient stone tablet supposedly dating to 1750 BC, bearing the inscription: "Iran is only weeks away from developing nuclear weapons." Another version has archaeologists discovering a 3,000-year-old tablet warning that Persia was weeks away from the bomb. Carlson is also accused of having his own agenda in cranking up the nuclear alarm. Once among Trump's most enthusiastic media champions, he has become one of the most consequential dissenting voices within the MAGA movement, and his break with Trump has been particularly pronounced over Israel and Iran. Carlson has argued that America should not subordinate its foreign policy to Israeli interests or be dragged into another Middle Eastern war. He has attacked Netanyahu's influence in Washington, questioned the rationale for American military intervention and challenged the longstanding assumption among Republican conservatives that supporting Israel is an unquestionable article of faith. The nickname "Qatarlson", popularised by his critics, including Laura Loomer and other pro-Israel conservatives, suggests that his criticism of Israel reflects Qatari influence rather than independent conviction. There are also larger ideological divisions at play here. One faction of MAGA believes America First means resisting foreign entanglements, particularly wars undertaken for Israel; another regards unwavering support for Israel as integral to U.S national security and conservative politics. Carlson has become a lightning rod in that battle, with critics accusing him of trafficking in conspiratorial anti-Israel rhetoric, while supporters view him challenging standard establishment thinking. title: âPhysically impossibleâ: Ukraine hits back at Musk over Starlink restrictions, disputes offensive drone strike claim
text: Elon Musk claimed that Ukraine breached Starlink's terms of service by using it for offensive strikes. A Ukrainian defence technology adviser has challenged Elon Musk âs claim that Ukraineâs military breached Starlinkâs terms of service by using the satellite network for offensive drone strikes, prompting SpaceX to restrict access to the high-speed technology. According to CNBC news report, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defence technology, disputed Muskâs explanation in a telegram post on Sunday. He argued that existing operational restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine would have made the type of attacks described by the SpaceX chief technically impossible. title: Trump faces backlash over plans to import Russian diesel ahead of US midterms
text: US President Donald Trump. US President Donald Trump is facing bipartisan criticism over his decision to allow Russian diesel into the US market, as rising fuel prices linked to the Iran war threaten to become a political liability for his Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections. Trump announced on Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by additional shipments in the coming months, to help ease global fuel shortages and bring down prices for American consumers. The move has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties, who argue that easing restrictions on Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with funds to continue its war against Ukraine. Watch 'It Was The Iran War...': Trumpâs Russia Oil Deal âBackfiresâ; Big GOP Revolt Before Midterms? The backlash comes just weeks after Trump signed legislation authorising fresh sanctions and tariffs against countries importing Russian oil and gas. A bipartisan group of seven senators on Sunday urged the president to reverse course, saying the US should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russian forces continue to kill Ukrainian civilians. âCongress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine,â the lawmakers said in a joint statement. The group included Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, along with Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. The US Treasury Department is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7 to facilitate the shipments, according to reports. Other Russian assets, including those held in American banks, remain frozen. What is in the Russia diesel deal? Trump said Russia would release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another one million tonnes thereafter. He also referred to a further three million tonnes to be delivered within a short period, depending on the condition of Russian refineries damaged in Ukrainian attacks. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the figures to state-owned news agency Tass, adding that exports could eventually reach three million tonnes per month. âLower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,â Trump wrote on Truth Social. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the arrangement in an interview with Fox News, saying it would operate through existing legal channels available to the administration to help bring down prices. He rejected claims that the agreement would violate US law. Some Republicans have also backed Trump's approach. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer described it as an example of the president thinking outside the box to address the financial pressure on Americans. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso said the sanctions legislation gave Trump flexibility and additional leverage in dealing with Putin. However, other Republicans have called for tougher action against Moscow. Senator Lisa Murkowski urged Trump to use the new law to increase pressure on Russia rather than allow it to earn additional revenue from diesel exports. Republican Representative Don Bacon also argued that buying Russian fuel was the wrong way to bring down prices. Democrats have been more sharply critical. Representative Steny Hoyer called the deal outrageous, while Representative Bill Keating described it as a disturbing capitulation to Putin. Senator Chris Van Hollen accused Trump of seeking to finance Russia's war against Ukraine after the Iran conflict drove up fuel prices. Fuel prices add to Trump's midterm challenge The dispute comes at a politically sensitive time for Trump, with next month's midterm elections set to determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress. The US-Israel war with Iran, which began at the end of February, has disrupted crude oil supplies and pushed up global energy prices. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for American farmers, ranchers and truckers, who depend on the fuel to operate machinery and transport goods. The average price of diesel in the US stood at $6.28 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association, down from a record $6.53 at the end of September. The rising cost of fuel has added to public dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the economy and the Iran war. Polls indicate that a majority of Americans disapprove of his performance on both issues, putting additional pressure on the administration to demonstrate that it can bring prices down before voters head to the polls. Analysts have questioned whether Russia can deliver the promised volumes and whether the shipments would significantly reduce costs for American consumers. The US consumes approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel per day, meaning the initial 300,000-tonne shipment would account for only a fraction of its daily demand. The deal has also drawn criticism from US allies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a gift to Putin, arguing that the arrangement would provide financial support to Russia while its war against Ukraine continues. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting have also criticised the move, calling for greater pressure on Moscow to end the conflict. Trump announces energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine Amid the controversy, Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an âenergy ceasefireâ, without providing further details. The proposed arrangement would halt attacks on the two countries' energy infrastructure. Zelensky welcomed the announcement but said Kyiv was awaiting details and confirmation from Moscow. âThe Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,â Zelensky wrote on X. He added that Ukraine expected Putin to follow through on Trump's announcement. There was no immediate response from Moscow. The energy ceasefire could offer a potential opening for reducing attacks on critical infrastructure, but the diesel arrangement has exposed divisions in Washington over how to balance domestic economic pressures with the US policy of pressuring Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. With fuel prices weighing on voters ahead of the midterms, Trump faces the challenge of delivering relief to American consumers without further alienating lawmakers who believe his Russia policy risks undermining efforts to end the war. title: India's record oil imports hit 5.6 million bpd as Middle East, Russia supplies rise: Report
text: India's crude oil imports hit a record 5.6 million barrels per day in October, but rising freight costs and competitive Gulf prices could make Russian supplies less attractive NEW DELHI: India's crude oil imports hit a record high of around 5.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, with refiners stepping up purchases from both the Middle East and Russia. While improved supplies through the Strait of Hormuz have boosted Gulf shipments, rising freight costs could make Russian crude less attractive in the coming months, according to energy intelligence firm Kpler. Middle Eastern supplies accounted for about 2.3 million bpd, while Russian shipments remained strong at nearly 2 million bpd, Kpler lead analyst Nikhil Dubey said, as quoted by PTI. The increase in Gulf supplies comes as more crude is moving through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil trade. Higher ship-to-ship transfers helped boost flows through the strait during September and October. Gulf producers are also offering competitive delivered prices to regain market share in India. This could make their supplies more attractive to refiners in the coming months, particularly as the cost of transporting Russian crude rises. However, a shift towards Middle Eastern supplies may depend on how the situation around Hormuz unfolds. "The situation remains volatile, and any renewed disruption to Hormuz flows could see refiners turning back to Russian barrels, even at higher freight costs," Dubey said. The October 16 waiver under the Graham Act could also ease concerns among some Indian buyers about the risks associated with purchasing Russian oil, giving them greater flexibility in sourcing supplies, he added. India imports nearly 90 per cent of its crude oil requirements, making the availability, transportation costs and final landed price of different grades important factors in procurement decisions. How Russia became a key supplier India's dependence on Russian crude rose sharply after Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022. With European refiners turning away from Russian supplies, Moscow offered steep discounts to attract customers. title: UN warns Russian attacks and winter hardship could displace more Ukrainians
text: As winter approaches, Ukraine faces dire challenges with essential services declining due to ongoing conflict. (Pic Credit: Reuters) Millions of Ukrainians are preparing for another difficult winter as attacks on essential infrastructure, damaged homes and escalating living costs increase the risk of further displacement, the United Nations migration agency warned on Friday. With temperatures expected to drop in the coming months, families across the war-torn country are struggling to ensure access to dependable heating, electricity and water after years of conflict, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. The warning comes after Russian missiles and drones targeted Ukrainian cities this week, amid concerns that the United States could reduce intelligence sharing and military assistance to Kyiv, according to the Reuters. âWinter is fast approaching in Ukraine, and for many Ukrainians, the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began,â Dejan Keserovic, IOM deputy chief of mission in Ukraine, told reporters in Geneva via a video link from Kyiv. Millions remain displaced as winter approaches According to the IOM's latest figures, nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced within Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. An estimated 3.8 million people have returned to their homes after being displaced, with many finding their properties damaged or partially destroyed. The agency said people who returned home within the past three months were the most likely to express an intention to leave again, highlighting growing anxiety over deteriorating living conditions. Meanwhile, European countries, including Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic, are currently hosting approximately six million Ukrainian refugees. Keserovic said host countries were expected to prepare for the possibility of another influx of Ukrainians if conditions in their homeland worsened. Russian attacks strain electricity, heating and water supplies Repeated Russian strikes on energy facilities and other critical infrastructure have placed Ukraine's electricity, heating and water networks under increasing pressure, the IOM said. Missile and drone attacks have also continued to kill and injure civilians across the country, adding to the challenges faced by communities already struggling with the effects of prolonged warfare. Access to reliable water supplies has emerged as a particular concern because water infrastructure depends heavily on electricity to function. The IOM said it had installed 31 solar power stations to help keep water systems operational in different parts of Ukraine. However, the agency cautioned that the scale of humanitarian needs remained substantial. Funding shortfall threatens winter relief efforts The UN agency also warned that a shortage of funding could undermine preparations for the approaching winter. Less than 7% of the IOM's Ukraine response plan for 2026 had received funding so far, leaving a significant gap between available resources and the assistance required. The agency stressed the urgent need for additional financial support to improve home insulation and help households withstand freezing temperatures. With damaged housing, unreliable utilities and rising living costs compounding the effects of the war, humanitarian agencies face mounting pressure to ensure vulnerable families can remain safe and warm during the coming months. Its resistance to electronic jamming has made it particularly valuable for military communications, helping Ukrainian forces coordinate operations, guide long-range attack drones and operate drones that deliver supplies to frontline troops. Any sustained disruption could therefore affect battlefield communications, drone operations and the delivery of supplies to troops. title: Rubioâs second India visit: An analysis of the motives
text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio during a Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai (Photo: PTI). US secretary of state Marco Rubio visited India for the second time this year from 20 to 21 October 2026. While strategic analysts have interpreted the visit differently depending upon their focus, its underlying motives need to be examined against the larger canvas of IndiaâUS relations. Notwithstanding the ties witnessing a roller-coaster shift since Feb 2025, the dialogues are continuing at various levels, indicating that both countries perceive that mutual cooperation is needed in the current geopolitical environment. Hence, his visit should be assessed in the context of broader strategic, economic and geopolitical interests shaping the relationship. During PM Modiâs visit to the US in February 2025, several initiatives were taken to deepen ties. These included the US-India TRUST (Transforming the Relationship Utilizing Strategic Technology) initiative, to catalyse government-to-government, academia and private sector collaboration to promote the application of critical and emerging technologies in areas like defense, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum, biotechnology, energy and space, while encouraging the use of verified technology vendors and ensuring protection of sensitive technologies. They also launched the US-India COMPACT (Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce & Technology) for the 21st Century, aimed at pushing transformative change across key pillars of cooperation with a results-driven agenda. Significantly, they expressed the ambition to doubling the bilateral trade by 2030. However, subsequent deterioration in relations exposed the trust deficit and the challenges of mutual expectations. To understand these better, it is essential to revisit past divergences that continue to shape the present. One significant issue was the US approach towards the Indian subcontinent, marked by three key dimensions. First, the USAâs soft approach towards Pakistan (which had joined SEATO and the Baghdad Pact), viewing the latter as an instrument to contain communism in Asia and as a potential influencer on China against Russia, ignoring Pakistan's nurturing of state-sponsored terrorist groups. Trump has a strong liking for the Pak Army Chief, whom Indian analysts hold responsible for the Pahalgam attacks. Second, hyphenating India and Pakistan and trying to influence their bilateral relations. Third, turning a blind eye to Pakistanâs nuclear programme and its proliferation activities. The US also had three concerns. First, soon after Independence, India was seen as being close to communist China and speaking for that country. Second, Indiaâs close relations with the Soviet Union and later with Russia. In the 1990s, India and Russia supported their mutual fight against terrorism as Taliban-controlled Afghanistan became a common security challenge. Third, India opposed the US intervention in Korea, Vietnam and Iraq. Now two more concerns have been added, which relate to mutual expectations. First is Trumpâs claim that he brought an end to the Indo-Pak War after OP Sindoor, while India maintains that no third power was involved and the war came to an end when the Pak DGMO spoke to the Indian DGMO. Significantly, India on the 7th May 2025 declared that it had no intention to prolong the war. Trump continues to claim, and Munir and Shabaz keep on flattering him. Second is the US pressure to stop buying Russian oil, while India maintains that market forces determine Indiaâs purchases. In 2025, Rubio had stated that this was a disturbing factor. The US tariff kept on increasing, and the trade deal appeared to be facing an impasse. There were statements from US officials hurting Indians. An officer of the US stated that the US would not allow India to develop like China, while the reported Vance statement for Indians in the US was severely criticised. The H-1B visa was also a source of concern. Trump administrationâs rhetoric on Indian economy, diaspora and the Russian oil trade was strongly opposed by Indians. Several analysts pointed out that the trajectory of the relationship plummeted to the lowest level in the last two decades. However, the situation changed as the US got concerned over the rising oil prices, particularly when the mid-term elections were approaching. While it had acquired Venezuelan oil, it could mainly be refined at Jamnagar. The refinery there can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products. Reports suggest that Trump has waived the sanctions on the purchase of Russian oil for some time. This is aimed at lowering oil prices and inflation needed for the mid-term elections. It was in this backdrop that Rubioâs second visit took place. While the US Embassy stated that the aim of the visit was to advance the US-India strategic partnership, strengthen commercial and investment ties, and reaffirm the US commitment to a prosperous and secure Indo-Pacific, it was to goad Relaince to purchase more Venezuelan oil, project the US interest in the Quad and indicate that the trade deal is about to be finalised. Besides, Reliance is not only investing in the US but it has a strong sales network covering Europe, which can substantially help the US in selling Venezuelan oil. He called India a refining superpower. Indian analysts felt that it was a damage control exercise. While the details of the actual agreements/understandings are not available, the US readout placed at the Embassy website and Rubioâs statement at the 250th American Independence Anniversary mirrored a changed approach towards India. Rubio pointed out three factors indicating why India is important for the US: it is the most populous country on earth and the oldest democracy and it is a strong geopolitical partner of the US. He also assured that the USAâs ties with Pakistan are not at Indiaâs cost and that the Quad remains a priority. In sum, while the motives of his visit were driven by American economic and geopolitical interests, Rubio reflected that the US was seeking Indiaâs cooperation. It has the potential to improve Indo-US relations if the US administration actually takes steps âto strengthen the Indo-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.â While the trust deficit cannot be reduced in one visit, it appeared to be a step in that direction. However, India need to remain cautious. There is a lesson for India: it must continue to maintain strategic autonomy, diversify its relations and avoid dependence on any one country. title: Russia hits Coca-Cola, McDonald's sites in Ukraine but Donald Trump staying silent

Russian attacks on American businesses operating in Ukraine have damaged facilities linked to Coca-Cola, McDonaldâs and PepsiCo in recent months, raising questions about why the Donald Trump administration has been more vocal in criticising Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure than in condemning attacks on US companies. Zelenskyy said the strike destroyed the warehouse, while McDonaldâs Ukraine confirmed that âa warehouse operated by one of our logistics partners in the Kyiv region was damaged in a drone attack on 25 September.â âAn attack drone â against ordinary food products,â Zelenskyy wrote on X. âThe Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers â for Russia, ordinary life in and of itself is simply a target.â The damage has affected operations at McDonaldâs restaurants in Ukraine, which are now offering a reduced menu. PepsiCo also confirmed in late August that a production facility in the Mykolaiv region had been damaged, although no casualties were reported. Hunder said the attacks were hitting American investors and commercial interests directly. âWe need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors that are being hit and are being targeted,â he said. US response under scrutiny The lack of a strong public response from the Trump administration has drawn criticism from some US lawmakers, including Democrats who have urged the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and condemn Moscowâs actions. However, companies operating in the country have differed over whether to speak publicly about the attacks. A former senior State Department official told CNN that some businesses were reluctant to disclose that their facilities had been targeted repeatedly. âSome businesses do want us to raise this,â Hunder said, adding that others âare treading very carefully.â The American Chamber of Commerce has raised the issue with visiting US lawmakers from both parties and asked them to bring it to the White House. Hunder said the organisation had also sought a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner last month to discuss the condition of American businesses in Ukraine, including the latest attacks. âWe didnât get any response on that,â he said. A White House official said Trump wanted the war to end and that his administration remained committed to efforts to secure peace. âThe president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that weâll ultimately get a peace deal done,â the official said, arguing that the US is âthe only country in the worldâ that can âplay a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end.â Trump had publicly expressed displeasure after a Russian strike on a US electronics factory in August 2025, saying he had told Russian President Vladimir Putin that he was ânot happy about itâ. Contrast with pressure on Kyiv The administrationâs response to attacks on American businesses contrasts with its pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy facilities. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure for rising fuel prices, which have also been driven up by the US-Iran war. CNN reported in February that the administration had warned Kyiv that strikes on a Russian Black Sea oil facility late last year had affected US investments in Kazakhstan. In recent weeks, the US has also threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and ammunition supplies to Ukraine if it continues attacking Russian energy infrastructure, according to sources cited by CNN. Last Friday, Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions and purchase diesel from Russia, despite US law. Hunder said he struggled to understand the administrationâs relative silence on attacks against American companies, particularly given its stated support for US businesses. âAny company, any business, wants to have some sort of protection. You would expect your government to stand up in your corner and fight the fight with you, especially if itâs a foreign military that is attacking the American companies,â he said. The former State Department official told CNN that officials in Washington often believe Ukraine-related discussions should be handled by Witkoff and Kushner, making it difficult for others to draw attention to the attacks. âThe idea that you would get a rationale backâ on why the US was silent about the attacks âis not something that people can expect,â they said. title: Another 'exploding pager' plot? Israel eyes strike on Tehranâs top military bosses
text: Netanyahu holds up pager at UN, recalls Israelâs Hezbollah attack Israel is considering a covert operation modelled on its 2024 exploding-pager attacks against Hezbollah to target Iran's top military and security leadership, potentially eliminating key commanders and disrupting the country's wartime command structure, amid growing uncertainty over the possibility of renewed US-Israeli strikes against Tehran. "According to a report published by the New York Post, former Mossad deputy head of global operations Oded Ailam said Israel could consider a pager-style operation targeting Iran's military establishment, describing the option as 'fully on the table'." Watch Netanyahu's TIME RUNNING OUT? Arab Parties Signal Major Move To Topple Israeli PM After Deadlock He identified four senior figures as the people exercising real power in Tehran, including Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ahmad Vahidi, Basij commander Hossein Taeb, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi and security official Mohsen Rezaei. Ailam argued that Iran's military establishment has emerged as the principal centre of power, with the country's political leadership struggling to maintain control over strategic decisions. He suggested that disagreements between military hardliners and political officials have also complicated Tehran's negotiations with Washington. The proposed operation draws parallels with Israel's September 2024 covert campaign against Hezbollah, widely referred to as Operation Grim Beeper, in which thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies used by the Iran-backed militant group exploded across Lebanon in two successive waves. The first wave began on September 17, 2024, when thousands of pagers used by Hezbollah operatives exploded almost simultaneously across Lebanon, particularly in Beirut's southern suburbs, the Bekaa Valley and southern Lebanon. The following day, September 18, a second wave targeted handheld walkie-talkies used by the group, triggering explosions in several locations, including during funerals. The two attacks killed at least 39 people and injured more than 3,400, according to Reuters. According to Reuters, Hezbollah had ordered approximately 5,000 AR-924 pagers, which were allegedly modified before reaching the group. Explosives were concealed inside the devices, allowing Israeli intelligence to turn ordinary communication equipment into remotely activated weapons. In December 2024, two former Israeli intelligence officers, speaking anonymously to CBS News' 60 Minutes, disclosed further details about the operation. They said the planning had begun nearly a decade earlier with booby-trapped walkie-talkies, while the pager component was developed from 2022 onwards. The report comes amid growing indications that Washington and Tel Aviv are preparing for a possible resumption of military operations against Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections.
