title: Russian strikes kill 12 in Ukraine after Trump announces diesel deal with Putin
text: A recent barrage of Russian airstrikes in Zaporizhzhia claimed at least 12 lives, including those of children. (Pic Credit: Reuters) Russian attacks killed at least 12 people, including three children, in Ukraineâs Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday. The strikes came a day after US President Donald Trump announced an agreement to purchase Russian diesel, a move Kyiv warned could help fund Moscowâs war against Ukraine. Russian aerial bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, leaving at least 14 people wounded, Zelenskyy said. Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange long-range aerial attacks, while their forces remain largely deadlocked along the front line, more than four and a half years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter an intensifying Russian bombardment campaign that has claimed more than 60 lives over the past four days. Trump announced on Friday that he had reached a deal to buy diesel from Russia, marking a significant departure from years of US pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The move also comes as his administration seeks to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. âToday, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,â Zelenskyy wrote on X on Saturday. He said the attacks showed that Moscow interpreted any easing of pressure as an opportunity to continue its military campaign and strike Ukrainian cities. âDifferent signals are needed,â he added. Trump had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call. However, the US president announced the diesel deal on Friday instead. Under the agreement, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes âimmediately thereafterâ, Trump said in an online post. Russia would then deliver another 3 million tonnes âwithin a short period of timeâ. The announcement appeared to contradict a sweeping Russia sanctions law Trump signed last month, which aimed to curb the oil and gas revenues that help finance Moscowâs war against Ukraine. Reacting to the agreement in a lengthy online post on Friday, Zelenskyy warned that Russia would repay the move with âfurther terror and perfidyâ. He argued that the deal amounted to an investment in the war that could prolong the conflict. âIt plays into Russiaâs hands â allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,â he said. title: Oil prices ease as Trump waives Russia sanctions, Middle East risks persist
text: Crude prices ease below $110 per barrel Oil prices fell on Monday as US President Donald Trumpâs decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia raised the prospect of additional fuel supplies entering the market. title: Ukraine's Starlink scare - a cautionary note for India?
text: Ukrainian officials and commentators are alleging that the Starlink restrictions might be connected to Washingtonâs pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes TOI Correspondent from Washington: The raging debate in India over Elon Muskâs bid to muscle Starlink into the country has received a cautionary call after Ukraine reported on Wednesday that its military units suffered disruptions due to unexpected restrictions on Starlink terminals, affecting high-speed connectivity used in combat missions. Ukrainian officials and commentators are alleging that the Starlink restrictions might be connected to Washingtonâs pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. âClearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,â Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military expert who advises President Volodymyr Zelensky on weapons technologies, wrote on a social media platform, as several US lawmakers and European leaders fumed about President Trump appearing to throw Kyiv under the bus after announcing a deal with Moscow to buy diesel. Watch Iran Vows Tougher Starlink Crackdown As Internet Curbs Tighten As Tehran Threatens Violators Starlink, operated by SpaceX (founded by Elon Musk) is a satellite internet constellation that provides high-speed, low-latency broadband internet access in underserved, rural, and remote locations where traditional cable or fiber-optic infrastructure is unavailable or unreliable. Musk and his company SpaceX have rendered matchless service to Ukraine, activating Starlink service to the country within days of the Russian invasion to help hospitals, emergency services and government offices stay connected during the war. By some accounts, Ukraine now has more than 50,000 Starlink terminals. Ukrainian officials are now accusing SpaceX of crippling its drone missions among other effects, although Musk defenders say the restrictions appear to affect only military-grade Starshield, which is operated by the US government and isn't under SpaceX's control. The Trump administration and Starlink have not responded to the charges at the time of writing, but the very possibility illustrates the dilemma facing India of opening itself to a technology controlled by a company â that too owned by a partisan political hack â operating within another countryâs political and regulatory system. Starlink has become a particularly contentious issue after Musk accused Indian business interests of blocking its entry to protect their monopolies, implicitly targeting Reliance Jio chairman Mukesh Ambani. New Delhi has rejected the suggestion that its regulatory framework is discriminatory. Starlink has secured important licences and authorisations but is reported to be awaiting security clearances and spectrum assignment before commercial operations can begin. A report titled Starlink and Risks for India from Takshashila Institution, released in April this year, has raised precisely this point: foreign control of connectivity and data security, and the vulnerability that comes from relying on a foreign private operator. Even ahead of Wednesdayâs developments, the report had noted that Starlink's service availability had been altered or restricted during conflicts (such as in Ukraine) or used to bypass state blockades during civil unrest (such as in Iran), while warning that a foreign corporate decision, technical failure, or external pressure could disrupt critical communications in India during a crisis. For Kyiv, the timing could hardly be worse. Russia launched scores of ballistic missiles and drone attacks against Ukrainian targets this week, striking energy infrastructure and leaving approximately 600,000 people without electricity. The country is heading into another winter under bombardment, with its air defences under enormous strain, and President Trump transparently intent on turning the screws on Kyiv in an effort to end the war, even if it is in Russiaâs terms. title: On eve of visit, Rubio cites India to defend Russia sanction pause
text: Countries like India are partners, need time to figure out right combo: Rubio WASHINGTON: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has defended President Donald Trump's decision to grant a 60-day waiver from sanctions linked to Russia, citing India as important partner to US, and its dependence on Russian energy, warning that imposing tariffs and sanctions simultaneously could have serious consequences for the global economy. Rubio, who will be in India on Monday, said that the US President wants to use a 60-day window to analyse what imposing the tariffs would mean. Watch âOUTRAGEOUS LIE!â: Rubio FIRES BACK At Zelensky Over âFalseâ Claims Of U.S. Costing Ukrainian Lives "These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries - India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said. "You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the US. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added. Rubio said that the US President was also taking into account the changing geopolitical situation since the Lindsey Graham bill was brought into law, especially with the increase in conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia. "I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are that are going on in the world right now," he said. On Friday, Trump invoked Section 115 of Graham Act, which authorises President to waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty under the law. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said in the order. Trump waived the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Act, which allowed him to increase the rate of duty on all goods imported into the United States from Russia to a rate of up to 500% ad valorem (relative to the value). title: Foreign investors withdraw Rs 34,843 crore from Indian stocks; second straight month of selling spree
text: Representational image Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) withdrew Rs 34,843 crore from Indian equities in October, marking the second consecutive month of substantial outflows amid concerns over high crude oil prices, global interest rates and the outlook for corporate earnings. However, foreign investors turned net buyers towards the end of the month, purchasing equities worth around Rs 6,300 crore between October 26 and 30. This followed net withdrawals of nearly Rs 2,700 crore in the week ended October 23, according to data from the Central Depository Services Ltd (CDSL). The latest buying indicates an improvement in near-term investor sentiment, although market experts cautioned that a single week of positive flows does not necessarily signal a sustained reversal. FPI outflows from Indian equities reach Rs 2.95 lakh crore in 2026 Foreign investors had withdrawn Rs 35,861 crore from Indian equities in September. Before that, they invested Rs 20,200 crore in July and Rs 29,631 crore in August. With October's withdrawals, cumulative FPI outflows from Indian equities in 2026 have reached Rs 2.95 lakh crore. Anand K Rathi, co-founder of MIRA Money, said foreign selling remained significant through October, reflecting concerns over elevated crude prices, global interest rates and corporate earnings prospects. âHigher crude prices pose risks to India's inflation and corporate margins, and attractive yields in the US continue to influence global capital allocation,â he said. Rathi added that the sustainability of the recent improvement in foreign flows would depend on greater clarity over global macroeconomic conditions, crude prices and the earnings outlook. He also pointed to the role of domestic institutional investors in absorbing foreign selling and supporting market stability. Fed decision, valuations among factors behind late-month buying FPIs were net buyers in three of the four trading sessions ending October 30 in the cash market, suggesting a possible improvement in their outlook towards Indian equities. VK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments, said the US Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged, attractive valuations in Indian large-cap stocks and signs of sustained domestic economic growth could have contributed to the shift in sentiment. The weakening of the global artificial intelligence trade could also be influencing portfolio allocations, he added. The improvement in foreign investment flows helped the Nifty reclaim the 23,000 mark. Vijayakumar said that while foreign investors continued to sell large-cap financial stocks, they were selectively accumulating pharmaceutical and healthcare shares, along with stocks of certain digital platform companies. Pabitro Mukherjee, deputy vice-president for research at Bajaj Broking, said the reversal in FPI flows was encouraging for market sentiment. Market participants will closely watch the outcome of the US midterm elections in the coming week, along with movements in Brent crude prices, developments in the US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, and quarterly corporate earnings announcements. title: Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's reliance on US tech, Europe admits 'can't replace capability'
text: EU leaders seek alternatives to Starlink as Ukraineâs battlefield communications face risks European Union leaders are grappling with how to reduce Ukraineâs dependence on Elon Muskâs Starlink satellite communications system after disruptions to its services raised concerns about Kyivâs reliance on US-controlled technology for battlefield operations. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe did not have an immediate alternative to the satellite network, which has become essential to Ukraineâs military communications, as leaders gathered for a summit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also in attendance. "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can't replace this capability," Kallas said before the talks. She added that the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked and needed to develop, stressing that the gaps had to be addressed "as soon as possible". The issue has gained urgency after Ukrainian officials reported restrictions and slower speeds on parts of the Starlink system this week, amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Trumpâs deal involving Russian diesel. Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to refrain from attacking Russian refineries and announced a truce on energy infrastructure attacks. However, Ukraine has continued to target Russian refineries. Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government rather than his company, SpaceX. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military-grade satellite service, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones. It also uses Starlinkâs civilian satellite network, but not for offensive operations. European leaders call for stronger satellite capabilities Several European leaders acknowledged that building an alternative to Starlink would take time, even as the latest disruptions highlighted the need to strengthen the continentâs satellite communications capacity. "Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters. "It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have, but not enough. So this is strategically something we have to discuss today." Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed the issue with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday, focusing on how European countries could provide similar services in the near future. British defence minister Wes Streeting also said he had raised Starlink with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, on Thursday. "It's not yet clear to us in the UK what happened, why the service interruption occurred. But I am reassured, and was reassured directly by Secretary Hegseth, that the service has been restored," Streeting told the BBC on Friday. Ukrainian officials reported slower speeds on the system on Wednesday, affecting connectivity. Some Ukrainian officials suggested Washington was behind the restrictions reported on certain Starlink internet terminals. Eutelsat shares jump as investors look to European alternatives The disruption has renewed investor interest in European satellite operators that could help reduce reliance on SpaceX. Shares in Eutelsat, the French satellite operator that runs the OneWeb network, rose 12 per cent on Friday, taking its gains for the week to 23 per cent. Paris-listed SES, another European satellite operator, gained 6.7 per cent. The gains followed a Reuters report citing two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter, which said an order to limit Starshield services in Ukraine had come from inside the White House. Analysts said the developments had strengthened the case for European satellite operators as governments increasingly sought alternatives to US technology. "The Starlink Ukrainian issue helped," Oddo BHF analyst StÃ©phane Beyazian said of the share price movements, according to Reuters. "But more generally, shares have been done so much due to the Starlink risk â now investors are reconsidering them as the European industry will not disappear to Starlink," he added. Eutelsat operates OneWeb, a network of around 600 low-Earth orbit satellites that provides broadband connectivity to governments, airlines and telecommunications operators. Backed by the French and British governments, OneWeb is widely viewed as Europe's leading challenger to Starlink, whose much larger satellite network dominates the global low-Earth orbit broadband market. Eutelsat chief executive Jean-FranÃ§ois Fallacher said in March that the company had sold its entire capacity in Ukraine. The company operates as a dual-use provider, with thousands of antennas active and devices capable of operating in environments affected by GPS jamming, Reuters reported. However, analysts cautioned that European systems could not immediately match Starlink's capabilities. "We donât see (Europe's IRISÂ² satellite project) fully replicating Starlinkâs capabilities in the short term, although SES and Eutelsat can already provide complementary satellite connectivity," ING analyst Jan Frederik Slijkerman said. Ukraineâs reliance on Starlink exposes a strategic vulnerability Starlink has played a central role in Ukraineâs war effort since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Ukraineâs then deputy prime minister and digital transformation minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, publicly appealed to Musk for connectivity in the early days of the invasion. The first 500 Starlink terminals arrived in Ukraine two days later, and Musk subsequently granted the Ukrainian government and military access to the network, initially free of charge. The system has enabled secure communications between Ukrainian military units and supported command, control, intelligence and surveillance operations. Its connectivity has also been particularly important to Ukraineâs extensive use of drones. However, the relationship has faced tensions over the years. In 2022, Musk refused a Ukrainian request to activate Starlink connectivity for a planned operation near Crimea, saying that doing so would make SpaceX explicitly complicit in a major act of war and risk escalating the conflict. More recently, Musk said Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the US government, with decisions on restrictions ultimately resting with the US military and the US president. The latest disruption has again drawn attention to the risks of Ukraine relying on a satellite network controlled by a private company whose military services are subject to US government decisions. For European leaders, the immediate challenge remains how to maintain Ukraineâs communications capabilities while developing alternative systems. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Over 33 killed as Russia's glide bomb attack targets two civilian buses in Ukraine
text: The attack came amid an intensifying Russian campaign of drone and guided-bomb strikes on cities in Donetsk's so-called âfortress beltâ, Over 30 people were killed and at least 18 others injured after Russia launched a glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on Thursday, according to Ukrainian authorities. The strike came a day after a major Russian aerial assault killed dozens across Ukraine, with much of the attack focused on the country's power grid. Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin said Russian forces had targeted public transport in Kramatorsk, accusing Moscow of deliberately striking civilians. Police said the attack took place on a street where two city buses were operating, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the location as a bus stop. âThese are not 'the consequences of war', nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,â Filashkin said. âRussia comes to Ukrainian land with death.â The attack came amid an intensifying Russian campaign of drone and guided-bomb strikes on cities in Donetsk's so-called âfortress beltâ, which Ukrainian officials regard as the backbone of the region's defences. Russia has demanded that Ukraine surrender the remaining parts of the region under Kyiv's control as a condition for ending the war, a demand Ukraine has rejected. How Russia's glide bombs are changing the war The war has highlighted the growing importance of autonomous systems and stand-off weapons, with Russia making extensive use of glide bombs. Unlike conventional unguided bombs, glide bombs use aerodynamic surfaces, including deployable wings, to extend their range after being released from aircraft. Guidance systems combining satellite and inertial navigation allow the weapons to hit targets with tactical accuracy while aircraft such as Russia's Su-34 and Su-35 fighters can release them from well inside Russian-controlled territory. This keeps Russian aircraft farther from Ukraine's air-defence systems. Russia uses conversion kits such as the Unified Gliding and Correction Module, or UMPK, to turn Soviet-era FAB-500 and FAB-1500 bombs into precision glide weapons. It has also developed purpose-built weapons such as the UMPB, which has improved aerodynamics and a range approaching 90km. title: Starlink vs Starshield: How Elon Muskâs two satellite networks differ
text: Unlike Starlink, Starshield is not commercially available SpaceX 's satellite technology powers internet connectivity across the world, but not all its satellites serve the same purpose. While Starlink provides commercial internet to millions of users, its lesser-known network, Starshield, is designed for military communications, intelligence gathering and national security operations. The distinction came into focus in October 2026, when Ukrainian officials reported disruptions to Starshield connectivity used by drone operators. According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, full connectivity was restored on October 24 after terminals reportedly stopped working at speeds above 160 kmph. What is Starlink? Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, providing connectivity to individuals, businesses and governments. The company says it has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, operating around 550 km above Earth, and serves customers across more than 160 countries. Its users include households, airlines, ships and government agencies. Ukraine has also relied heavily on Starlink for communications since Russia's invasion in 2022. Starlink is owned and operated by SpaceX, and customers can purchase terminals and subscription plans. What is Starshield? Announced in December 2022, Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network designed for US military and national security agencies. It uses Starlink technology but incorporates additional security features, hardened hardware and specialised systems for sensitive government operations. Its three main functions are: Earth observation: Satellites equipped with optical and radar sensors for intelligence and surveillance. Secure communications: Encrypted connectivity for military users through specialised terminals. Hosted payloads: Carrying government equipment and technology aboard satellites. Unlike Starlink, Starshield is not commercially available, and much of its operations remain classified. How are the two networks connected? Starlink and Starshield use similar technology, but their satellites are physically separate. However, Starshield satellites can access the Starlink network when required, allowing US national security customers to use its wider infrastructure. This interoperability is not available to ordinary commercial users. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said Starlink's terms prohibit its use for offensive drone strikes, while decisions on Starshield operations rest with the US government. The US government is the customer and, in some cases, the owner of the infrastructure. SpaceX builds the satellites and operates the underlying Starlink network. It also operates some Starshield satellites under government contracts.

title: Russia ships 20 million barrels of oil to Asia via Arctic route amid shipping disruptions: Report
text: Russia's Arctic oil shipments exceeded 2025's full-season total of 13 million barrels, with another 5-10 million barrels expected by the end of the current navigation period Russia has shipped nearly 20 million barrels of oil to Asia through the Northern Sea Route (NSR) since the start of the navigation season in July, almost 50 per cent more than during the corresponding period last year, as disruptions to traditional shipping corridors make the Arctic route more attractive, traders said and data showed. The volume shipped through the route by mid-October has already exceeded the 13 million barrels exported during the entire 2025 navigation season. Shipments could rise by another 5-10 million barrels before the current navigation period ends, according to preliminary estimates by traders, cited by Reuters. The NSR connects Russia's western ports with Asian markets through Arctic waters. Although the route is more hazardous and expensive to navigate, requiring icebreaker assistance, disruptions involving the Suez Canal, the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea have improved its appeal this year. Rising tanker freight rates, fuelled by the wars involving Iran and Ukraine, have added to the pressure on shipping costs. With conventional routes facing security risks and supply disruptions, Asian refiners have been looking for alternative sources of crude oil, making the higher cost of Arctic shipping more competitive against longer or riskier alternatives, traders said. For Moscow, the route also offers a strategic alternative to European waters, where tankers carrying Russian oil have faced repeated seizures this year. The expansion of Arctic shipments comes as Russian crude supplies to India face tighter availability and growing competition from China. Meanwhile, India remained the world's largest destination for Russian crude oil in September, although imports fell nearly 29 per cent from July levels as Chinese refiners stepped up purchases and tightened the availability of Russian supplies, according to ship-tracking data from Kpler. The report noted that Arctic shipments offer a more direct and potentially economical route to northern China during the navigation season. This could intensify competition between Chinese and Indian refiners for Russian crude, particularly as shipping costs and tighter supplies reduce the price advantage India previously enjoyed. India has relied heavily on Russian crude since 2022, when Moscow redirected oil exports away from Europe. However, the changing economics of Russian oil have prompted Indian refiners to consider alternatives, including supplies from the Middle East and Latin America. Gazprom Neft plans to increase Arctic shipments Gazprom Neft, one of Russia's major oil producers, plans to increase shipments through the NSR by around 35% this year compared with 2025, its chief executive Alexander Dyukov told journalists in Moscow on Friday. The route is also being used to transport liquefied natural gas (LNG) and other goods to Asian markets. LNG shipments are expected to increase this year following the launch of deliveries from the Arctic LNG project. Russia is seeking to expand the route's role in its trade with Asia. President Vladimir Putin said at an economic forum in Vladivostok in September that the country expects annual cargo turnover through the NSR to double to 70 million metric tonnes by the end of the decade. The increase in oil traffic is also being supported by Vostok Oil, Rosneft's major oil project in northern Russia, which began operations last month and is already contributing to rising volumes along the route. title: Netanyahu pushing Donald Trump for nuclear strike on Iran? US commentator makes big claim
text: File photo: US President Donald Trump and Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu US media personality and political commentator Tucker Carlson has claimed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing US President Donald Trump to launch a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Washington could take a decision on the use of nuclear weapons within days. In a detailed post on X on Monday, Carlson claimed that the proposed target could be Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence allegedly believes Tehran has restarted its nuclear enrichment programme. He argued that conventional US weapons would not be able to penetrate the mountain's granite to reach underground tunnels where enrichment activity is supposedly taking place. "Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran," Carlson wrote. He further claimed that Netanyahu had been pushing for such an operation and quoted an unnamed source as saying, "Bibi calls Trump about it every day." Carlson's post did not provide independently verifiable evidence for the claims about a possible nuclear strike or the alleged pressure being exerted by Netanyahu. Carlson claims Netanyahu wants war to continue Carlson linked the alleged push for military action to Netanyahu's political position following last week's elections in Israel. He claimed the Israeli prime minister would struggle to form a government without Trump's direct intervention and could face investigations and possible jail if he lost office. "Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war," Carlson wrote. He also alleged that several senior US officials were backing Netanyahu's position and opposed a negotiated settlement with Iran. Carlson named US defence secretary Pete Hegseth and Centcom commander Brad Cooper, while also claiming that secretary of state Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe were following the Israeli prime minister's lead. Carlson further claimed that former US president Barack Obama had opposed the Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha during a recent meeting. He did not provide details or evidence to substantiate that assertion either. The commentator also said that Netanyahu had travelled secretly to Abu Dhabi on September 27 to seek the United Arab Emirates' support for a final military operation against Iran, but that the Emiratis had refused. Warning over regional and global consequences Carlson warned that another escalation could have serious consequences for the Gulf region and the global economy, pointing to damage to oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions to energy and fertiliser markets. He claimed that 11 of the approximately 850 supertankers used to transport oil globally had been badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October. On the consequences of a possible nuclear strike, Carlson alleged that a ground explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Persian Gulf and affect the water supply of 100 million people. He also warned that the use of a nuclear weapon by the US could set a precedent for other countries. Carlson claimed that Russia had told at least two governments that a US nuclear strike on Iran would give it the freedom to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. He also cited possible nuclear escalation involving North Korea and South Korea. He further alleged that the US administration had quietly revised its nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called "battlefield nukes" easier. Trump weighing diplomacy as Iran talks continue Carlson's claims come amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to resume negotiations between Washington and Tehran, even as the possibility of renewed military action remains under discussion. US President Donald Trump and Netanyahu spoke by phone on Saturday about the state of negotiations with Iran and the possibility of returning to military operations, according to an Axios report. The report said Netanyahu was pressing Trump to launch fresh strikes after Tuesday's US midterm elections, while the US president wanted to allow negotiations to continue. An Israeli source described the conversation as "tough", while a US source called it "direct". Trump later described the conversation as a "very good talk" and confirmed that Iran was among the subjects discussed, without providing further details. Trump has said negotiations with Iran were "going fine" and that he was not "in much of a hurry". However, he also indicated that the US still needed to address one or two Iranian nuclear sites, specifically referring to Pickaxe Mountain. "We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly," Trump said. Meanwhile, US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter last week to Iran's national security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, regarding the possibility of restarting negotiations. Qatari mediators also held discussions with Iranian officials for a third consecutive day on Sunday in an effort to facilitate an agreement to resume direct talks between Washington and Tehran. Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said no agreement had been reached and that progress depended on the US responding to Tehran's questions. "We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," Araghchi said. Carlson, meanwhile, claimed that Trump was listening to Vance and US envoy Steve Witkoff, who he said believed a deal with Iran could still be reached. title: UK budget offers Â£100 energy relief as Iran war threatens growth and raises costs
text: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, holds up the traditional red ministerial box outside No 11 Downing Street before departing to the House of Commons to deliver the first budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government British finance minister John Healey on Wednesday announced a Â£100 one-off energy payment for 20 million lower- and middle-income households, retained the Â£20,000 annual tax-free cash ISA limit and raised taxes on savings and property income in his maiden budget. The measures aim to ease the impact of the Iran war on household finances while encouraging investment and managing the country's rising debt. Healey said the government had to respond to the economic fallout of the conflict, which has pushed up energy prices and weakened growth prospects. âMy choice in the budget today is to give families and businesses some breathing space now,â he told parliament. The budget also extends a cut in the sales tax on electricity bills and abolishes a charge on gas bills. The measures come as disruptions to global oil and gas supplies, including bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, threaten to raise household energy bills over the winter. Cash ISA limit stays at Â£20,000 Healey reversed plans to reduce the annual tax-free limit for cash Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs) from Â£20,000 to Â£12,000 for people under 65 from next year. The earlier proposal, introduced by former finance minister Rachel Reeves, aimed to encourage more people to invest in stocks and shares and support Britain's stock market. The decision to retain the existing limit is expected to benefit banks and building societies, which use cash deposits to support lending, including mortgages. The government will explore ways to encourage first-time investors to buy stocks and shares through a proposed new 'Starter' ISA. However, some experts have criticised the plan for potentially adding complexity to investment products. The government also announced a two-percentage-point increase in the tax rates on savings and property income from April 2027. Tax on savings income will rise to 24%, 44% or 49% for basic-, higher- and additional-rate taxpayers, respectively. The changes are expected to raise Â£590 million in 2031-32, with the government estimating that around half of the additional revenue will come from the wealthiest 10% of households. Banks to fund energy support Banks will face a higher surcharge on their profits to help fund the energy support package. The rate will double to 6% for 15 months from January. âAmid global economic storms, I am looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families,â Healey said. The budget also includes tax cuts for businesses in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors, including pubs and clubs. These will be funded by higher levies on gaming machines. Healey announced additional funding to tackle homelessness and pledged Â£10 billion more in economic and military support for Ukraine. âToday we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes,â he said. Growth forecast cut as Iran war weighs on economy The UK's economy is forecast to grow by 1.2% in 2026, according to the independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). However, growth in 2027 is now expected to be 1%, down from the earlier forecast of 1.6%, reflecting the economic impact of the Iran war. Inflation, which had been expected to fall towards the Bank of England's 2% target, has instead risen to 3.5% and is forecast to climb further over the next year or two. Higher inflation could prompt the central bank to raise interest rates, increasing borrowing costs for households, businesses and the government. Economists said the budget was unlikely to reverse Britain's prolonged period of weak growth and pressure on living standards. âNone of what was announced today is likely to shift the dial on what is set to be a truly terrible decade for living standards,â said Ruth Curtice, chief executive of the Resolution Foundation. Defence spending and public debt Healey confirmed that the government has a target date of 2030 to raise defence spending to 3% of gross domestic product (GDP), in line with the commitment made by NATO members. Defence spending currently stands at 2.7% of GDP. The chancellor said he would explain how the government plans to meet the target when it publishes its three-year spending plans next year. The commitment is particularly significant for Healey, who resigned as defence secretary earlier this year over concerns about funding. Meanwhile, public debt remains a major constraint on government finances. The UK's debt has exceeded Â£3 trillion for the first time, equivalent to more than $4 trillion, while debt servicing accounts for around 8% of government spending. title: US threatens to cut Ukraine intelligence, weapons supplies over Russian energy strikes
text: US President Donald Trump met Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The United States has threatened to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and halt European purchases of American weapons for Kyiv unless Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stops attacks on Russian energy facilities, CNN reported, citing two European officials. The reported warning comes as US President Donald Trump says Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an âenergy ceasefireâ, even as Zelenskyy accuses Moscow of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Russia, meanwhile, has yet to explicitly confirm that it has accepted the proposed arrangement. According to two European officials cited by CNN, the US administration has warned Ukraine and its European allies that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing and halt a mechanism through which European countries purchase American weapons for Kyiv. The warnings were reportedly conveyed over the weekend by the State Department and the Pentagon, including through direct communications between the US military and Ukrainian commanders. A US official said American negotiators had reminded Kyiv that Washington was providing weapons and intelligence and that Ukraine should not take actions that hurt American consumers. Another source familiar with the matter said the US had threatened to cut intelligence sharing. The Financial Times first reported the threats. The reported warnings come amid Trump's anger over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, which have added to tensions between the US president and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump has repeatedly called for both countries to stop targeting energy facilities, citing the impact of the war on global fuel prices. Those pressures have been compounded by the US war with Iran. The potential suspension of support could have serious consequences for Ukraine. American intelligence helps its forces detect incoming Russian ballistic missiles and identify launch sites, giving them more time to respond. A halt to weapons purchases under the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Nato allies finance the purchase of US arms for Ukraine, could also affect supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles, which Kyiv needs to defend against intensifying Russian missile and drone attacks. A Nato official told CNN on Monday that weapons supplies through PURL were continuing. The US had previously suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine in March 2025 after a heated meeting between Trump and Zelenskyy at the White House. Sharing resumed after Kyiv agreed to a proposed US ceasefire during talks in Saudi Arabia. Against this backdrop, Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to what he called an âenergy ceasefireâ, offering little detail about its terms. The announcement appeared to catch Kyiv by surprise, while Moscow has yet to explicitly confirm that it has accepted the arrangement. Zelenskyy says Russia continued attacks Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure but accused Moscow of continuing to strike Ukrainian energy facilities even after Trump's announcement. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been âhorribly surprisedâ by Russian strikes on a power plant in Kharkiv, a gas production facility and a civilian gas station in the hours after the US president announced the proposed ceasefire. The Ukrainian president later told Fox News Channel's âAmericaâs Newsroomâ that Kyiv had refrained from attacking Russian energy sites since Sunday's announcement and was ready to honour the arrangement. He described the proposed halt to energy attacks as âa good first stepâ towards ending the war. But Zelenskyy expressed doubt over whether Russian President Vladimir Putin would reciprocate. âIâm not sure that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin is ready,â he said. âEven after yesterdayâs messages from (Trump) ... Putin attacked our gas infrastructure,â Zelenskyy said. âWhen we speak about energy ceasefire, it means only one thing: that they donât attack our energy infrastructure and we donât respond on their energy infrastructure.â Trump's announcement on social media had declared that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding, âDo not break it!â However, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined on Monday to confirm whether Moscow had agreed to the arrangement, saying only that âContacts are ongoing". Zelenskyy's comments came amid a separate dispute over elections in Ukraine. Trump recently suggested that Kyiv should choose a new leader, prompting the Ukrainian president to say that a 60-day ceasefire could allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections. Zelenskyy has argued that elections are currently unfeasible because of continued Russian attacks. He has called for a âfull ceasefireâ, saying the security situation makes it impossible to organise a vote while strikes continue day and night. title: A Nevada manganese mine that left arsenic and lead in the ground is undergoing an estimated $257 million cleanup; a 3.5-acre park has now opened on the former site, with more than 3,000 homes planned nearby
text: Nevada mine site gets a new park amid $257 million cleanup and plans for 3,000 homes (Image Credit: Nevada Division of Environmental Division) What was once a mining site associated with potentially harmful industrial waste is now making way for neighbourhood parks, walking trails and thousands of homes. In Henderson, Nevada, a former manganese mine that operated for decades and left behind contamination is being transformed into a large residential community. The opening of Greenbow Park marks a new phase in that redevelopment. According to the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP), the Three Kids Mine site has been the subject of extensive environmental assessments and a cleanup programme, with the estimated remediation cost reaching approximately $257 million. From wartime manganese production to an abandoned mining site The Three Kids Mine has a history dating back more than a century. Manganese ore was discovered at the site in Clark County, Nevada, in 1917. However, mining operations took place intermittently, including between 1942 and 1943 and again from 1953 to 1961. Manganese was an important industrial mineral, particularly during World War II, when demand increased for materials used in military equipment and steel production. According to the NDEP, an on-site processing mill was constructed in 1942 to meet the renewed demand for manganese during World War II. The mill reopened in 1951, and mining resumed in 1953. Mining continued until the open pits were exhausted, and operations permanently stopped in 1961. The end of mining, however, did not mean the end of the site's environmental problems. Former mine features included open pits, waste rock, an ore yard, processing facilities and tailings ponds. Environmental assessments identified dust, residues and processing waste containing lead, arsenic, manganese and petroleum. The contamination raised concerns about the condition of the land and the work needed before it could be considered suitable for redevelopment. Why the cleanup carries a $257 million price tag The scale of the environmental work is reflected in the estimated cost. The NDEP's November 2023 Record of Decision placed the total estimated cleanup cost at approximately $257.5 million. The wider Three Kids Mine property covers around 1,165 acres, although the former mining operations affected a smaller portion of the site. The area affected by the former mining operations covered approximately 410 acres, distinguishing the contaminated mine area from the larger property earmarked for redevelopment. Environmental investigations and feasibility studies were undertaken to identify contaminants and determine the appropriate remediation measures. The federal Three Kids Mine Remediation and Reclamation Act was enacted in July 2014, creating a framework for transferring federally owned land through the City of Henderson Redevelopment Agency so that assessment, remediation and reclamation could take place. The land transfer was completed in February 2024, while major cleanup activities began in May 2024. The NDEP also established a perimeter air monitoring plan to monitor air quality during the work. The contamination identified at the site was not limited to lead and arsenic. Investigations also identified manganese, petroleum-related materials and other industrial waste. The environmental work therefore involved addressing several types of contamination rather than simply clearing away the remains of the old mine. Greenbow Park brings a new public space to the former mine One of the most visible signs of the transformation is Greenbow Park, a new 3.5-acre recreational space that has opened on the former mine property. According to FOX5 Vegas, the park is part of the Aries master-planned community in Henderson. Its facilities include pickleball courts, playgrounds, shaded gathering areas and more than 3,000 feet of trails. Visitors can also enjoy views of the Las Vegas skyline from the walking routes. The park adds recreational space to an area being developed into a residential neighbourhood. Its opening is significant because the former industrial property is now being incorporated into a community designed around housing, outdoor activities and shared public spaces. Rather than leaving the former mining land as an isolated industrial site, the redevelopment is intended to give it a new role in Henderson's expanding urban landscape. More than 3,000 homes planned across 24 neighbourhoods Greenbow Park is part of a much larger development plan. The Aries master-planned community is expected to include more than 3,000 homes spread across 24 residential neighbourhoods. The redevelopment covers more than 1,100 acres, making it a substantial addition to Henderson's residential growth. The community is being developed on the former Three Kids Mine property, with housing and recreational facilities planned as part of the wider project. The transformation also highlights the challenges involved in bringing previously industrial land back into urban use. Former mining properties can offer substantial redevelopment opportunities, but their conversion requires careful environmental assessment, remediation and long-term planning. There is also an important distinction between the progress of the redevelopment and the environmental project's official status. While Henderson's redevelopment director told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that remediation work had been completed, the NDEP's public project page continues to describe the overall cleanup as ongoing and lists site closure reports and monitoring documents. For Henderson, the opening of Greenbow Park offers a visible glimpse of what the former mine site could become. A property once associated with manganese production and industrial contamination is gradually taking on the appearance of a residential community, with parks, trails and thousands of homes planned as part of its next chapter.

title: After 28 years & 51,000-km trek around the world, Karl Bushby is back in UK
text: Karl Bushby is back in UK HULL (ENGLAND): Karl Bushby was taking the final steps Monday of his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world and return to his mother's home in northern England. Bushby was surrounded by journalists as hundreds of people cheered his arrival at City Hall. "Sorry to keep you waiting," he joked. "Is that it, is it done?" Bushby was a 29-year-old ex-paratrooper when he walked from his home to a Royal Air Force base near Oxford and caught a flight to South America. He returned as a 57-year-old - softer, greyer and weathered, but far more worldly. "They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here," Bushby said. "The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn't do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth." Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov 1, 1998, and has walked 50,000 kilometres across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane - or any transport - to propel him forward. He had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument among his fellow special forces troops about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic red tape often brought his adventure to a halt for long periods. Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic. "You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that," he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years." He dodged war in the dangerous Darien Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 90-km Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that allowed travel only a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian embassy in Washington, DC, which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Bushby planned to meet with family, including his son, Adam, whom he has only seen a few times over the journey. He was expected to meet his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time. Then he was off to push his two-wheeled cart the final steps across Hull and reunite with his mother, Angela, whom he hadn't seen in a decade. "It's been a week of lasts," Bushby told the crowd. "The last day in the tent. The last day on the road. After 28 years you couldn't ask for more than this. This is the last of the last few steps almost to my mother's house." You use AI every day. title: In 1998, he left home as a 29-year-old adventurer; in 2026, 28 years, 4 continents, 1 journey with over 50K km trek around the world later, Karl Bushby walks back home to his mother in Hull
text: Who is Karl Bushby? 28 years, 4 continents, 1 journey with over 50K km trek around the world later, the British adventurer walks back home to his mother in Hull Who do you picture when you imagine an adventurer on his feet? Someone like Forrest Gump, with an extraordinary talent for running? Well, in reality, Karl Bushby might just be your best shot at that fictional character. But Karl Bushby isnât your typical adventurer. Most people, if they ever seriously think about walking around the world, let the thought drift away and move on. Karl couldnât. In 1998, when he was just shy of 30, he stepped out of his childhood home in Hull, northern England, full of ambition and, to be honest, a bit of stubbornness. He promised himself heâd walk the entire way: no planes, trains, or cars; only come back to Hull when the journey was complete. That wasnât just bravado; it became a rule he never broke, no matter how complicated or dangerous things got. Fast-forward nearly three decades â 28 years, to be precise â and Karl finally made it back on November 2, 2026, with a staggering 50,000 kilometers under his boots. He didnât cross just one or two continents; he covered four, trudged through 30 countries, and faced obstacles that might have stopped anyone else in their tracks. The world threw jungles, deserts, and freezing oceans at him, unpredictable politics and visa nightmares, wild animals, and weather that could kill. Still, Karl pushed on. By the time he walked up to his mum Angela Bushbyâs front door, he was 57: more seasoned, certainly more tired, but still chasing the same goal he set out with decades ago: coming home on foot. Karlâs story doesnât read like a typical adventure for glory. He wasnât gunning for a Guinness World Record or a magazine cover. The finish line wasnât an abstract place; it was real and familiar â his mumâs house. So, who is Karl Bushby? And what sort of person spends 28 years walking toward one destination everyone else would drive to in ten minutes? Karl Bushby: Who is he? Born in Hull in March 1969, Karl Bushby grew up in the Sutton Park neighborhood. Per AP News, life wasnât easy for Karl growing up. He had severe dyslexia, which made school a battlefield. He got picked on and found solace first in birdwatching and wandering outside. His family had their share of adventure, too: his dad was an army guy, and his brother followed that path. Karl joined the British Army, serving twelve years with the Parachute Regiment, and picked up the endurance and grit that would one day push him across the world. What was the Goliath Expedition ? The seed for his journey came from a simple conversation: a birthday card from his dad, mentioning that soldiers were debating whether you could walk from London to New York via the Bering Strait. While others laughed it off, Karl took it seriously. He traced a route on a map, connecting England with the southern tip of South America and looping back home. Instead of letting it go, he turned that wild idea into his own lifeâs mission. He called it the Goliath Expedition, which is a name fitting for a quest that would take more than half his life. When he started, Karl had about $500 and a backpack. On November 1, 1998, he left from Punta Arenas in Chile, carrying a backpack and limited supplies, heading north through South and Central America, all the way up to North America, over the Bering Strait into Russia, then on through Asia and Europe back to the UK. Over 28 years, the journey covered approximately 50,000 kilometres across four continents and 30 countries. Imagine pushing a two-wheeled cart, dubbed âThe Beastâ, through jungles, deserts, and frozen seas â almost never alone, but always on his own. From the DariÃ©n Gap to the frozen Bering Strait: The biggest challenges Karlâs journey was filled with stories most of us wouldnât believe. For instance, the DariÃ©n Gap, which is infamous for its dense rainforest and dangerous gangs. He got through it, dodged trouble, and even spent over two weeks locked up after crossing a restricted border. The Bering Strait crossing in 2006 was another monster challenge: Karl and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer pushed sledges across shifting ice between Alaska and Russia, facing minus-30 temperatures, nearly falling into the frigid sea, and stumbling across a polar bear. After all that, Russian authorities detained them for illegal entry. Russia would become his biggest bureaucratic challenge. Tight visa rules and political dramas meant Karl had to get creative. Once, after being denied a visa in 2012, he protested by walking all the way from LA to Washington, DC, just to make his case to the Russians. In 2024, he even swam across the Caspian Sea, rather than loop back into Russia or pass through Iran. That wasnât a short swim; it was about 300 kilometers over a month. Every new obstacle seemed to demand something even crazier or more inventive from him. Why did the journey take 28 years instead of the planned 12? Bushby originally expected his expedition to take around 12 years. However, the reality proved considerably more complicated. Why? To put it simply: life happened. Visa hang-ups, border closures, wars, and money issues slowed him down. The 2008 financial crisis hit his sponsors hard, and COVID forced its own long pauses. Bureaucracy and border regulations turned his route into a tangled mess, leaving him stranded and waiting for permissionâ¦ sometimes for months or years. When Karl finally got to the edge of the UK, there was one last challenge. Eurotunnel authorities wouldnât let him walk through the Channel Tunnelâs service corridor, so he figured out another way. He swam across the English Channel, taking breaks when he could, pushing through 20 hours in the water over three days â in just last month. He landed at Shakespeare Beach, Dover, then finished the last 400 kilometers on foot before reaching Hull. An emotional homecoming after 28 years Coming home was more than just the physical arrival. He got a heroâs welcome in Hull, with hundreds gathering at Queen Victoria Square. Then, the real heart of the journey: knocking on his mumâs door. Angela hadnât seen him in about ten years, and he reunited with his son Adam and met his granddaughter for the first time. The moment was raw and real; it was everything heâd walked for. One of the most humane aspects of Karlâs journey has been the fact that his decade-spanning trip was never a solo one. He points to the kindness of strangers along the way: the people willing to help, share, and cheer him on. Their support was vital. After spending almost 30 years on the road, heâs admitted that adjusting to regular life wonât be easy. His journey became more than what he did; it shaped who he is. Thatâs what makes Karl Bushbyâs story so powerful. For years, the world tried to stop him: jungles, desert, ocean, political walls, and plain old exhaustion. Instead, Karl just kept putting one foot in front of the other until the only thing standing between him and home was his mumâs front door. And he walked right through. You use AI every day. title: "It's really over": BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War directorâs heartbreaking admission leaves fans facing the end
text: The end of BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War marks more than the conclusion of a major anime project. For director Tomohisa Taguchi , it also closes a creative chapter that lasted seven years. After spending years bringing Tite Kubo's celebrated manga back to television, the director is beginning to feel the weight of its conclusion. His latest comments offer a personal look at the emotions behind the anime's final chapter and the changing future of its production studio, Pierrot Films. Tomohisa Taguchi reflects on his seven-year journey with BLEACH For Taguchi, the connection with BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War began long before viewers saw the final episodes. He revealed that the project first came his way around 2019, giving him seven years to work on an anime that has remained close to the hearts of longtime fans. Now that the production has reached its conclusion, the reality of moving on is becoming harder to ignore. In a recent comment shared by Anime Tokki, the director spoke about the emotional impact of watching Pierrot Films move its production focus towards other projects. He said: "Watching Pierrot films shift its production to other projects, the feeling that 'it's really over' has finally sunk in. I was approached around 2019, so I spent 7 years with BLEACH TYBW." His words highlight how much time and creative energy went into bringing the final arc of Tite Kubo's manga to the screen. For audiences, the ending means saying goodbye to Ichigo Kurosaki's latest journey. For the people behind the scenes, it also means leaving behind years of planning, production and collaboration. The director's reaction carries particular weight because BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War was not simply another anime assignment. The revival brought back a franchise that had been absent from television for a decade, creating enormous expectations among viewers who had followed the original series. BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War marks a major chapter for Pierrot Films The final arc has been released in four parts, beginning in October 2022. Each instalment brought viewers closer to the long-awaited conflict between the Soul Reapers and Yhwach's Quincy army. The final instalment, titled The Calamity, premiered on July 25, 2026, with Pierrot Films handling animation production. The studio's involvement also reflects a wider change in its approach to anime production. Pierrot Films was introduced as a dedicated production branch in 2024, with plans to work on manga adaptations aimed at adult audiences as well as original projects. BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War became one of its major productions. The final two episodes were pushed back to October to allow more time for production quality. The concluding episode aired on October 26 in Japan, bringing the Thousand-Year Blood War adaptation to its end. Taguchi's comments offer a reminder that an anime's ending affects more than its audience. Behind every major battle, emotional scene and dramatic reveal is a team that has spent years bringing the story to life. For fans, the conclusion closes an important chapter in Ichigo's story. For Taguchi and the production team, it marks the end of a seven-year commitment. And as Pierrot Films turns towards new projects, the director's words capture the bittersweet feeling of finally moving on from a world that has occupied so much of his working life. title: Trump waives US sanctions, tariffs on Russian oil & gas - what it means for India
text: Trump announced the waiver just days before several provisions of the legislation were due to take effect. In what is being seen as a big relief for India and China, US President Donald Trump has waived sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, citing the national interest of the United States. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 gave Trump the authority to impose broad sanctions on Russia and levy steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India. The legislation, principally backed in Congress by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, provided for tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on goods entering the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas. It also covered countries that knowingly purchased Russian oil or gas 30 days after the law's enactment, as well as those among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions. Also Read | The return of Middle East oil: Has Iran lost control of Strait of Hormuz & why are crude prices still up? What Trump announced Trump announced the waiver just days before several provisions of the legislation were due to take effect. He had signed the bill into law in mid-September. âI am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,â Trump said in an executive order issued on Friday evening. In the order, Trump said he had submitted a certification to Congress stating that granting the waiver at this stage was in the US national interest. The executive order comes as Trump has adopted a warmer stance towards Russia while publicly criticising Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. He has even suggested that Ukraine needs a new leader. The proposed Russia sanctions had also raised concerns among countries that rely heavily on Russian oil imports. India, one of the largest buyers of Russian crude, was among the countries that expressed concerns about the legislation. What it means for India Russia continues to be the single largest supplier of oil for India. A waiver of tariffs of up to 100% which may have come into place in the coming days means that India can continue importing oil in large numbers from Moscow without any economic fallout. If 100% tariffs had been imposed by the Trump administration, then it would have hit exporters as the US is the largest trading partner for India. At the same time, any sanctions may have rendered Russian crude economically unviable which would have added to the supply crunch at a time when Middle East tensions continue. Manoj Mishra, Partner and Tax Controversy Management Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat sees the waiver of the proposed 100% tariffs as a significant relief for India on both trade and energy security fronts. âAvoiding steep additional tariffs reduces the risk of disruption to energy sourcing amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East. Given that the US is Indiaâs largest trading partner, the waiver also helps shield Indian exporters from potential adverse impacts across sectors,â he says. âImportantly, it eases a source of uncertainty in bilateral trade negotiations and creates a more conducive environment for advancing the IndiaâUS trade deal. However, businesses will continue to seek greater tariff clarity and predictability to support long-term export planning and supply-chain decisions,â he adds. The Middle East is a big supplier of energy needs for India - crude oil, LPG and LNG. Shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have been hit, leading India to diversify its energy basket more aggressively. Russian oil has played a big role in Indiaâs crude oil imports at this time, with numbers hitting record highs a few months ago. In fact, Russia gradually became Indiaâs largest crude supplier since the start of Moscowâs war with Ukraine, when European sanctions prompted Russia to sell oil to India and China at deep discounts. Last year, Donald Trump imposed 25% penal tariffs on India for its crude oil purchases from Russia, taking the total tariff figure to 50%. India did not stop buying crude from Russia, but after the US imposed sanctions on two Russian oil majors, the imports started coming down. In February this year, announcing while lowering tariffs on India to 18% and removing the 25% penal tariffs, Trump claimed that India would stop buying oil from Russia. India never made any such statement, and before a clear trend on its crude purchases from Russia could emerge, the Middle East conflict erupted. In between, the US waived sanctions on Russian crude to lower global crude oil prices, but even with those waivers lapsing, India continued to procure from Russia to meet its energy needs. The Trump administrationâs move to sign the sanctions bill last month was also hinted to have been weighing on the India-US trade deal talks. With sanctions now being waived off, some movement may also be seen on that front, especially with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal recently hinting that a draft is almost ready. Competing for oil with China But even as the threat of tariffs related to Russian oil recedes, India may still have to compete aggressively with China for crude from Moscow. Indian refiners expect Russian crude supplies to become even tighter in October and November as exports decline and competition from China intensifies, reports suggest. Also Read | Beijingâs billion-barrel weapon: Why India must prepare for China-driven oil prices The shortfall is likely to push the world's third-largest crude importer towards more expensive alternatives for the remainder of the year. In recent months, China, the world's largest crude importer, has increased its purchases as the Iran war disrupted supplies from the Middle East. "Demand from China has been really high. They were willing to book cargoes in advance and to pay firmer prices compared to Indian refiners," a source involved in the sale of Russian crude told Reuters recently. title: Brent crude tops $110 as fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia raise concerns over oil supplies
text: Crude prices hold above $110 per barrel Oil prices edged higher on Thursday, with Brent crude trading above $110 a barrel. The rise came after fresh Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia prompted US to order some diplomats and their family members to leave American missions in the Kingdom. At the same time, concerns over shipping safety and oil supplies in the region also persisted. WTI crude was trading at $98.05, up 90 cents or 0.93%, while Brent crude stood at $110, up $1.15 or 1.06%. US officials told Reuters that the state department also plans to withdraw family members from several other American missions in the region. The latest security concerns followed a series of attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on Wednesday. At least one person was killed and eight others wounded in an attack on a civilian airport in Dammam. A drone attack on a Saudi oil field killed two people. Explosions were also reported in Sirik, in southern Iran, on Wednesday. Iranian media said that the nature and origin of the blasts were unknown. Shipping risks extend beyond Strait of Hormuz The threat to energy supplies has extended to maritime routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz. Kpler data showed at least 18 attacks on shipping over the past two weeks. LSEG analysts warned that Iran was targeting tankers further afield, including in the Gulf of Oman. Such attacks were jeopardising Gulf crude loadings and ship-to-ship transfers that support regional loadings. Iran's leadership also issued fresh statements amid the tensions. Foreign minister Abbas Araqchi told the Financial Times on Wednesday that Iran was fully prepared to defend itself. President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that the US could not expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran. US crude inventories fall, distillate stocks rise US crude inventories declined by 3.06 million barrels last week to 412.5 million barrels, according to data released by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) on Wednesday. The fall was greater than the 820,000-barrel draw expected by analysts in a Reuters poll. Distillate inventories, which include diesel and heating oil, increased by 1.68 million barrels to 104.3 million barrels during the week. Analysts had expected these stockpiles to fall by 1.16 million barrels, EIA data showed. Separately, the Trump administration is offering to loan up to nearly a third of the US emergency heating oil reserve, which holds one million barrels. The department of energy announced the move on Wednesday as the administration seeks to contain prices that have risen amid diesel shortages linked to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Elsewhere, Russian President Vladimir Putin met US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. The meeting came as Washington renewed efforts to end Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two. The Kremlin said Putin had agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
