title: Polandâs top court turns into battleground as Tusk and pro-Trump president clash
text: File photo: Demonstrators attend a protest outside the premises of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, after the tribunal said on its website that the tribunal's president Bogdan Swieczkowski, who was a deputy justice minister under the PiS government, had been suspended Polandâs long-running battle over judicial independence has escalated into a confrontation between prime minister Donald Tusk and president Karol Nawrocki, after the suspension of the Constitutional Tribunalâs leadership triggered protests and a police deployment outside the court in Warsaw. The latest flashpoint came on Friday, when Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced the one-month suspension of Tribunal president Bogdan ÅwiÄczkowski and his deputy, BartÅomiej SochaÅski, and said she would take charge of the institution. The move followed a dispute over the appointment of new judges, whom ÅwiÄczkowski had refused to allow to take their seats. Watch 'Tusk Coup' Battle Explodes: Protesters Return In Huge Numbers, Poland's Top Court Under Danger Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS) and a vocal supporter of US President Donald Trump, abandoned a visit to Senegal and returned to Warsaw. He described the suspension of the Tribunalâs leadership as a âforcible takeover of a constitutional institutionâ. PiS leaders also condemned the move, accusing Tuskâs government of attempting a coup. Police were deployed outside the court as hundreds of protesters gathered. Officers said their presence followed concerns about possible threats to judges and staff and risks to public order. Police also reported three arrests after people tried to enter the court complex. Tusk defended his governmentâs actions, saying it was seeking to restore the rule of law after years of political interference in the judiciary under PiS, which governed Poland for eight years until 2023. âThis process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,â Tusk said in a post on X on Saturday. In a televised address, he said that âshouting, lies, and brawling cannot be the source of law in Polandâ. A decade-long dispute over the judiciary The Constitutional Tribunal rules on whether legislation complies with Polandâs constitution, giving control over its composition significant political and legal consequences. The current dispute has roots in 2015, when PiS came to power and challenged judicial appointments made by the outgoing government. Polandâs Constitutional Tribunal subsequently found that only three of five appointments made by the outgoing parliament had a valid legal basis. The incoming PiS majority appointed replacements, including for seats that had already been lawfully filled, while then-president Andrzej Duda refused to swear in the three validly elected judges. During its eight years in office, PiS introduced wider judicial changes that critics said increased political influence over the courts. In 2021, the European Commission warned that the partyâs actions posed a âsystemic risk to the rule of law in Polandâ and froze EU funding over concerns about judicial independence. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2021 that the participation of an improperly appointed judge had deprived a company of its right to a tribunal established by law. In December 2025, the European Unionâs top court also ruled that Polandâs Constitutional Tribunal did not meet the requirements of an independent court. Tusk returned to office in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence. But efforts to reverse the changes have been complicated by the continued presence of PiS-appointed judges and Nawrockiâs role in the appointment process. This year, parliament elected eight judges to the Tribunalâs 15-member bench. Nawrocki administered the oath to three but withheld it from five others, who took their oaths without his presence. ÅwiÄczkowski subsequently refused to allow the five to begin their work. The latest confrontation followed the appointment of Maciej Berek, a former minister in Tuskâs cabinet, who was prevented from taking his seat last week. The choice has also drawn criticism from within the governing camp, with some questioning whether appointing a former government minister is consistent with promises to depoliticise the judiciary. Legal experts have raised questions about the latest intervention, too. Korwin-Piotrowskaâs authority to suspend the Tribunalâs president and deputy has been disputed, with her claim based on her length of service as a judge overall rather than seniority within the Tribunal. A standoff with no clear resolution The confrontation has exposed a difficult question for Tuskâs government: how to restore the Tribunalâs independence without creating new doubts about the legality of its actions. Marcin Matczak, a Polish lawyer, told Al Jazeera that PiS was seeking to retain control of what he described as its remaining institutional stronghold, while the government wanted to restore balance to the Tribunal. He warned that the use of police in a dispute involving the court could set a precedent for future governments. The US ambassador to Poland, Tom Rose, urged all sides to avoid escalation, warning that large crowds outside the Tribunal could make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The standoff comes as Poland faces security concerns linked to Russiaâs war in neighbouring Ukraine and sabotage attacks that Tusk has attributed to Moscow. Tusk has accused his opponents of finding support among pro-Russian forces, an allegation that further sharpens the political divide. With parliamentary elections due next year, the dispute over the Tribunal is likely to remain central to the debate over Polandâs political direction and its relationship with the European Union. title: Watch: China-North Korea bridge opens after 12-years delay
text: New Yalu River Bridge connects Dandong in northeastern China with Sinuiju in North Korea China and North Korea on Thursday officially opened a long-delayed bridge linking their border cities, reviving a major trade route after more than a decade of stalled construction and signalling renewed efforts to strengthen economic ties. The four-lane, 3-km New Yalu River Bridge connects Dandong in northeastern China with Sinuiju in North Korea. Officials from both countries attended the opening ceremony virtually, while trucks bearing Chinese and North Korean flags waited on the bridge. Watch North Korea Fires Submarine Missiles In Latest Show Of Force Amid Tensions With South | WATCH Chinese premier Li Qiang said the two countriesâ relationship had entered a ânew stageâ, describing the crossing as a landmark of their traditional friendship. North Korean premier Pak Thae Song said the bridge would help advance prosperity and improve peopleâs well-being, according to the countriesâ state media. The opening comes as Pyongyang has strengthened its ties with Moscow, including through military support for Russiaâs war in Ukraine, prompting questions about Beijingâs influence over its longstanding ally. A decade-long delay The bridge was completed on the Chinese side in 2014 and was initially expected to open that year. But work on the North Korean side stalled, leaving the crossing unused for more than a decade. The delay fuelled speculation that Pyongyang was wary of becoming more dependent on Beijing or unhappy with Chinaâs support for United Nations sanctions over North Koreaâs nuclear programme. The new crossing is expected to ease pressure on the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, built in 1943, which carries more than 70% of official trade between the two countries. The older bridge accommodates rail and road traffic, but vehicles can cross in only one direction at a time. Even before the new bridge opened, Chinese traders were reportedly rushing to move cargo across the old crossing. A report by Daily NK said shipments surged after Chinaâs National Day holiday, as traders sought to send goods before the new route began operating amid fears of steep tolls and other fees. Authorities have not announced the new bridgeâs toll rates. Traders are expected to weigh the cost of using the wider crossing against the older route, meaning improved capacity may not automatically translate into cheaper shipments. Beijing seeks to retain its influence China remains North Koreaâs largest trading partner and a vital economic lifeline. About 98% of North Koreaâs external trade was with China in 2025, according to figures cited in the reports. But Kim Jong Un has increasingly prioritised ties with Russia, sending troops and conventional weapons to support Moscowâs war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance. The opening of a road bridge between Russia and North Korea last month underscored that growing partnership. The New Yalu River Bridge could help Beijing reinforce its economic role as Pyongyang broadens its external partnerships. Analysts say it may improve logistics and facilitate trade, although its impact will depend on how the crossing is used and what charges authorities impose. The opening marks a practical change for cross-border commerce and is also a test of how Beijing and Pyongyang manage a relationship shaped by economic dependence, political interests and North Koreaâs growing engagement with Moscow. text: Lucknow Development Authority Lucknow: The Lucknow Development Authority (LDA) will build multi-level parking facilities at four city locations at a cost of Rs 431 crore. The projects, aimed at easing traffic congestion and addressing parking shortages, will be built in Vivek Khand and Patrakarpuram in Gomti Nagar, near Ekana Stadium, and at Ambedkar Park. The proposal followed a request from the fire department after the fire incident in Aliganj. title: 'Dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists': PM Modi hails ISRO after successful GSLV-F18 launch carrying NVS-03
text: PM Modi hails ISRO after successful GSLV-F18 launch carrying NVS-03 navigation satellite NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday congratulated Indian Space Research Organisation ( ISRO ) scientists and engineers following the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission carrying the NVS-03 navigation satellite, saying the mission would strengthen India's indigenous satellite navigation system, NavIC . In a post on X, PM Modi said, "Congratulations to our scientists and engineers at ISRO on the successful launch of GSLV-F18 carrying NVS-03. Watch ISRO As âResidual R&D Boutiqueâ?: Staff Bodies Seek âWritten Clarityâ On Private Space Sector Shift Also read: Success launch of navigation sat NVS-03 with desi atomic clock will make NaVIC up & running, and give military strategic independence This mission marks an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system. Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people. The dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud." The successful launch is expected to strengthen India's strategic autonomy by helping restore the operational capabilities of NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to global navigation systems such as the US-operated GPS and Russia's GLONASS. The NVS-03 satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock, alongside imported atomic clocks, marking an important step towards reducing India's dependence on foreign technologies for satellite-based navigation. Atomic clocks provide highly precise time signals that are essential for determining location, navigation and timing. NavIC, which was originally designed around a seven-satellite constellation, had been operating with only three active satellites, below the minimum requirement of four satellites for standalone positioning services. This had limited its use for critical applications, including military navigation, precision positioning and coordination of naval assets. An operational NavIC constellation is particularly important for India's armed forces, which require reliable Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals for missile guidance, precision-guided weapons, troop movement, combat aircraft and naval operations. Dependence on foreign navigation networks can pose strategic vulnerabilities during conflicts, as access to such services could potentially be restricted or disrupted. India experienced the limitations of relying on foreign satellite navigation systems during the 1999 Kargil war. With NVS-03, India aims to strengthen the availability of indigenous navigation services for both civilian and strategic applications. NavIC is designed to provide coverage across India and up to 1,500 km beyond its geographical boundaries. Three satellites were placed in geostationary orbit, while four were placed in inclined geosynchronous orbits. However, the constellation's operational strength declined over time as ageing satellites could not be replaced as planned. The launch of NVS-02 on January 29, 2025, also failed to deliver the intended results after a pyro valve signal loss in the engine prevented the satellite from reaching its designated orbit. The successful deployment of NVS-03 is expected to address some of these operational limitations and strengthen India's efforts to establish an independent satellite navigation capability. title: SC upholds war injury pension for Army man in Op Rakshak
text: Chandigarh: The Supreme Court has dismissed an appeal filed by the Union of India challenging the grant of âwar injury pensionâ to an Army personnel who developed rheumatoid arthritis (seropositive) while posted at Kargil during Operation Rakshak, holding that the ministry of defence could not deny pensionary benefits when its policy did not distinguish between operations notified by the govt. A bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe, while upholding the decisions of the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) and the Punjab and Haryana high court, also directed that while notifying operations under Category E(i) of the MoD policy, Govt must declare in clear terms whether the pensionary benefits contemplated under the policy would apply to such notifications. Narender Kumar, who was enrolled in the Indian Army on Dec 30, 1996, was posted in Kargil from July 13, 2003, to July 6, 2005, when he was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis (seropositive). He was later diagnosed with two other spinal disabilities while posted in West Bengal. The Release Medical Board, while discharging him from service on January 31, 2013, conceded all three disabilities as aggravated by military service at 70% for life, rounded off to 75% for life. Having rendered more than 16 years of service, he was granted disability pension consisting of service element and disability element. Six years after his discharge, he approached the AFT seeking war injury pension under Part II, Category E(i), Para 4.1 of the MoD policy letter dated Jan 31, 2001, contending that the disability was a direct consequence of his posting at Kargil during Operation Rakshak. MoD argued his disability was not covered under Category E(i) of the policy. The AFT, in April 2024, allowed his application, holding that the disease originated in Jan 2005 when he was serving at Kargil and that the entire Jammu and Kashmir area was an operational area. The Punjab and Haryana high court dismissed the ministryâs challenge in Aug 2025. Before the Supreme Court, additional solicitor general Archana Pathak Dave argued the respondentâs claim did not fall under Category E(i). The Centre maintained that Category E(i) would cover only operations specially notified by the govt, such as Operation Sindoor or Operation Snow Leopard, and not ongoing operations such as Operation Rakshak, which covers the entire Jammu and Kashmir, or Operation Rhino, covering the entire Assam. Kumarâs counsel, advocate Ajay Sehoran, submitted that Operation Rakshak at Kargil was an integral part of operations specially notified by the govt under Category E(i). Referring to Army Order 1 of 2003, the counsel argued that battle casualties included casualties occurring while operating on the International Border or Line of Control due to natural calamities and illnesses caused by climatic conditions. Examining the scope of Category E(i), the Supreme Court observed, âSub-Category E(i) is intended to give flexibility to our defence administration as it is natural that all war-like situations cannot comprehensively commence and conclude within the specified eight Sub-Categories (a) to (h).â The bench added: âGoing by the plain language of the policy, once a notification is issued for a specific operation, Category E(i) is invoked, unless there is something indicative either in the Policy or in the notification so issued.â It added, âExcept for the oral statement of the Ld. ASG that Operation Rakshak is not intended to be covered under Category E(i), there is no other interpretative aid for us to exclude Operation Rakshak from the scope of Category E(i).â The Bench observed, âIf the policymaker interprets its own policy against the plain language or in a manner that could be discriminatory, arbitrary, irrational or goes against the very purpose and object of the policy, the courts will disregard the interpretation offered by the policymaker.â The Supreme Court held that Category E(i) was enabling in nature and that when the language of the policy was unrestrictive, it was not for the court to limit its application through an interpretative process, particularly when the policy concerned grant of pensionary benefits. The bench also observed that the MoD policy letter of 2001 was clear and that when there was no distinction between notifications issued under Category E(i), the benefit of the policy could not be denied. The bench, however, added that âwhile notifying operations as contemplated under Category E(i), the Government must declare in clear terms whether the pensionary benefits contemplated under Para 4.1, Category E(i) of the MoD Policy letter dated 31.01.2001 would be applicable to such notification or not.â You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in Chandigarh Stay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. title: âNot uniqueâ: Iran seeking to expand attacks in UK to military sites, MI5 chief warns after RAF Fairford incident
text: File photo: UK's RAF Fairford base Iran is seeking to expand its attacks in Britain to include military installations, with the suspected plot against the US-run RAF Fairford air base in September being ânot uniqueâ, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said on Tuesday. Speaking in his annual assessment of threats to the UK, the head of Britain's domestic security service said Tehran was increasingly looking beyond its traditional targets, including Iranians opposed to the country's Islamic authorities, to strike more difficult targets such as military sites. âThe RAF Fairford incident ... is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world,â McCallum said, according to Reuters. The comments came as British detectives continued investigating the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran during this year's war. Security alert at RAF Fairford The suspected plot triggered a major security operation on September 27, when scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the air base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts moved into the area. Police later said they had found a quantity of gasoline, described as an accelerant, in three vans at the site. No explosives were found. British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which prompted the US to withdraw its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that the suspected plot was âalmost certainlyâ directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Earlier, he said that Tehran was âhighly likelyâ to have been behind the suspected plot. Seven men in their 20s have been arrested and released on bail under investigation. McCallum said he could not comment on the Fairford incident because the investigation was ongoing. He nevertheless pointed to a broader shift in Iran's activities. âA major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites,â he said. McCallum also referred to arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites in Britain, which the UK has attributed to Iranian proxies. I ran has denied involvement in the suspected Fairford plot, although it has previously said it considers any military base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. MI5 flags Russia's activities and AI threats McCallum also warned about Russia's activities against Britain and its allies, describing Moscow as the leading state aggressor, according to Reuters. He said Russia was escalating its use of hybrid warfare against countries supporting Ukraine, employing tactics that fall short of conventional military conflict. He cited an attempted drone attack on a cargo plane at a German airport and a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure as examples. âIt's no accident that Russian aggressors are trying to unsettle other European homelands at a time when their military progress in Ukraine is minimal and horrifically costly,â McCallum said, according to Reuters. Russia has denied involvement in hostile acts in Britain. The MI5 chief also said state threats had quadrupled over the past decade, leaving the agency devoting more resources to them than during the Cold War. He identified the potential misuse of artificial intelligence as another major security concern, particularly the risk that terrorists could use the technology to develop biological weapons or create new pathogens. McCallum's assessment outlined a range of threats facing Britain as authorities investigate the suspected Iranian plot and monitor hostile activities attributed to foreign states. title: Black Sea in crossfire: Bulgaria says Russia behind drone strikes that sank two ships
text: The two ships hit on Tuesday were the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo vessel Dignity and the Chelsea-3, a Ukrainian-owned ship registered in Odesa and sailing under the Maltese flag. Bulgaria on Wednesday said Russia was likely behind a series of drone attacks on four commercial ships in the Black Sea, which sank two vessels over the past week. However, it admitted it had no proof of Moscowâs involvement. Rescue teams are still searching for 11 crew members missing after Tuesdayâs strikes, while five sailors have been rescued. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told Parliament that the attacks appeared to benefit Russia, as one of the vessels was Ukrainian-owned. The strikes targeted ships in Bulgariaâs exclusive economic zone and nearby waters, raising concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the region. Watch Fresh Black Sea Ship Fire Sparks Alarm As Eight Go Missing Near NATOâs Eastern Flank âThere is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia â and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it,â Radev said. The two ships hit on Tuesday were the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo vessel Dignity and the Chelsea-3, a Ukrainian-owned ship registered in Odesa and sailing under the Maltese flag. The Dignity sank after being hit by a military strike. Four sailors, three Syrian nationals and one Egyptian, were rescued and brought to the port of Varna, district governor Mario Smarkov said. All four were in relatively good condition and had no injuries. A fifth sailor was expected to arrive later on Wednesday. The search for 11 missing crew members from the two vessels is continuing. Five other crew members were rescued following the attacks. Bulgaria seeks NATO support Bulgaria has requested international assistance to investigate the attacks on commercial vessels. It has also sought Nato support to strengthen surveillance, monitoring and response capabilities against drone strikes. Radev said the country was suffering significant economic and financial damage from the incidents. Sofia is also seeking to coordinate with neighbouring Romania and Turkey on measures to protect shipping in the Black Sea. On Tuesday, Radev summoned the Russian ambassador to Sofia over the attacks. The ambassador said she had no information from Russiaâs defence ministry about the incidents but did not rule out the possibility that âthese attacks represent a provocation by a third party.â Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova called for an immediate halt to hostilities in the Black Sea and a moratorium on drone attacks against commercial and civilian infrastructure. âThe unprecedented attacks demonstrate that the war has reached the Black Sea and that the conflict is intensifying,â Yotova said in a television interview on Tuesday. She said she had taken coordinated steps with her Romanian and Turkish counterparts in response to the growing risks in the region. âThe aim is a moratorium on the use of drones over the Black Sea against commercial and civilian infrastructure and to halt hostilities over the sea,â Yotova said. Ukraine blames Russia for attacks Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha blamed Russia for the strikes in a post on X on Tuesday. âRussia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea,â Sybiha wrote. âThe Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength,â he added. Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the alliance would continue working closely with its allies in the Black Sea. He said Nato had strengthened its posture along its eastern flank and would continue monitoring the security situation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also condemned the attacks, saying the Black Sea âhas become another front of escalationâ in Russia's war in Ukraine. European council president Antonio Costa expressed solidarity with Bulgaria and said the growing number of Russian hybrid activities would be discussed at the European Council meeting scheduled for Thursday and Friday in Brussels. Series of attacks raises security concerns Tuesdayâs strikes came a week after drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgariaâs exclusive economic zone. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew of a vessel sailing under the flag of Pulau. A day before the latest attacks, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire after a drone strike in the Black Sea off Romania and later sank. Romanian authorities said two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. In a separate incident, Radev confirmed an attack on Starlink satellite communication antennas near the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Tuesday. title: Russia begins diesel exports after Trump deal amid global oil market concerns
text: Russian diesel reaches global markets after Trump deal, Kremlin says (representative image) Russian diesel has begun reaching global markets following an agreement with US President Donald Trump, the Kremlin said on Thursday, adding that the supplies could help stabilise oil markets but would not be sufficient to fully achieve that goal. "The diesel has started reaching global markets and is expected to have a positive effect on stabilising oil markets, although it will not be enough to fully stabilize them," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, according to Reuters. Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets to help lower fuel prices. Moscow subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from October 10 following the agreement. Russian diesel shipments resume Data from financial information provider LSEG showed on Wednesday that Russia had resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk. According to the shipping data cited by Reuters, a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel was loaded on October 13 and was heading towards Morocco. Trump said on Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to US and global markets. He also said another 500,000 tonnes would be supplied in November, followed by a further 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter". However, the initial volume would amount to less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone. US Energy Information Administration data puts daily consumption in the sector at around 2.94 million barrels. The additional volumes announced by Trump would amount to less than four days of demand for US transport. Trump is seeking to bring down US diesel prices ahead of the country's midterm elections on November 3. Ukraine, European officials criticise deal The agreement has drawn strong criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European officials and some Republican politicians in Trump's own party. Russia, meanwhile, has rejected European criticism of the diesel arrangement as "cynical", arguing that European countries continue to purchase some Russian oil and liquefied natural gas. The deal comes amid tensions over efforts to secure an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Kremlin accuses Kyiv of undermining peace efforts Separately, the Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were running counter to US efforts to initiate peace talks, following a drone attack on a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight. Peskov said Moscow did not believe Kyiv had complied with the energy ceasefire announced by Trump on Sunday. Ukraine had said it paused strikes on Russian oil refineries for three days but resumed them after Russia continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "The Ukrainian regime in Kyiv continues to strike these facilities, thereby, of course, coming into serious contradiction with the peace efforts of the United States and of the American negotiators who are indeed making very vigorous efforts to somehow initiate the peace process. But so far, these vigorous attempts have been thwarted by the unwillingness of the Kyiv regime â and of (President Volodymyr) Zelenskyy personally â to make peace," Peskov said. The news agency Associated Press (AP) reported that the drone strike started a fire at the Ryazan refinery, around 300 kilometres southeast of Moscow. A senior Ukrainian official confirmed that Ukraine had hit the facility, while Russia's Defence Ministry and regional governor reported the attack. Russia had previously said the scope of the energy ceasefire had not been defined. On Wednesday, it said it had struck seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities, according to Reuters. The competing claims over compliance with the ceasefire could not be independently verified. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine between midnight and Thursday morning. Ukraine's Emergency Services said three people were killed and six injured in a Russian drone attack on the central Kirovohrad region, while the Ukrainian Air Force said its air defences had intercepted 536 Russian drones during the overnight assault. title: Asian shares are mixed with tech stocks volatile, and oil falls on Trump's Russian sanctions waiver
text: Asian shares remain mixed Asian shares were mixed Monday as volatility in technology stocks persisted, while U.S. equity futures edged higher ahead of another week of American corporate earnings results. Oil prices fell more than 2% after U.S. President Donald Trumpâs decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia, including on Russian energy. A sell-off of technology shares from Asia to Wall Street recently put downward pressure on stock markets, as investor concerns grow over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom. South Koreaâs benchmark Kospi index was up 1.8% to 5,768.01 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 17% over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy. Samsung Electronics was up 1.2%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix added 0.4%. Japanâs Nikkei 225 lost 0.6% to 64,916.70. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 2.6%, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 2%. âWeâve been arguing for a while that volatility in tech stocks would pick up as the AI bubble continued to inflate: sharp and short-lived sell-offs were common as the âdotcomâ bubble inflated, for example, even as the market ultimately made very large gains on net,â Capital Economics Head of Markets for Asia Pacific Thomas Mathews wrote in a commentary Monday. Hong Kongâs stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.4% higher to 3,730.92, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5% for its economy in the July-September quarter. CXMT, Chinaâs leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7% despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months. Australiaâs S&P/ASX 200 was 0.4% higher at 8,845.70. Taiwanâs Taiex fell 0.6%. Indiaâs Sensex slipped 0.9%. Indonesiaâs benchmark stock index fell over 5% at its peak, to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11% on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its âemerging marketâ status. On Friday, Wall Streetâs benchmark S&P 500 declined 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite sank 2.1%. Investors this week are watching for more big corporate earnings results from the U.S., including Meta, Netflix, General Motors, Tesla and IBM. Strong company earnings have been one factor thatâs been keeping U.S. stocks robust lately. As technology shares face rising uncertainties, experts say government bonds might stand to benefit as investors look for relatively safe assets, though the bond market had also been turbulent over the past few weeks. The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury eased to around 5.07% early Monday, compared with roughly 5.13% Friday. It had hit 5.35% earlier this month at its highest level since 2002, as inflation worries from the Iran war-driven energy shock and growing U.S. government debt pushed yields higher â investors demanded more in return because of the additional risks. title: Middle East conflict may end, but energy crisis will drag on: IEA chief explains
text: IEA's Birol does not expect energy markets to return to pre-war levels in 2027 With oil prices edging towards $120 a barrel and winter adding to concerns over fuel supplies, the global energy crisis could outlast the Iran war itself. International Energy Agency (IEA) executive director Fatih Birol has warned that energy markets are unlikely to return to their pre-war conditions in 2027, urging governments and businesses to put energy security first. Speaking at the Singapore International Energy Week conference on Monday, Birol said that the conflict, which began in late February, had upended expectations of a surplus in the energy market this year. Instead, disruptions to global energy flows have tightened supplies and pushed up oil benchmarks and refined fuel prices. "I am afraid I don't see any credible pathway that the markets will go next year, where we were before this war has started," Birol said. He called on countries and companies to prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, with energy security taking priority while they also consider what comes next. Watch Houthis BOMBARD Saudi Oil Field, Riyadh Airport; Claim Attacks On Riyadh's Mercenaries In Yemen "So therefore, we all need to get prepared, taking the energy security as a number one priority in our government, business world, but without forgetting what is the next chapter for the countries and for companies that are all here today," he said. Oil prices near $120 a barrel add to economic pressure The pressure on oil markets has already been visible in prices. More Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia sent Brent crude futures soaring to $117 a barrel on Friday, their highest level in nearly six months. Prices eased to $115 per barrel on Monday but still remained about 59% above their pre-war level. "Oil prices are flirting with $120 a barrel and the prices for products are even much higher," Birol said. While he declined to predict where oil prices would go next, he warned that costs at these levels were becoming a major burden for several economies. "I can tell you that the current price of oil is, for some countries, for example in Europe, maybe not so high and affordable. But in many parts of the world, having almost $120 oil prices is having a major impact on trade deficits." Winter demand and refinery maintenance threaten fuel supplies Oil is not the only concern. As winter approaches, Birol is also worried about the availability and cost of refined products, particularly diesel, which is used for heating in parts of the West. Demand for diesel typically rises during the colder months, just as several refineries are scheduled to undergo maintenance, adding another pressure point for fuel markets. "I am worried on top of that for refined products because we are entering...winter season. Some parts of the world, where typically diesel demand goes high and several refineries are going through maintenance period." Europe faces a difficult winter Europe, meanwhile, faces a difficult winter on the gas front. Countries have decided to cut imports of Russian gas, while the Iran war has added to the strain by disrupting gas exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. "In Europe, we are facing a tough winter because European countries have decided to cut gas imports from Russia and with the additional problem now rising from the Iran war, namely Qatar and the Emirates not being able to export gas as they were before, will put significant pressure on gas markets." The energy crisis could also give nuclear power a fresh push. Birol expects a "strong comeback" for the sector as countries grapple with the current situation. The IEA's recent survey found that 90 gigawatts of nuclear power capacity was under construction, the highest level in the past four decades, he said. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Russian officer helped Ukraine kill over 300 troops by leaking military secrets: Report
text: Lev Stupnikov served as chief signals officer in Russiaâs 36th Motor Rifle Brigade. Photo credit: X account @ddfmarketing1 A Russian army lieutenant secretly supplied Ukraine with troop positions, military plans and other sensitive information, helping Kyiv kill more than 300 Russian soldiers. Lev Stupnikov, who served as chief signals officer in Russiaâs 36th Motor Rifle Brigade, used his access to military communications and operational details to help Ukrainian forces identify targets and launch deadly strikes against his own unit. Stupnikovâs first major operation came in February 2024, when Russian soldiers and senior officers gathered for a training exercise near the front line in eastern Ukraine. He photographed the troops, estimated their numbers and sent the exact coordinates of the field to his Ukrainian handler. After being warned to leave the area, he moved away as Ukrainian forces launched a barrage of missiles. His phone buzzed. âWere there explosions? Send a photo.â âThereâs just meat,â he answered, according to Wall Street Journal. Stupnikov later counted and informed Ukraine handlers that 68 Russian soldiers had been killed and 60 wounded. Ten of the dead were officers, including Colonel Gusein Musayev, commander of the 36th Motor Rifle Brigade. The strike marked the beginning of a series of attacks aided by Stupnikovâs intelligence. His position as the battalionâs chief signals officer gave him access to troop movements, commandersâ communications, surveillance feeds and battle plans. He passed on radio frequencies, locations of Russian units and details of planned operations, helping Ukrainian forces work out where troops were deployed and when they intended to advance. Stupnikov sabotaged military equipment He also undermined his brigade from within. He disabled cameras monitoring Ukrainian territory and tampered with a battery pack connected to a drone controller, causing it to overheat and malfunction during a mission. His information helped Ukraine launch further attacks. In March 2024, Ukrainian forces killed several Russian officers at a brigade gathering identified by Stupnikov. In May, they struck the basement of a former hotel where two Russian assault units were staying, killing 20 soldiers, including a captain. Other intelligence led to an attack on a brigade command post during a meeting of senior officers. The repeated losses raised suspicions among Russian commanders. Stupnikovâs own commander complained that operations were failing and wondered whether a spy had infiltrated the ranks. Stupnikov feared he would soon be exposed after the danger became clear as he accidentally sent his Ukrainian contact a map screenshot showing the location of his own basement. A subsequent strike hit the building, but he survived. His escape across the front line In July 2024, Stupnikov received instructions from his Ukrainian contacts to leave his weapons behind and reach an agreed location near the village of Mykilske. Guided by a Ukrainian drone, he crossed no-manâs-land, navigating destroyed vehicles, craters and suspected mines. Ukrainian troops tracked his progress through thermal camera footage and waited for him on the other side. When challenged for the agreed password, he replied, âPeanut shop.â He was searched, blindfolded and taken to safety. Before leaving, he handed Ukrainian forces a smartphone containing access codes to several communication channels, allowing them to continue accessing live feeds from Russian drones and surveillance cameras. Stupnikov later joined the Russian Volunteer Corps, a Ukrainian army unit made up of Russians opposed to Vladimir Putinâs rule. He is now fighting against the Russian forces he once served. title: Scientists find twin and triplet embryos inside two eggs laid by one wild Burmese python in Florida, marking a first for snakes
text: Image AI generated Scientists have discovered twin and triplet embryos inside two eggs laid by a single wild Burmese python in southern Florida, marking the first recorded instance of triplet embryos in a snake. The unusual finding emerged from a clutch of 37 eggs laid on 17 May 2024 by a radio-tagged female python in Big Cypress National Preserve. While 32 eggs hatched normally, researchers found two non-viable eggs containing five embryos in total, all of which had died before hatching. According to the study published in Ecology and Evolution titled â First Record of Twin and Triplet Embryos Found in the Clutch of a Wild Burmese Python in Southern Florida â, the discovery raises questions about how multiple embryos develop within a single snake egg and how often such occurrences happen in the wild. What did scientists discover inside the Burmese python eggs The unusual clutch was laid on 17 May 2024 by a female Burmese python measuring 313.7 centimetres in snout-to-vent length. The eggs were deposited within a hardwood hammock in Big Cypress National Preserve, where researchers were already monitoring python reproduction and survival as part of a long-term study. The clutch was monitored in its natural location, allowing scientists to observe the development and eventual hatching of the eggs. On 14 July 2024, researchers removed the female from the clutch before the expected hatching period to install an enclosure designed to prevent hatchlings from escaping. The enclosure consisted of a polyvinyl chloride frame covered with two nested mesh laundry bags. Non-viable eggs were removed during the process, while trail cameras were used to monitor the remaining eggs remotely. Hatching began on 17 July, and researchers collected, weighed and measured the emerging hatchlings over five days; the process completed on 22 July 2024. PC: First Record of Twin and Triplet Embryos Found in the Clutch of a Wild Burmese Python in Southern Florida How were the twin embryos inside Egg A different in their development The first unusual egg, identified as Egg A, contained two female embryos. When researchers examined it on 22 July, they found a two-centimetre slit in its shell, indicating that the hatching process, known as pipping, had begun. Both embryos were attached to the same yolk and had died. Their development, however, was not identical. One embryo had developed more extensive pigmentation but showed significant skeletal and developmental abnormalities, while the other had a more normally developed body and intact organs. The second egg, identified as Egg B, contained three embryos at different developmental stages. Unlike Egg A, this egg remained intact, with no signs that hatching had begun. Two of the embryos were similar in size and weight, while the third was considerably smaller and less developed. The researchers recorded that the smallest embryo weighed just 5.6 grams and had a compressed body, particularly around the head and neck. The sexes of all three embryos could not be determined. All were connected to the same yolk, much of which remained unabsorbed. What is monozygotic twinning, and how does it occur in reptiles The study also examined how multiple embryos might develop inside a single reptile egg. Researchers explained that twinning can occur when one fertilised egg divides into two independent embryos, a process known as monozygotic twinning. Another possibility is dizygotic twinning, in which two separately fertilised eggs, each with its own yolk sac, become enclosed within the same eggshell. Scientists have previously proposed that differences in embryo size and egg dimensions could help distinguish between these processes. In the Burmese python clutch, however, both unusual eggs were similar in size to the other eggs, and all embryos were connected to a single yolk. The two embryos in Egg A also had similar body masses, observations that suggested a possible monozygotic origin. However, the researchers cautioned that physical characteristics alone could not establish how the embryos originated. They noted that yolk sacs may fuse to form a common yolk sac, meaning further genetic testing would be necessary to determine the embryos' origins conclusively. Why are twin and triplet embryos so rare in wild Burmese pythons The researchers noted that multiple-embryo eggs are reported in other reptiles, including lizards, turtles and crocodiles, but documented cases in snakes have been considerably more limited. Earlier reports of snake twins had largely involved captive-bred individuals or wild-caught females that laid eggs in captivity. The first documented Burmese python twins came from a captive-bred clutch in which two eggs each contained a pair of embryos. Neither pair survived to hatch. Before the southern Florida discovery, the scientific literature had not documented triplet embryos in snakes. The researchers also highlighted that the frequency of such eggs in wild Burmese pythons remains unknown. Previous observations of wild python clutches in southern Florida had not identified similar cases. The female involved in the study had also laid a clutch in May 2022 of 19 viable eggs and one non-viable egg, none of which contained multiple embryos. The authors described the occurrence as uncommon based on their observations and stressed that further research is needed to establish how frequently it happens, whether such embryos can survive to hatching and how these unusual reproductive events affect the species' overall reproductive output. Although none of the five embryos in the 2024 clutch survived, the discovery provides a documented example of both twin and triplet development in eggs laid by a wild snake.

title: Queenslandâs Kuridala copper town prospered during World War I, but a 1918 cyclone damaged its smelter before the plant closed in 1920
text: Representative Image of the historic Hampden Smelter and railway, highlighting their role in Kuridalaâs mining prosperity (AI-generated image) Kuridala, about 65â70 km south of Cloncurry in Queensland, grew into an important copper-mining settlement before and during World War I. Its development was closely tied to the Hampden Smelter and a railway connection that helped transport ore from the surrounding mining district. But the townâs prosperity depended on the copper industry, leaving it exposed to changing prices, operational disruptions and financial pressures. Queensland Places records Kuridalaâs population at about 1,500 in 1913 before reporting 774 by 1921. The Queensland Heritage Register gives different figures, recording a population of 2,000 by 1920 and 800 by 1924. How the Hampden Smelter and railway helped build Kuridala Kuridala developed through several name changes. The Queensland Heritage Register records that the settlement was surveyed as Hampden in 1910 and known as Friezland by 1912 before officially becoming Kuridala in October 1916. Queensland Places gives an earlier sequence that begins with Gulatten, followed by Friezland and Kuridala. According to the Heritage Register, the final name was intended to avoid confusion with another Queensland settlement, although anti-German sentiment has also been suggested as a possible factor during the war. Railway development and copper processing were central to the townâs growth. The railway reached Cloncurry in 1908, with an extension serving the Hampden area opening in 1910. The Hampden Smelter began operating in March 1911 and continued until 1920, allowing copper ore from nearby mines to be processed locally. The smelter helped support a substantial settlement, with businesses and public services developing around the mining industry. By 1913, Kuridala had about 1,500 residents, according to Queensland Places. The town had hotels, shops, an ice works, a printery, a hospital, churches and a school. These facilities reflected the needs of a community whose employment and commercial activity were closely connected to mining and smelting. World War I sustained the regionâs prosperity rather than initiating Kuridalaâs growth. The Queensland Heritage Register describes the conflict as bringing four years of prosperity to the Cloncurry district and notes that the period was particularly prosperous for the company operating the smelter. Queensland Places identifies 1918 as a high point for the settlement. It records a daily school attendance of 280 children, while the Heritage Register describes the school as having up to 280 pupils. Why Kuridala declined after World War I Kuridalaâs fortunes changed as the conditions supporting copper production weakened. British wartime price controls ended in 1918, and the Queensland Heritage Register says the change forced the company into difficulties. In December 1918, a cyclone damaged the smelter and its powerhouse. Smelting was postponed until September 1919. The plant processed about 69,598 long tons of ore in 1920, equivalent to approximately 70,715 tonnes, according to the Heritage Register. The smelterâs closure was also connected to financial difficulties. The Heritage Register records that the Commonwealth Bank withdrew funds against copper awaiting export, after which the company halted all operations. Queensland Places also identifies the collapse in copper prices in 1920 as a factor in the townâs decline. Population figures from the period differ between the sources. Queensland Places reports 774 residents by 1921, while the Heritage Register records 2,000 by 1920 and 800 by 1924. As mining and smelting activity contracted, facilities that had supported the settlement were moved elsewhere. The hospital, picture theatre and courthouse were relocated to Mount Isa, while the ice works also followed. The Queensland Heritage Register records that the company ceased to exist in 1928, after offering its assets for sale in 1926 and their subsequent purchase by Mount Elliott. Kuridala today: the heritage significance of the Hampden Smelter The remains of the Hampden Smelter are central to Kuridalaâs historical significance. The Queensland Heritage Register identifies the site as evidence of the copper industry that helped shape the Cloncurry district. Its surviving industrial remains also have research potential for understanding the technology, organisation and operation of early 20th-century copper smelting. Kuridalaâs history records the rise of a mining settlement supported by railway access and industrial investment, followed by the contraction of its principal industry. The surviving smelter remains, and historical records document the townâs place in Queenslandâs copper-mining history. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Economy, not ideology
text: . When populists and autocrats lose, is the vote on political theory or economic reality? Thereâs a view, supported by research, that democracy is in danger. Per Swedenâs V-Dem Institute, the average person has about the same democratic freedoms now as in 1978. So, itâs tempting to read election results from Brazil and Serbia as an endorsement of democracy. In Brazil, voters narrowly denied Flavio Bolsonaro, a candidate with undisguised authoritarian tendencies, and gave Lula another term. In Serbia, they roundly defeated strongman Aleksandar Vucic. The Serbian result has got outsized attention â itâs a country of just 65L people and $112bn GDP â because the winning side is a student protest movement, fronted by academics, doctors, etc. Yet, this may not be the democratic revival many are hoping for. Rather, as Harvard Prof Steven Levitsky pointed out in 2024, such results could chiefly be anti-incumbency. Even Lula in Brazil lost the first round to Bolsonaro, before staging a spirited fightback. The trend has been clear since 2020, when Covid, and economic disruption, led govts to adopt easy-money policies. The resultant inflation worked for billionaires, but left the middle class, and everyone below, worse off. Levitsky noted that citizen distrust and discontent were running high, and in 41 of 55 polls between 2020 and 2024, the incumbent lost: âalmost certainly a product of and part of Covid inflationâ. Were young Serbians, who campaigned against Vucic for two years, fighting for an ideology or their economic future? Weâve seen how Labour won a landslide in UK, only to become unpopular within months. In Germany, Social Democrats arenât in a happy place either. Or look at US, which ousted Trump, a populist, for Biden, only to vote him back four years later. And now, with US midterms scheduled for Nov 3, it looks like Americans will pounce on the chance to clip Trumpâs wings in Congress. Why? Because, far from addressing their cost-of-living crisis, as he promised, heâs worsened their economic pain with the war on Iran. Israel, another test case for democracy, votes today. And while polls donât show Netanyahu winning outright, whoever wins is unlikely to go soft on Palestinians. In fact, young Israelis, first-time voters, donât appear to have much sympathy for Gazans either. What they are weary of is endless war and psychological hardship. And corruption. People everywhere are asking elected leaders, âWhat have you done for us, for our future?â And incumbents are losing because they usually donât have a convincing answer. title: US intelligence confirms image shows China's secret spaceplane in orbit; design resembles X-37B
text: The US Defense Intelligence Agency has unveiled a detailed satellite image showcasing China's experimental reusable spaceplane currently in orbit The US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has confirmed that a satellite image released in a newly declassified report shows China's experimental reusable spaceplane in orbit, offering a clearer view of a spacecraft whose design closely resembles the US Space Force's X-37B. The higher-resolution image, captured by a satellite operated by Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor, was included in the DIA's latest unclassified assessment of security challenges in space, released on October 26. Although a lower-resolution version had circulated publicly since 2024, the spacecraft's identity had not been confirmed at the time. Watch Project 18A: Indiaâs â¹75,000 Crore Plan for Bigger, Deadlier Next-Gen Navy Destroyers The image shows a compact, shuttle-like vehicle with wings, twin vertical tails, an open payload bay and a rear-mounted module with solar panels deployed on either side. Its overall configuration resembles the X-37B, an uncrewed reusable spaceplane operated by the US Space Force, although the Chinese vehicle appears to have longer wings. âA key capability for reusable space activities are spaceplanes like this PRC [Peopleâs Republic of China] Spaceplane captured by Maxar. Spaceplanes can launch into orbit to place objects in space or even test them and return to earth [sic],â reads the caption to the picture in DIAâs report. The exact date and circumstances of the satellite's observation have not been publicly disclosed in the DIA report. However, the image carries a 2024 copyright date, placing it within the period when China's spacecraft was conducting its third orbital mission. China has conducted four spaceplane missions since 2020 China is understood to have conducted four orbital missions using its experimental reusable spaceplane since 2020. The latest mission began on February 7, 2026, and the spacecraft remained in orbit as of the latest available reports. The vehicle's activities have attracted attention because it has reportedly released smaller objects into orbit and carried out operations involving other spacecraft. During its third mission, which lasted from December 14, 2023, to September 6, 2024, the spaceplane was observed releasing multiple smaller objects. Their identities and purposes remain unknown. Analysis of open-source orbital tracking data by astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell also indicated that the spacecraft involved in the latest mission released and subsequently recaptured a smaller object during a series of orbital operations. These activities point to its ability to interact with objects in space, although its precise mission objectives remain undisclosed. The spacecraft is commonly referred to as Shenlong in Western reports, but its official designation and the model shown in the image have not been definitively established. The DIA report states that âChina has two primary spaceplane models: the Shenlong and Tengyun,â without specifying which one appears in the photograph. China's Shenlong programme has been discussed publicly since at least 2007, when images emerged of what was believed to be a prototype or test vehicle mounted beneath an H-6 bomber. Separately, the state-run China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation unveiled its Tengyun reusable spaceplane concept in 2016. The proposed system was designed around a two-stage-to-orbit approach involving a carrier aircraft, rather than relying entirely on a conventional rocket launch. It remains unclear whether the planned Tengyun test targeted for 2025 took place. How China's spaceplane compares with the US X-37B The Chinese vehicle shares several visible design features with the US Space Force's X-37B, including a winged body, payload bay and a configuration intended to support a return to Earth. Both spacecraft are uncrewed and designed for reusable orbital operations. The US has built two X-37B vehicles, which have flown a total of eight orbital missions since 2010. The spacecraft can carry experiments and payloads into orbit before returning to Earth for recovery and refurbishment. Much of its operational activity remains classified. China's spaceplane is also understood to launch aboard a conventional rocket before operating in orbit and returning to Earth for a runway landing. A secretive Chinese airbase in the country's northwest, featuring an exceptionally long runway, has been identified in reporting as a possible landing site for the vehicle, although the full details of its recovery operations remain unclear. The image does not establish whether the Chinese spacecraft carries weapons or is being used for offensive missions. However, its ability to manoeuvre, deploy objects and potentially interact with other spacecraft has raised questions about the military applications of reusable spaceplanes. DIA warns of growing competition in space The DIA's report places reusable spaceplanes within a wider assessment of expanding space capabilities and the potential risks they pose to US and allied assets. In general, âspaceplanes are â¦ reusable and feature enhanced maneuverability, making them more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,â DIAâs report notes. Such vehicles can potentially deploy small satellites, conduct experiments, inspect other spacecraft and return payloads to Earth. Their ability to alter trajectories and approach other objects also makes them useful for missions that conventional satellites may find more difficult to perform. The report also discusses China's development of counterspace capabilities, including ground-based laser weapons that could disrupt, degrade or damage satellites in low Earth orbit. âChina has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,â the DIA said. âBy the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.â The assessment also points to China's testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles, satellite servicing and refuelling technologies, and robotic systems that could potentially interact with spacecraft in orbit. China has expanded its space-based intelligence and surveillance capabilities in recent years, while the United States and Russia are also developing systems that can manoeuvre close to other satellites. Such activities have raised concerns about the potential for interference with, or attacks on, space assets. The DIA report also explains the economic rationale behind reusable technology, noting that conventional space access has relied heavily on expendable launch vehicles and spacecraft. âIn general, access to space traditionally requires expendable spacecraft: single-use launch vehicles, satellites, and one-time use capsules designed to maximize performance. Reliance on expendable vehicles has made access to space expensive and exclusive,â DIAâs report explains. âReusable technologies, while even more difficult and expensive to develop and build, stand to greatly reduce the cost of spaceflight by recovering, refurbishing, and reusing rocket stages, fairings, and capsules. â The newly released image provides a clearer look at China's experimental spaceplane, but its full capabilities, payloads and intended military role remain unknown. Its resemblance to the X-37B, combined with reported orbital manoeuvres and object deployments, underscores the growing role of reusable spacecraft in the increasingly competitive space domain.

title: âWorldâs firstâ: Ukraine claims heavy-lift drone rescued wounded soldier from frontline
text: Ukraine leveraged a heavy-lift hexacopter drone to successfully evacuate a wounded soldier from a perilous frontline area (92nd Assault Brigade) Ukraine has turned a heavy-lift drone into a flying ambulance, lifting a wounded soldier out of a frontline kill zone where mines and Russian drone activity had made a ground evacuation too dangerous. According to Ukraineâs official military news agency ArmyInform, Ukrainian forces have evacuated a wounded soldier from a frontline position using a heavy-lift hexacopter after Russian drone activity Znd mined terrain made a ground evacuation too dangerous. The operation, carried out using a drone supplied by Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence, is being described by Kyiv as the worldâs first such evacuation and highlights how aerial drones could offer a new way to rescue troops from heavily contested battlefields. According to The War Zone (TWZ), the operation involved personnel from Ukraineâs 92nd, 30th and 14th Mechanised Brigades, the 10th Army Corps and Gurzuf Defence. The wounded infantryman belonged to the 30th Mechanised Brigade, while a UAV operator from the same formation piloted the heavy-lift hexacopter. The soldier remained in contact with the operator throughout the extraction. TWZ reported that the aircraft was supplied free of charge by Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence. Military specialists worked with the company to adapt the drone for the mission, with the technical solution designed to keep the aircraft stable and prevent excessive swaying or tipping during flight. The footage shows the soldier securing himself beneath the hexacopter with a harness before being lifted into the air. Unlike a conventional medical evacuation helicopter, the drone carried him suspended beneath its frame, without an enclosed cabin or a protected medical compartment. The military said the soldier was rescued successfully and was undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, with his life no longer in danger. Ukraine has increasingly relied on unmanned ground vehicles to deliver supplies and evacuate casualties from exposed positions. However, mines, mud and cratered terrain can prevent ground robots from reaching wounded troops, while hostile drones and artillery make movement through frontline areas dangerous. An aerial platform offers a potential alternative by bypassing ground obstacles and reaching positions inaccessible to ground vehicles. Why this is a big deal The operation highlights a potential shift in how wounded soldiers could be evacuated from modern battlefields, where drones, landmines and artillery make conventional rescue missions increasingly dangerous. The approach could also expand the role of heavy-lift drones beyond carrying supplies and equipment. If successfully developed for repeated frontline use, these platforms could provide military commanders with another option for recovering injured troops from positions inaccessible to ground vehicles. However, the method has significant limitations. The footage shows the soldier suspended beneath the aircraft, leaving him exposed during flight. The harness-based approach could also prove difficult for unconscious personnel or those too severely injured to secure themselves. The aircraftâs range, endurance and ability to operate reliably under enemy fire remain unclear.

title: 'Politicisation of energy flows harmful': Jaishankar calls for diversified supply chains at G20
text: Jaishankar speaks at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, calling for diversified supply chains and the de-politicisation of energy markets External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday called for reducing political interference in energy markets and diversifying global supply chains, saying disruptions were placing a disproportionate burden on developing countries. Speaking about the message he delivered at G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said the discussions covered geopolitical conflicts, energy and food security, and resilient supply chains. âLook, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications,â ANI quoted him as saying. He added that âthere are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway.â Watch India, Azerbaijan Hit Reset Button, Jaishankar Meets Aliyev After Operation Sindoor Fallout On energy security, Jaishankar warned against disruptions in fuel distribution and their impact on developing economies. âThis distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful,â he said, adding that âthe Global South was bearing the brunt of the energy shortages and that something needs to be done.â He also flagged risks to food security, citing disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea regions. At the meeting's concluding session on supply chains, Jaishankar called for wider diversification of manufacturing and production across countries. âToday we need more diversified supply chains,â he said, advocating âmore globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing.â In a post on X after the session, he said securing supply chains was central to the global economy's well-being and called on the G20 to promote âthe right to industrialiseâ and resist âpredatory practicesâ. âDiversification and de-risking, including in connectivity, is the key to supply chain resilience, threatened by pandemics, conflicts, climate events and mishaps,â he said. title: 'Some still allow political calculations': Jaishankar's veiled swipe days after Rubio backs Pak ties
text: Jaishankar said some countries continued to allow political calculations to take precedence despite lessons of history. NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said that the use of terrorism as an âinstrument of statecraftâ was unacceptable and could never be justified, warning that the threat persisted because some countries did not demonstrate âzero toleranceâ. Speaking at the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan on the occasion of UN Day, Jaishankar said some countries continued to allow political considerations to take precedence despite the lessons of history. âTerrorism is another deadly threat to peace. Its usage as an instrument of statecraft is simply unacceptable. It can never be justified. It can never be rationalised. Yet, it continues because not all states really display zero tolerance,â he said. Watch India, Azerbaijan Hit Reset Button, Jaishankar Meets Aliyev After Operation Sindoor Fallout âDespite history holding so many lessons, some still allow political calculations to take precedence. The world must therefore develop sharper awareness about this common threat, and it must come together with stronger resolve and counter-terrorism in all its forms and manifestations,â he added. Jaishankar did not name any country in his remarks. Earlier this week, US secretary of state Marco Rubio defended Washingtonâs engagement with Pakistan saying the US needed to maintain relations with countries with which it had disagreements. Speaking to Network18, Rubio said Pakistanâs possession of nuclear weapons and its geographical position made engagement necessary. He also argued that maintaining ties could give Washington greater influence over Islamabadâs decisions, including on terrorism. âIn the case of Pakistan, itâs a country that we have to have a relationship with, a country that possesses nuclear weapons. Itâs a country that from a geographic standpoint, we need to be able to interact with them in much the same way as govt of India has to have and has a relationship and meets with leaders from Iran,â Rubio said. â... It could be a positive thing because if... we can speak to them, it perhaps puts us in a position to help discourage the kinds of things India is worried about,â he added. Rubio also urged businesses to view India-US ties as a strategic partnership spanning technology, trade and security. He said the two countries were âperfectly alignedâ on issues shaping the 21st century, while acknowledging that differences would persist. Jaishankar also stressed the importance of peace amid ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, warning that wars in one part of the world can have far-reaching consequences for global security, economies and societies. "We cannot remain helpless spectators. India expresses global sentiment when we urge that dialogue and diplomacy are the only solution," the external affairs minister said. Emphasising the interconnected nature of global peace, he said, "Let us consider the indivisibility of peace. Now, war anywhere threatens peace everywhere." Jaishankar said India was making efforts towards peacebuilding and remained open to working with other partners to advance these efforts. The minister also highlighted the link between peace, economic progress and shared prosperity, warning that unequal development in an interconnected world could fuel further instability. "Progress and prosperity are the flip side of conflict and violence, and they too are equally indivisible. The world cannot advance half prosperous and half denied in an era of intricate supply chains, of globalised markets, and of common resources. This is simply a prescription for continuous instability," he said. His remarks came a day after India condemned a deadly attack on a church in Karak, Jordan, on October 23, which killed seven people and injured 34 others.
