title: Australia eyes Israelâs Iron Dome: Why is Canberra building a missile shield?
text: Israelâs Iron Dome is a short- to medium-range air defence system developed by Israeli defence company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems (Photo: AP). Australia is considering acquiring missile interceptors developed for Israelâs Iron Dome as part of efforts to establish an air defence system, officials told a parliamentary committee on Thursday. Defence officials said Australia aimed to have a ground-based missile defence system in place by the early 2030s, citing lessons from rapidly changing warfare in Ukraine and the Middle East. The options under discussion include the US Patriot missile defence system and interceptor missiles developed by Israeli defence company Rafael Advanced Defence Systems for Iron Dome. The interceptors have recently been used in a new system developed for the US Marine Corps and are jointly manufactured with US company Raytheon, AFP reported. The Iron Dome Israelâs Iron Dome is a short- to medium-range air defence system developed by Israeli defence company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. According to Rafael, the system has recorded more than 10,000 successful interceptions since 2011, with a success rate exceeding 90 per cent. It is designed to intercept a range of aerial threats, including rockets, artillery shells, mortars, cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The company says the system can operate in different weather conditions and respond to multiple incoming threats simultaneously. Watch Project 18A: Indiaâs â¹75,000 Crore Plan for Bigger, Deadlier Next-Gen Navy Destroyers The Iron Dome Iron Dome system is part of a wider family of air defence systems that includes C-Dome, its naval variant, and I-Dome, a mobile configuration. These systems are designed to protect civilian population centres, military forces, maritime assets and strategic infrastructure. According to the company, Iron Domeâs architecture can be integrated with other sensors and command-and-control systems as part of a layered air defence network. Rafael also says the United States Marine Corps selected the system to strengthen its expeditionary air defence capabilities. Truck-mounted, medium-range interceptors were tested by the US Marines in Guam in June during a regional military exercise that Australia also participated in, AFP reported. Australia does not supply weapons to Israel, and potential purchases of Israeli defence equipment have come under political scrutiny. âThe government will always seek to deliver the most suitable military technology,â government minister Murray Watt told the committee when asked about the issue. Air Marshal Robert Chipman said the defence force would make recommendations to the government next year following a competitive selection process linked to the Talisman Sabre military exercise in 2027.

title: Fireworks, flags and celebrations as student-led movement wins in Serbia; can they deliver reforms?
text: In Serbia, can a leaderless student movement, with little experience of governing, turn its electoral victory into lasting political change? Celebrations swept across Serbia after Gen Z-backed candidates defeated president Aleksandar Vucicâs ruling party in a historic election, ending his long grip on power. In Belgrade, crowds filled central squares, cars draped in Serbian flags honked their horns and fireworks lit up the sky as jubilant protesters dismantled barricades around a pro-government encampment near parliament. But beyond the celebrations, a key question remains: Can a leaderless student movement, with little experience of governing, turn its electoral victory into lasting political change? Watch ON CAM: Celebrations & Chaos! Political Earthquake In Serbia As Vucic Loses; Serbia Streets Go Wild The election follows nearly two years of student-led demonstrations sparked by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station in 2024, which killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and cronyism for the disaster, turning the tragedy into a wider campaign for accountability. From street protests to political power Visuals circulating on social media showed crowds taking to the streets of Belgrade and other Serbian cities soon after the election results were announced. The student movement built nationwide support without a single leader and eventually fielded 250 candidates, including academics, lawyers, doctors, farmers, actors and musicians. Its agenda centres on anti-corruption measures, judicial reform and stronger public institutions. The candidates have proposed an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, transparent appointments to state-owned companies and tighter scrutiny of public infrastructure contracts. However, unity could prove difficult once the movement begins governing. â(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia's culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,â Katarina Popovic, a professor at the University of Belgrade told news agency Reuters. âWe just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system,â she added. Can the new government deliver reforms? Under Serbiaâs constitution, the student-backed candidates have 90 days to form a government after parliament is convened following the announcement of final election results. The immediate challenges include passing a year-end budget, addressing rising public and private debt, reforming the police and intelligence services, and strengthening the judiciary. The students' victory "is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movementâs limited governing experience could make the transition challenging," Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday. The IMF projects Serbiaâs economy to grow 3 per cent in 2026 and 4 per cent in 2027, while inflation rose to 4.1 per cent in September from 2.2 per cent in August. The central bank has held its benchmark interest rate at 5.75 per cent since 2024. âThe new government would have to fight its corner,â warned Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior, referring to the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is expected to remain a formidable opposition force. The movement has also promised economic changes, including action against retail monopolies to lower food prices, tax relief for lower-income groups, affordable housing initiatives and cheaper medicines. Kosovo, Russia and the European Union Foreign policy could be another test. The student-backed candidates oppose recognising Kosovoâs independence, declared in 2008, while relations with the European Union remain strained over stalled accession talks and the need to normalise ties with Pristina. The movement has also said it does not intend to impose sanctions on Russia, Serbiaâs traditional ally and a major gas supplier. At the same time, the European Commission has offered support for reforms involving the rule of law and media freedom. âI am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing,â said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement, according to Reuters. title: Noida clears decks to allot 13,000 more abadi plots in urban villages
text: The 2031 master plan envisages acquisition of 15,279 hectares of land Noida: Noida Authority has amended its Master Plan 2031 to resolve pending cases involving the allotment of 5% developed residential plots to farmers. The amendment provides for earmarking these plots on land adjoining existing village abadi areas and is expected to pave the way for allotment to nearly 13,000 farmers who gave up their land for development projects but are yet to receive developed plots that were part of the compensation package. Noida, Greater Noida and Yamuna authorities currently follow a policy of giving farmers 5%, 6% and 7% of developed plots respectively in return for acquired land. Allotment has been planned in several cases, but farmers claim nearly 12,800 beneficiaries are still awaiting developed plots. âSince the master plan 2031 is nearing full implementation, identifying suitable locations for planning and allotting the remaining plots has become difficult. In view of farmersâ demand for an early resolution of these cases, the Authority has decided to amend the master plan to allow 5% abadi plots on land adjoining existing village abadi,â a Noida Authority official said. Officials said the Authority will now invite objections and suggestions from the public before sending the proposal to the state government for approval. Once the amendment is approved, the Authority will acquire suitable land and allot plots to eligible farmers. Over the past decade, Noida has seen multiple protests by farmers seeking 64.7% additional compensation and 10% developed plots. The most recent was held on Oct 7, when farmers under the banner of BKU (Manch) protested outside the Authorityâs Sector 96 office and demanded developed plots in return for land acquired for planned development. The demand stems from the Allahabad High Courtâs Oct 2011 order in the Gajraj versus State of UP case, which directed payment of an additional 64.7% compensation over and above the amount already paid to farmers, besides allotment of developed residential plots equivalent to 10% of the acquired land. So far, Noida Authority has paid enhanced compensation to farmers, but developed plots have not been allotted to many of the affected farmers because of a shortage of land. The 2031 master plan envisages acquisition of 15,279 hectares of land. According to a 2021 CAG audit, the Authority acquired nearly 12,375 hectares in 69 villages between its formation in 1976 and 2020. In Feb 2024, UP govt constituted a three-member high-powered committee to examine the issue. The panel, comprising revenue board chairperson Rajneesh Dube, then Noida district magistrate Manish Kumar and Meerut divisional commissioner Selva Kumari J, examined the farmersâ demands and submitted its report in Aug 2024, which concluded that, based on documentary evidence and its analysis, the demands were not found to be justified or practical, and that it was not possible to form an opinion on some of the issues raised by farmers. The amendment is likely to accelerate construction and push up land values in Hajipur, Salarpur, Bhangel and Sorkha villages that are located close to developed sectors. However, the scale of growth will depend on the identification availability of land and the allotment process. title: War in space? China may deploy orbital lasers to blind US satellites by late 2020s - report
text: A future war could begin by blinding an enemy before the first missile is fired. China may be preparing to take that fight into space, with weapons capable of threatening the satellites that guide precision strikes, track enemy forces and keep modern militaries connected. According to a new report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), China could field space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s, potentially expanding its ability to disrupt, damage or disable adversary satellites. The assessment warns that Beijing is also developing more powerful ground-based systems capable of threatening satellites operating in higher orbits, raising concerns over the vulnerability of US military assets in space. Watch Project 18A: Indiaâs â¹75,000 Crore Plan for Bigger, Deadlier Next-Gen Navy Destroyers The DIAâs report, Challenges to Security in Space, released on October 26, warns that China is expanding its counterspace arsenal, combining directed-energy weapons with anti-satellite missiles, electronic warfare and manoeuvrable spacecraft. The report identifies the late 2020s as a potential timeline for China to field space-based directed-energy systems, although it does not confirm that such weapons are already operational in orbit. Directed-energy weapons are systems that use concentrated energy, such as high-powered lasers or high-power microwaves, to disrupt, disable or damage a target without firing conventional ammunition. In space warfare, these weapons could be used to temporarily blind a satelliteâs optical sensors, interfere with its electronic systems or cause permanent damage to sensitive components. Unlike conventional anti-satellite missiles, which physically collide with and destroy their targets, directed-energy weapons can potentially affect satellites without creating large amounts of space debris. Their effectiveness, however, depends on factors such as the weaponâs power, distance from the target, targeting accuracy and the satelliteâs vulnerability. The DIA said the Peopleâs Liberation Army (PLA) considers directed-energy weapons particularly useful because they can produce both reversible and irreversible effects against satellites. Reversible attacks could include jamming satellite signals or temporarily blinding optical sensors, while more powerful systems could permanently damage sensitive components. âChina and Russia will continue to pursue new and improved counterspace capabilities to exploit a perceived US and allied reliance on space-based assets,â the report concluded. Why satellites are critical in modern warfare Satellites have become a backbone of modern military operations, enabling armed forces to communicate across vast distances, track enemy movements, guide precision strikes and detect incoming missile threats. Their disruption could weaken a militaryâs ability to gather intelligence, coordinate forces and respond rapidly to changing battlefield conditions. Satellite-based navigation systems, such as GPS, provide positioning, navigation and timing data used by military aircraft, naval vessels, ground forces and precision-guided weapons. Surveillance satellites help identify troop concentrations, monitor naval movements and assess enemy deployments, while secure satellite communications allow commanders to exchange information with forces operating across different theatres. Satellites also play a critical role in missile warning, with specialised sensors detecting heat signatures associated with missile launches and transmitting alerts to defence networks. Losing access to these capabilities could delay threat detection and complicate military responses. For the United States, which relies heavily on space-based infrastructure to support global military operations, the threat is particularly significant. In a potential conflict over Taiwan or elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, China's ability to disrupt satellite services could complicate US force coordination and targeting.
